The Buddha said: the countless Buddhas of the eight directions, above and below, each in turn sent bodhisattvas who flew to where the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity was to hear the scriptures and make offerings, each yielding place to the other in turn. And so likewise below: in the countless Buddha-lands of the eight directions below, each direction again like the flowing sands of the Ganges — one grain of sand, one Buddha, and their number again was such as this — each of those Buddhas sent forth countless bodhisattvas, past all reckoning, who all flew to where the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity was, came forward and bowed in homage to Amitābha Buddha, touched their heads and faces to the Buddha's feet, stepped back, and sat listening to the scriptures; and when they had heard the scriptures through, all the bodhisattvas were greatly joyful, and rose and bowed in homage to the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity and departed. The Buddhas above again in turn sent bodhisattvas who flew to where the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity was to hear the scriptures and make offerings, yielding place to one another: those who came before departed to make way for those who came after, and those who came after made offerings in the same way, with no end or ceasing at any time:
It is like the lands as many as the sands of the Ganges; thus are the Buddha-lands of the East.
Each and every one sends bodhisattvas, who bow their heads to the Buddha of Immeasurable Awakening.
West, south, north and the four faces are all the same, lands as numerous as Ganges sands.
All these Buddhas send their bodhisattvas, who bow their heads to the Buddha of Immeasurable Awakening.
These bodhisattvas of the ten directions fly, all with garments
composed of
a
sleeve
less
yoke
plus
precept ] as their flowers.
With heavenly silk and every kind of offering, they go to honor the Buddha of Immeasurable Awakening.
All the bodhisattvas gather in great assembly, bowing their heads to the Light Without Boundary.
Three times they circle, then stand with palms joined, praising the Land's Honored One, the Buddha of Immeasurable Awakening.
All hold flowers and scatter them upon the Buddha, hearts pure, extolling the Immeasurable One.
Before the Buddha they stand and speak for themselves: may my land be even as this one.
The flowers they scatter rest in the empty sky, joined into a canopy a hundred yojanas wide.
Its stem is wondrous, adorned and well arrayed, covering all the assembled host.
All the bodhisattvas go and arrive there; such honored lands are hard to meet.
If a person such as this hears the Buddha's name, at peace and secure, he gains great benefit.
We of this kind attain such virtue; all these lands obtain what they hold dear.
When I reckon my own land, it is like a dream; for countless kalpas I will purify this soil.
I see bodhisattvas circling the World-Honored One, majestic in spirit, mighty, with life without end.
The Buddha's assembly in that land is wholly pure, inconceivable through countless kalpas.
Then the Buddha of Immeasurable Life smiled, and thirty-six billion nayutas
of rays of light came forth from his mouth, shining throughout countless lands.
Then the light returned and circled the Buddha; three times round, and it entered from his crown.
Its color suddenly was seen no more; both devas and humans were filled with joy.
Maudgalyayana rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, and bowed his head in inquiry.
He said to the Buddha: For what cause do you smile? We beg the World-Honored One to speak its meaning.
Grant me the prediction of my own true nature; in compassion bring me to the hundred marks of merit.
All who hear these sounds leap up with joy, every one of them.
The voice of Brahma and the voice of thunder, the eight-toned voice, deep and weighty.
The Buddha granted Maudgalyayana the prediction, saying: now I will speak to you; listen with care.
Bodhisattvas from all the worlds come to bow in homage at Sukhavati, the Land of Bliss.
Hearing with joy, they practice it widely, and swiftly attain the pure abode.
Having arrived in this adorned and pure land, they at once gain the full divine feet.
Their eyes see through all, their ears hear all things; and they also gain knowledge of past lives.
The Buddha of Immeasurable Awakening grants them their prediction: in a former life I had my primal vow.
All who hear the Dharma taught will swiftly be reborn in my land.
All that I vowed is now fulfilled; those who come to be born from the countless lands
all arrive here without exception, and in one life attain non-retrogression.
If a bodhisattva should raise a further vow, wishing to make his land like mine,
let him also think to save all beings, causing each vow to reach the ten directions.
Swiftly and speedily he may pass beyond and arrive at the world of the Land of Peace and Bliss.
Arriving at the land of immeasurable light, he makes offerings to countless Buddhas.
Serving a hundred million Buddhas, he flies and transforms throughout all lands.
Reverent and joyful, he departs, and returns again to Sukhavati.
No one without such merit can hear the name of this sutra.
Only those of pure precepts can come to hear this true Dharma.
Those who have seen the Hero, the World-Honored One, in former lives come to believe in this matter.
Humble and reverent, hearing and practicing it, they leap up with great joy.
The evil, the arrogant, the lazy, the slothful — these find it hard to believe in this Dharma.
Those who saw the Buddha in former lives take joy in hearing the World-Honored One's teaching.
It is like one born blind in the dark who wishes to lead and guide others on the way.
The hearers, and even the Great Vehicle — how much less the common and ordinary folk.
The Heaven of Heavens knows their minds; the hearers do not comprehend the Buddha's course.
The pratyekabuddhas likewise; only the Perfectly Awakened One knows this.
Though all were made Buddhas, their pure wisdom and wisdom-in-emptiness
would pass beyond this by a hundred million kalpas; the Buddha's wisdom none can reach.
Let them expound and discuss for countless kalpas, to the end of life they still would not know it.
The Buddha's wisdom has no boundary; by such practice purity is attained.
Only one who receives my teaching believes this; only such a person can understand it clearly.
He who can receive all that the Buddha has spoken — that is the first proof.
A human life is hard to obtain; a Buddha's presence in the world is very hard to meet.
Faith and wisdom cannot be forced; if one hears and sees, let him strive with diligence.
Hearing this Dharma and not forgetting it, one is honored and wins great rejoicing.
Such a one is near and dear to my goodness; for this reason he brings forth the resolve for the path.
Though the whole world were filled with fire, one should pass through it to hear this Dharma.
He shall become a guide, a World-Honored One, and ferry all across birth, old age, and death.

The Buddha said to Ānanda: “When the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity had finished preaching the scriptures for all the bodhisattvas and arhats, among the devas and humans there were those who had not yet attained the path of the stream-enterer, and they attained the path of the stream-enterer. Among them were those who had not yet attained the path of the once-returner, and they attained the path of the once-returner. Among them were those who had not yet attained the path of the non-returner, and they attained the path of the non-returner. Among them were those who had not yet attained the path of the arhat, and they attained the path of the arhat. Among them were those who had not yet attained the stage of the non-retrogressing bodhisattva, and they attained the stage of the non-retrogressing bodhisattva.

Amitābha Buddha, following each one's own past lives and the vows his heart cherished when he sought the path, great or small as each wished, preached the scriptures to him and at once granted him the prediction, causing him swiftly to open and understand and attain the path. All were bright in wisdom, each delighting in what he loved. Whatever scripture or path they wished for, there was none who did not take joy in it and recite and practice it; each recited the scriptures and the path from memory, fluent and never wearying, without end or limit. Among the bodhisattvas and arhats there are those who recite the scriptures, and their voices are like thunder. Among them are those who expound the scriptures, like a swift wind and violent rain. Then the bodhisattvas and arhats, expounding the scriptures and practicing the path, were each and every one like this. Through a whole kalpa to its end there was never a time of idleness or fatigue; all were wise and valiant, their bodies all light, and in the end they had no pain or itch. At all times, walking, standing, sitting, or rising, they were vigorous and valiant. Like the king among lions: in the deep forest, when he has somewhere to go, in that hour none dares stand against him. In the land of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity, the bodhisattvas and arhats, expounding the scriptures and practicing the path, are all valiant, with no thought of doubt or difficulty. What they do in their minds is done without forethought, a hundred thousand million times over. This is the mighty king among lions. Such a mighty king among lions, a hundred thousand million times over, is still not equal to my second disciple Maudgalyayana in valor, by a hundred thousand million times. In the land of Immeasurable Purity, the bodhisattvas and arhats all surpass my second disciple Maudgalyayana.

The Buddha said: “Maudgalyayana in his valor is without peer among all the arhats in all Buddha-lands. Maudgalyayana's flight and progress, his wisdom and valor, his penetrating sight and hearing, his knowledge of the events of the eight directions, above and below, past, future, and present — a hundred thousand million times over, all gathered into one, that wisdom and valor, when set among the arhats in the land of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity, its virtue is still not equal to that of a single arhat in the land of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity in wisdom and valor — by a thousand million times.”

At that time there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Ajita. Ajita the bodhisattva rose, came forward, knelt long with palms joined, and asked the Buddha: “In the land of Amitābha Buddha: “among the arhats: “are there indeed any who have passed into parinirvāṇa? I wish to hear of it.”
The Buddha told Ajita the bodhisattva: “If you wish to know, are there as many stars as this in the four continents? Do you see them?”
Ajita the bodhisattva said: “Yes, indeed; I see them all.”

The Buddha said: “My second disciple, Maudgalyayana, flying over the four continents, in one day and one night counted all the stars and knew how many there were. As many as the stars of the four continents, so very many, past all reckoning — still that is a hundred thousand million times over but a few of the arhats in that land.”
The Buddha said: “Suppose from the great ocean of the world one drop of water were taken away: could that make the ocean water less?”
Ajita the bodhisattva said: “Take from the great ocean a hundred thousand million billion bushels and stones of water, and still it cannot make the sea less.”

The Buddha said: “In the land of Amitābha Buddha, among all the arhats, though there be those who pass into parinirvāṇa, it is like taking one small drop from that great ocean — it cannot make the arhats who remain any less, so as to be known as fewer.”
The Buddha said: “Take one stream of water from the great ocean: could it make the sea water less?”
Ajita the bodhisattva said: “Take from the great ocean a hundred thousand million billion streams of water, and still it cannot make the sea water less, so as to be known as diminished.”

The Buddha said: “In the land of Amitābha Buddha, among all the arhats, though there be those who pass into parinirvāṇa, it is like taking one stream from that great ocean — it cannot make the arhats who remain less, so as to be known as fewer.”
The Buddha said: “Take one Ganges River from the great ocean: could it make the sea water less?”
Ajita the bodhisattva said: “Take from the great ocean a hundred thousand million billion Ganges Rivers, and still it cannot make the sea water less, so as to be known as diminished.”

The Buddha said: “In the land of Amitābha Buddha, the arhats who have passed into parinirvāṇa are countless; and those who remain, newly attaining arhatship, are also countless — there is no increase or decrease at all.”
The Buddha said: “Suppose all the waters of the world flowed together into the great ocean: could that make the sea water increase?”
Ajita the bodhisattva said: “It cannot make the sea water increase. And why? Because the great ocean is the king among all the good waters of the world; that is why it is so.”

The Buddha said: “The land of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity is likewise. Though all the countless Buddha-lands of the eight directions, above and below, and all their countless devas and humans, and the winged and crawling creatures, were all to be reborn in the land of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity, their number would be very great and many, past all reckoning. Yet the bodhisattvas and arhats and the assembly of monks in the land of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity remain as always, one and the same Dharma, no different, without increase. And why? Because the land of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity is the most joyful; among the countless Buddha-lands of the eight directions, above and below, it is the king among all bodhisattvas. The land of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity is the heroic land among all countless Buddha-lands. The land of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity is the treasure among all countless Buddha-lands. The land of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity is the most enduring among all countless Buddha-lands. The land of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity is the most outstanding among all countless Buddha-lands. The land of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity is the most vast among all countless Buddha-lands. The land of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity is the most wholly natural and unconditioned among all countless Buddha-lands. The land of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity is the most joyful, bright, fair, and blissful, without limit. Why is the land of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity alone supreme? Because when he was a bodhisattva seeking the path, his vows were valiant, his diligence never slackened, and his accumulated virtue brought it about; that is why it is so.”

Ajita the bodhisattva was greatly joyful; he knelt long with palms joined and said: “The Buddha speaks of the land of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity: the arhats who have passed into parinirvāṇa are very many; the excellence and goodness of that countless land is beyond measure, bright and fair, most lovely, without peer — and is it alone so?”

The Buddha said: “The bodhisattvas and arhats of the land of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity dwell in seven-treasure houses; some dwell in the empty sky, some dwell on the ground. Among them are those who wish to make their house the highest, and the house is then high. Among them are those who wish to make their house the largest, and the house is then large. Among them are those who wish to make their house stand in the empty sky, and the house then stands in the empty sky — all naturally, according to their will, whatever they do. Among them are some who cannot make their houses do as they wish. And why? Those who can are all those who in former lives, when they sought the path, were compassionate of heart, diligent, and gave themselves to every good; the weight of their virtue brought it about. Those who cannot are all those who in former lives, when they sought the path, were not compassionate of heart nor diligent, did few good deeds and had little virtue; each naturally obtains accordingly. The clothing, bedding, food, and drink they receive are all naturally equal; it is for this reason that they are not the same. Virtue differs in greatness and smallness, and so the valiant are made known and seen by the assembly.”
The Buddha told Ajita the bodhisattva: “Do you see the dwelling place of the king of the Sixth Heaven?”
Ajita the bodhisattva said: “Yes, indeed; I see it all.”

The Buddha said: “The lecture halls and houses of the land of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity surpass the dwelling place of the king of the Sixth Heaven a hundred thousand million times over. In the land of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity, all the bodhisattvas and arhats have penetrating sight and hearing, and all see and know the events of the eight directions, above and below, past, future, and present. They also know all the countless devas and humans above and below in the heavens and the world, and the winged and crawling creatures; they know all the good and evil thoughts of their minds. What their mouths wish to say, they all know in what year and in what kalpa they will gain deliverance, attain the human path, be reborn in the land of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity, and be known to practice the bodhisattva path and attain the path of the arhat — all this they know beforehand. In the land of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity, the bodhisattvas and arhats all have light from the crowns of their heads, and each has its own radiance, great or small.

Among those bodhisattvas there are two most honored, who always sit beside the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity, one on either side, seated in attendance and discussing the teachings. The Buddha of Immeasurable Purity always sits face to face with these two bodhisattvas, deliberating the events of the eight directions, above and below, past, future, and present. Whenever the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity wishes to send these two bodhisattvas to the countless Buddha-lands of the eight directions, above and below, the two bodhisattvas at once fly there, arriving wherever their hearts wish, at whatever Buddha's land in whatever direction. These two bodhisattvas fly together, and their flight is as swift as the Buddha's, their valor without peer. One bodhisattva is named “Maudgalyayana,” and the other is named “Mahāsthāmaprāpta, foremost in the light of wisdom.” The light from the crowns of these two bodhisattvas blazes upon other regions, and a thousand Sumeru-mountain Buddha-lands are always in great brightness. The light from the crowns of all those bodhisattvas each shines for a thousand million myriad li. The light from the crowns of the arhats each shines for seven zhang.”

The Buddha said: “If among the people of the world, good men and good women, there is anyone in urgent fear or terror, or caught up in the affairs of the magistrate, let him simply take refuge in this bodhisattva Maudgalyayana. There is nothing from which he will not be freed.”

blocks.text: The Sutra of the Buddha's Immeasurable Purity and Equal Enlightenment, Scroll Three

inline.s: The Buddha told Ajita the bodhisattva: “The light from the crown of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity is a light of utmost brightness. The sun, moon, stars, and planets all abide in the empty sky and no longer turn or move in their courses, and they have no bright radiance; their light is all obscured and no longer appears. The light of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity shines throughout that land, and its blaze illumines other Buddha-lands, always in great brightness; there is never a time of darkness. In that land there is no first day or second day; no fifteenth day or month; no fifth month or tenth month; no five years or ten years; no hundred years or thousand years; no ten thousand years, hundred million years, hundred million ten-thousand years, or ten billion ten-thousand years; no hundred thousand million ten-thousand years; no thousand million million ten-thousand years; no one kalpa or ten kalpas; no hundred kalpas or thousand kalpas; no ten thousand kalpas or a hundred thousand kalpas; no ten million kalpas; no hundred thousand million ten-thousand kalpas.”

The Buddha said: “The light of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity is a light without limit. The light of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity: after countless kalpas, and again countless kalpas upon countless kalpas, and countless kalpas past all reckoning of kalpas — the kalpas are countless, and there is never a time of darkness. The land of Immeasurable Purity and all its heavens never have a time of decay. And why? Because the life of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity is exceedingly long and the land is most excellent; that is why it is so.”

The Buddha said: “The honored life of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity: after kalpas beyond number, kalpas that are ever countless, he has no time of parinirvāṇa. The Buddha of Immeasurable Purity, teaching in the world, wishes to deliver all the devas and humans and the winged and crawling creatures of the countless Buddha-lands of the eight directions, above and below, and wishes to bring them all to be reborn in his land and all to attain the path of nirvāṇa. All those who practice as bodhisattvas he wishes to make Buddhas, every one. And when they have become Buddhas, he causes them all in turn to teach again the devas and humans and the winged and crawling creatures of the eight directions, above and below, and again wishes them all to become Buddhas. And when they become Buddhas, they again teach countless devas and humans and crawling creatures, causing them all to attain the path of nirvāṇa. All those whom he teaches as disciples, in turn teach one another and in turn deliver one another, until they attain the paths of the stream-enterer, the once-returner, the non-returner, the arhat, and the pratyekabuddha. Turning and delivering one another, they all attain the path of nirvāṇa, all in this way.

The Buddha of Immeasurable Purity has never yet wished to pass into parinirvāṇa. The deliverance wrought by the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity, turning thus, abides again for countless kalpas — countless kalpas, past all reckoning of kalpas, and never a time of parinirvāṇa. The countless devas and humans and the winged and crawling creatures of the eight directions, above and below, who are born in the land of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity cannot be counted. Those who become arhats and attain the path of nirvāṇa are also countless, past all reckoning.

The grace and virtue of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity, and all that he gives, extend through the eight directions, above and below, without end or limit, most deep and greatly immeasurable; the excellence and goodness of it cannot be spoken. The scriptures and the path brought forth by the wisdom and teaching of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity are proclaimed throughout the eight directions, above and below — countless, in the heavens and the world below, very many beyond numbering. The number of those scriptures is very great, past all reckoning, wholly without limit.”
The Buddha told Ajita the bodhisattva: “Do you wish to know whether the life of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity is without limit?”
Ajita the bodhisattva said: “I wish indeed to hear and know it.”

The Buddha said: “Listen clearly. Suppose that all the devas and humans in the countless Buddha-lands throughout the eight directions, above and below, and the winged and crawling creatures as well, were all brought to the human path and all made into pratyekabuddhas and arhats, sitting together in single-minded meditation, and that the whole of their wisdom were gathered into one heroic might, and that together they wished to calculate and know the length of Amitābha's life — to know how many thousands, myriads, and billions of kalpas it spans. None of them could calculate or know the utmost length of Amitābha's life.”

The Buddha said: “Suppose again that all the devas and humans, and the winged and crawling creatures, in the Buddha-lands of a thousand Mount Sumerus in each of the other directions, all likewise attained the human path and were all made into pratyekabuddhas and arhats, all sitting in single-minded meditation, and that their wisdom were joined together into one heroic might, and that together they wished to count the bodhisattvas and arhats in Amitābha's Buddha-land — how many thousands of myriads and billions there are. None of them could count them either.”

The Buddha said: “Amitābha's lifespan is exceedingly long and vast; vast is its radiance, supremely deep its goodness, without limit and without bottom. Who could believe and know it? The Buddha alone knows it.”

When Bodhisattva Ajita heard the Buddha's words, he was greatly delighted; kneeling long, pressing his palms together, he said: “The Buddha has said that Amitābha's lifespan is exceedingly long, and that his awesome spiritual power, great wisdom, and radiance are lofty and excellent — that it is thus, and none besides?”

The Buddha said: “When Amitābha at last enters parinirvāṇa, Bodhisattva Lokeśvararāja will then become a Buddha, presiding over the wisdom of the Way and the teaching of the Dharma. All the devas and humans and the winged and crawling creatures in the world, in the eight directions, above and below, whom he brings across, he will cause all to attain the way of the Buddha's nirvāṇa. His goodness and merit will be again like those of the Great Master Amitābha: he will abide for countless kalpas, countless kalpas, kalpas beyond all reckoning. Kalpas beyond all reckoning. In accordance with the Great Master's Dharma, he will then pass into parinirvāṇa. Next, Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta will likewise become a Buddha, presiding over wisdom and teaching the Dharma to all. The merit of those he brings across will again be like that of the Great Master Amitābha. He will abide for countless kalpas and will never enter parinirvāṇa. Handed on from one to the next, they receive the scripture and the Way in utmost clarity. The land is supremely good; its Dharma is thus, and never is it cut off, nor can it ever be exhausted.”

Ānanda, kneeling long with palms pressed together, asked the Buddha: “The Buddha has said that in Amitābha's Buddha-land there is no Mount Sumeru. On what then do the first heaven of the Four Heavenly Kings and the second heaven of Trāyastriṃśa depend and dwell? I wish to hear it.”

The Buddha told Ānanda: “Do you harbor doubt concerning the Buddha? The eight directions, above and below, are boundless and limitless, without edge or measure. If a single man were to measure out all the ocean waters beneath the heavens, he might yet drain them to the bottom; the Buddha's wisdom is likewise thus. The eight directions, above and below, are boundless and limitless, without edge or measure.”

The Buddha said: “What I know and see by wisdom: all the Buddhas of the past who bear my name, Śākyamuni Buddha — they are as the flowing sands beside the Ganges, one grain of sand, one Buddha. And those who have but now begun to come, wishing to seek Buddhahood, who bear my name, Śākyamuni Buddha — they too are as the flowing sands beside the Ganges, one grain of sand, one Buddha. The Buddha sits facing due south and sees the present Buddhas of the south who bear my name, Śākyamuni Buddha — again as the flowing sands beside the Ganges, one grain of sand, one Buddha. The Buddhas of the past, future, and present in the eight directions, above and below, who bear my name, Śākyamuni Buddha, are each as the flowing sands beside ten Ganges, one grain of sand, one Buddha. Their number is thus, and the Buddha foresees and knows them all.”

The Buddha said: “In ages past, since countless kalpas ago — one kalpa, ten kalpas, a hundred kalpas, a thousand kalpas, ten thousand kalpas, a hundred million kalpas, a trillion kalpas, ten trillion kalpas — there have been Buddhas in those kalpas. Of the Buddhas of the past: one Buddha, ten Buddhas, a hundred Buddhas, a thousand Buddhas, ten thousand Buddhas, a hundred million Buddhas; and among those hundred million Buddhas there have been Buddhas, each with his own name and title, names of different kinds, and none that bore my name. And in the kalpas that have but now begun to come, the Buddhas yet to come: in one kalpa, ten kalpas, a hundred kalpas, a thousand kalpas, ten thousand kalpas, a hundred million kalpas, a trillion kalpas, ten trillion kalpas, there is one Buddha, ten Buddhas, a hundred Buddhas, a thousand Buddhas, ten thousand Buddhas, a trillion Buddhas, and among those ten trillion Buddhas there are Buddhas, each with his own name, names all different, not the same as the names of those other Buddhas; and only once in a long while is there one Buddha who bears my name, Śākyamuni Buddha. And in the countless Buddha-lands of the eight directions, above and below, the present Buddhas, and then those of other directions and other Buddha-lands: in one Buddha-land, ten Buddha-lands, a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, a hundred million, a trillion, ten trillion Buddha-lands, in those Buddha-lands there are Buddhas, each with his own name, names all different and manifold, and none the same; and none bears my name. Among the countless Buddhas of the eight directions, above and below, only now and then is there one who bears my name, Śākyamuni Buddha. Throughout the eight directions, above and below, in past, future, and present, the interval between them is utterly empty and far, far away, boundless and limitless; yet the Buddha's wisdom reaches through it all, exceedingly clear. He gathers the ancient and knows the present; he knows the beginningless past and beholds what is not yet; he foreknows the limitless, beyond all reckoning. However countless the Buddhas, and however great their awesome spirit and honored radiance, he knows them all. The Buddha's wisdom, virtue, and the Way are joined in clarity, and there is none who can question the Buddha about the scripture and the Way to its utmost end. The Buddha's wisdom can never be measured out and exhausted.”

When Ānanda heard the Buddha's words, he was seized with great dread and the hairs of his body stood on end. Ānanda said to the Buddha: “I dare not harbor doubt concerning the Buddha. The reason I asked the Buddha is this: in the Buddha-lands of other directions there is in every case a Mount Sumeru, and the first heaven of the Four Heavenly Kings and the second heaven of Trāyastriṃśa all depend on it and dwell there. I feared that after the Buddha enters parinirvāṇa, should there be devas or humans, or monks, nuns, laymen, or laywomen, who come and ask me, ‘Why is it that in Amitābha's Buddha-land alone there is no Mount Sumeru? On what do the first heaven of the Four Heavenly Kings and the second heaven of Trāyastriṃśa depend and dwell?’ — how should we answer them? If I did not ask the Buddha now, after the Buddha has gone, what words should I use to answer and reply to them? The Buddha alone knows this; no one else can explain it. For this reason I asked the Buddha.”
The Buddha said to Ānanda: “What you say is so. On what do the third Yāma heaven, the fourth Tuṣita heaven, and up to the seventh Brahma heaven depend and dwell?”
Ānanda said: “All those heavens dwell naturally in empty space; they have nothing on which they depend.”

The Buddha said: “That Amitābha's Buddha-land has no Mount Sumeru is likewise so. The first heaven of the Four Heavenly Kings and the second heaven of Trāyastriṃśa dwell naturally in empty space; they have nothing on which they depend.”

The Buddha said: “The Buddha's awesome spirit is most weighty: he acts freely as he wishes. When his mind wishes to do something, he does not plan it beforehand. These heavens all dwell naturally and always in empty space — how much more so the Buddha, whose awesome spirit is honored and weighty, acting freely as he wishes to act?”

When Ānanda heard the Buddha's words, he was greatly delighted; kneeling long with palms pressed together, he said: “The Buddha's wisdom knows the affairs of the eight directions, above and below, past, future, and present — boundless and limitless, without edge or measure, most lofty, great, and wondrous, transcending all; excellent and good, supremely bright and fair, beyond all comparison; his awesome spirit and honored weight cannot be withstood!”

The Buddha told Bodhisattva Ajita: “Among the people of the world, good men and good women who wish to be born in Amitābha's Buddha-land are of three grades; the merit they cultivate differs in greatness, so that one grade does not reach to another.”

The Buddha said: “What are the three grades? The highest, the first grade: one should leave home and forsake wife and children, cut off desire, and live as a monk, entering the way of non-action. One should walk the bodhisattva path; and for one who lives as a monk, keeping and practicing the scripture of the six pāramitās, the scripture and the precepts must not be broken. With a kind mind one should strive diligently and should not give way to anger; one should not have dealings with women. Pure in the fasts and precepts and pure in mind, without greed or longing, with utmost sincerity one vows and wishes to be born in Amitābha's Buddha-land, and should hold that thought with all one's heart, never letting it cease. Such a person, even while seeking the Way in this present life, will of himself, in his sleep, dream of Amitābha and of the bodhisattvas and arhats. When his life is about to end, Amitābha, together with the bodhisattvas and arhats, will fly forth to welcome him, and he will be born in Amitābha's Buddha-land. There, in a seven-jeweled pond, he will be born by transformation within a lotus, and will naturally receive a body that grows tall; he will become an avaivartika bodhisattva. Then, with all the bodhisattvas, and in their turn and company, he will fly about, making offerings to the countless Buddhas of the eight directions, above and below; his wisdom will be brave and keen, he will delight to hear the scripture and the Way, and his mind will be joyful. The seven-jeweled dwelling in which he lives will be in empty space, and he will act freely as his mind wishes, dwelling near to Amitābha.”

The Buddha said: “Those who wish to be born in Amitābha's Buddha-land, who strive diligently and uphold the scripture and the precepts, and who practice and carry out the supreme Dharma as set out above — when they are born in Amitābha's Buddha-land, they may be honored by the multitude. This is the highest, the first grade.”

The Buddha said: “Those of the middle grade: if a person wishes to be born in Amitābha's Buddha-land but cannot leave home and forsake wife and children, cut off desire, and live as a monk, he should uphold the scripture and the precepts and not let them be broken. He should further practice giving and generosity, always believe and receive the Buddha's words with deep sincerity and utter faithfulness, feed monks, and build Buddha-halls and raise stūpas. Burning incense, scattering flowers, lighting lamps, and hanging banners of varied silks — in such practices he should have no greedy attachment. He should not give way to anger; pure in the precepts and pure in mind, with a kind heart he should strive diligently, cutting off the thoughts of desire, wishing to be born in Amitābha's Buddha-land. If for one day and one night he does not let this thought cease, then such a person, in this present life too, will in his sleep and dreams see Amitābha. When his life is about to end, Amitābha will by transformation cause him to see Amitābha and that land for himself; and being born in Amitābha's Buddha-land, he may attain wisdom and courage.”

The Buddha said: “Suppose that a person practices giving in this way, and afterwards should regret it in the midst of it, his heart in doubt: he does not believe that giving and generosity and doing good works will bring him blessing in later lives; he does not believe that there is a Buddha-land of Immeasurable Purity; he does not believe that he can be born in that land. Even so, if that person keeps the thought unceasing — believing for a while, not believing for a while — his will wavering with no firm ground to stand on, yet continuing to bind up the good he does — by the name of that vow he will in the end attain birth. When his life and his illness are about to end, Amitābha will by transformation make a likeness of himself and cause that person to see it with his own eyes. He will no longer be able to speak, but his heart will be glad and leap up, and he will think in his mind: I regret that I did not know to increase my fasting and do more good; now I shall be born in Amitābha's Buddha-land. That person will then repent in his heart, and by repenting his offenses are somewhat reduced; nothing further is required of him. When his life ends, he will be born in Amitābha's Buddha-land. But he cannot come before Amitābha; instead, on the way he will see, at the edge of Amitābha's Buddha-land, a natural city of the seven treasures, and his heart will be greatly glad. Stopping there on the way, in that city, in a seven-jeweled pond he will be born by transformation within a lotus, and receiving a body will naturally grow tall. In that city he will remain five hundred years; the city is two thousand li across each way, and within the city too there are seven-jeweled dwellings. Within those dwellings, inside and out, there are naturally seven-jeweled bathing pools. In the bathing pools there are natural flowers all around, and above the bathing pools there are rows upon rows of seven-jeweled trees, all giving forth the five tones. At mealtimes there is naturally food before him, a hundred flavors, whatever he wishes to have. Such a person is happy in that city, and the things in that city are like the natural things of the second heaven of Trāyastriṃśa. Yet that person cannot leave the city, and cannot see Amitābha; he sees only his radiance, and in his heart reproaches himself, leaping up with joy. Nor can he hear the scripture, nor see the monks, nor see or know what the bodhisattvas and arhats in Amitābha's Buddha-land look like, what manner of beings they are. Such a person is but little at ease in comparison. The Buddha does not make everything one does come to one naturally either; it is by one's own mind that one inclines toward the Way and enters that city. When that person in his former lives was seeking the Way, his mind and mouth were at variance, his words and thoughts lacked sincerity, he doubted the Buddha's scripture, and did not believe or turn toward it, so that he ought naturally to have entered the evil paths; but Amitābha, in pity, drew him away by his awesome spirit. That person will remain in the city five hundred years before he can come out. Then he will go to where Amitābha is and hear the scripture, but his mind will not open and understand, nor may he hear the scripture among the bodhisattvas, arhats, and monks. Because the dwelling in which he lives stands on the ground, he cannot make that dwelling rise high in empty space as he wishes. And he is still very far from Amitābha, and cannot come near to him. Such a person's wisdom is not clear, he knows but little of the scripture, his heart is not joyful, and his mind does not open and understand. After a long, long time, he will of himself attain wisdom, open and understand the scripture; bright and strong and brave, his heart will be joyful, and next he will be as the highest, the first grade above. Why is this? Because when that person in his former lives was seeking the Way, he did not much keep the fasts and precepts but broke the scripture and the Dharma; his mind was in doubt and did not believe the Buddha's words. He did not believe deeply in the Buddha's scripture, nor believe that giving and generosity and doing good will bring him blessing in later lives. And he regrets it in the midst of it, not believing that he can be born in Amitābha's Buddha-land, and doing good works without wholehearted sincerity. For these reasons he is the second, the middle grade.”

The Buddha said: “Those of the third grade: if a person wishes to be born in Amitābha's Buddha-land, but has no means of giving and generosity, and cannot burn incense, scatter flowers, light lamps, hang silken banners, build Buddha-halls, raise stūpas, or feed monks, then he should cut off desire, be without greed or longing, with a kind heart strive diligently, not give way to anger, and be pure in the fasts and precepts. Being thus pure, he should single-mindedly hold the thought and wish to be born in Amitābha's Buddha-land; and if for ten days and nights, day and night, he does not let it cease, then at the end of life he will be born in Amitābha's Buddha-land, and may again be most honored, wise, and brave.”

The Buddha said: “After a person has done this, if he should afterwards give rise to regret in the midst of it and his mind be in doubt, not believing that doing good will bring him blessing in later lives, not believing that he can be born in Amitābha's Buddha-land — even so, that person will still in the end attain birth. When his life and his illness are about to end, Amitābha will cause that person, in his sleep and dreams, to see the land of Amitābha's Buddha-land, and his heart will be glad, and he will think in his mind: ‘I regret that I did not know to do more good; now I shall be born in Amitābha's Buddha-land.’ But though that person only thinks this in his mind, he can no longer speak; then he repents of himself, and by repenting his offenses are lessened and reduced, and his repentance can no longer reach beyond that. When his life ends, he will be born in Amitābha's Buddha-land. But he cannot come before him; instead, on the way he will see a seven-jeweled city two thousand li across, and his heart alone will be glad, and he will stop within it. Again, in a seven-jeweled pond he will be born by transformation within a lotus, and will naturally grow tall. That city is again of the same kind as the city before: like the natural things of the second heaven of Trāyastriṃśa. That person too will remain five hundred years in the city, and only after five hundred years will he be able to come out and be born where Amitābha is; his heart will be greatly glad. Yet when he hears and receives the scripture, his mind will not open and understand, his mind will not be glad, his wisdom will not be clear, and he will know but little of the scripture. The dwelling in which he lives stands on the ground, and he cannot make it rise high in empty space as he wishes. And he is far from Amitābha in the same way as before. Those of the second grade who are in doubt — after a long, long time they too will attain wisdom, open and understand the scripture; brave and joyful in heart, they will next be as the highest, the first grade above. Why is this? It is all because in former lives, when they were seeking the Way, they regretted in the midst of it and doubted, believing for a while and not believing for a while, not believing that doing good would afterwards bring them merit and blessing. All this they receive of themselves; according to their merit, whether weighty or not, each naturally inclines to his own place. In expounding the scripture and walking the Way, the excellence of their virtue is ten thousandfold different, and one transcends and does not reach another.”

The Buddha said: “Those who wish to seek the bodhisattva path and be born in Amitābha's Buddha-land should in the end all attain to be avaivartika bodhisattvas. Avaivartika bodhisattvas should all have the thirty-two marks and the purple-golden color, and the eighty secondary characteristics; all should become Buddhas. According to the wishes of their minds, in whatever direction and in whatever Buddha-land they wish to become a Buddha, they will never again enter hell, or become beasts or hungry ghosts. According as they strive in seeking the Way, whether early or late, in the end all things are equal; if they seek the Way without resting, they will surely attain it, and will not lose what they have wished and vowed.”

The Buddha told Bodhisattva Ajita and the devas, kings, and people: “I say to you all: those who wish to be born in Amitābha's Buddha-land, even if they cannot greatly strive in meditation and uphold the scripture and precepts, should in the main do good. First, one must not take life; second, one must not steal; third, one must not commit sexual misconduct or violate the wives of others; fourth, one must not deceive; fifth, one must not drink wine; sixth, one must not speak with a double tongue; seventh, one must not speak harshly; eighth, one must not speak falsely; ninth, one must not be jealous; tenth, one must not be covetous. One must not be stingy in heart, must not give way to anger, must not be foolish, must not indulge the cravings of the mind, must not regret in the midst of it, and must not be in doubt.

One should be filial and obedient, one should be utterly sincere and faithful, one should receive the Buddha's scripture deeply, and should believe that doing good will bring one blessing in later lives. If one upholds and practices this Dharma without breaking or losing it, then according to what his mind wishes he may be born in Amitābha's Buddha-land. Above all one should keep the fasts and precepts, with a single pure mind, and day and night always hold the wish to be born in Amitābha's Buddha-land. If for ten days and ten nights one does not let it cease, I will in pity take them all and cause them all to be born in Amitābha's Buddha-land.”

The Buddha said: “Should people of the world wish to emulate the wise and practice good in the home as a way of life, living together with wife and children, and amid the bonds of affection and desire they are anxious in mind. If their household affairs are many and hurried, so that they have no leisure for the great fasts and precepts, then with a single pure mind, though they cannot leave the home, when they have a moment of leisure they should of themselves rectify their minds, keep good thoughts in mind, and devote themselves single-mindedly to walking the Way. And if for ten days and ten nights they cannot do even this, then let them think it over well and consider: if they wish to deliver themselves, they should at least cut off their thoughts and put away their cares, not dwell on household matters, not share a bed with a woman, rectify themselves in body, cut off desire in mind, single-mindedly keep the fasts pure, and with utmost thought wish to be born in Amitābha's Buddha-land. If for one day and one night they do not let this cease, then at the end of life they will all be born in that land, born by transformation within a lotus in a seven-jeweled bathing pool, and may attain wisdom and courage. The seven-jeweled dwelling in which they live will be as their minds wish to act, and they may be next to the highest, the first grade above.”

The Buddha said to Bodhisattva Ajita: “All the countless devas and humans of the eight directions, above and below — monks and nuns, laymen and laywomen — who are born in Amitābha's Buddha-land: the whole assembly of them, all together in the seven-jeweled bathing pools, each and every one of them sits upon a single great lotus, and each declares his own virtue and good. Each tells of how, when he was seeking the Way in former lives, he upheld the scripture and precepts and the good Dharma he practiced; of where he came from and was born, the whole story from beginning to end; of the scripture and Way he delighted in; of the scripture he knew and the wisdom he had; and of the merit he carried out and practiced. From highest to lowest, in turn, all are included, so that one may know whether their knowledge of the scripture is clear or unclear, deep or shallow, great or small, and whether their virtue is fine or coarse, thick or thin; the way of nature distinguishes them all. Their talents and wisdom, their courage and strength, they look upon one another and illuminate one another; in courtesy and righteousness they are harmonious and compliant, all rejoicing and leaping up, wise and brave, and none falls short of another.”

The Buddha said: “Such a person takes no thought beforehand to increase his virtue; in doing good he is slack, and he does not believe it. He leans and dawdles, thinking it will do as it is; but when the time comes for the whole assembly to gather and expound the scripture and walk the Way, he is naturally pressed and hurried, and his answers come late. The wisdom of the Way is lofty and transcendent, brilliant and keen in talent, lofty and brave — yet he alone is poor and weak at the edge, and only when the matter is upon him does he repent. But repentance comes too late; afterwards, what good can it do him? He can only grieve and pine in his heart and long to be their equal.”

The Buddha said: “The bodhisattvas and arhats in Amitābha's Buddha-land, the whole great assembly of the great Way, gather of themselves together, restrain their minds and master their thoughts, rectify their bodies, and walk upright. They sport and penetrate everywhere, all following one another in flight, going out and coming in in ordered ranks, making boundless offerings, glad in heart and joyful, delighting to contemplate the scripture and walk the Way together, harmonious and well trained in letters, keen in talent and wisdom, their will like empty space, striving diligently and making vows, their minds never again turning back in the midst, their intent never again reversing, never at any time slackening. Though in seeking the Way they seem outwardly slow, inwardly they are swift and urgent; calmly, within empty space, they hit the mark exactly, outer and inner answering to each other, naturally well ordered, restrained and upright, body and mind pure and clean, without desire or craving, without any evil or stain. Their vows and aspirations are all settled and excellent, neither increased nor diminished; they seek the Way in harmony and uprightness, not straying into the crooked, measuring themselves by the Dharma of the Way, following the scripture's rules and commands, never daring to transgress or stumble, as if by the plumb line. They roam through the eight directions, above and below, without edge or measure, freely as they wish, reaching the boundless and limitless; all thus walk the Way, vast and broad in aspiration, spacious and free, their minds on the Way with no other thought, without worry or care. Naturally non-acting, empty and still, calm and at peace without desire, they do virtuous deeds and make good vows, seeking with all their hearts, holding pity and compassion, striving in both outer and inner, perfectly joined in courtesy and righteousness, penetrating and without transgression, harmonious and fitting, embracing within and without, crossing over and delivered, daring to rise into nirvāṇa, forever joined with the Way and virtue in clarity, naturally preserving one another, joyful and ever more joyous, ever more true. True and utterly white and pure, their vows are lofty and unsurpassed, pure and still and at peace, a serene joy without end, good and excellent beyond compare. Lofty is its radiance, shining and shining; once it opens and is understood, it is clear and penetrating — the mark of the natural within the natural, the root and foundation of the natural. Naturally it becomes five lights up to nine colors; the five lights up to nine colors interweave and revolve, changing through hundreds and thousands of transformations, the most excellent of the natural. Naturally it becomes the seven treasures, and spreading across it becomes the ten thousand things; the essence of light interweaves in brightness, all bringing forth excellence, most beautiful beyond all end. If that land is as beautiful as this, why not strive to do good? Think on the naturalness of the Way, resting in neither above nor below, penetrating without edge or measure, casting off the will into empty space — why does each not strive diligently, and of himself seek with all his might? So may he transcend and pass beyond, and be born in the land of Amitābha, the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity; cutting across the five paths, the evil paths close of themselves, and he rises on the Way without limit, easy to go where none has gone. That land does not go against one; it is drawn along naturally. Why not cast off the affairs of the world and seek the Way and its virtue? So may one attain the utmost long life, with bliss and life without end. Why busy oneself with the affairs of the world, and with the many shared sorrows that are never constant, while the people of the world, shallow and common, contend together over matters that are not urgent? Together here, amid the utmost evil and bitterest suffering, they toil body and mind to make a living and keep one another alive; with no noble and no base, no rich and no poor, no old and no young, no man and no woman — all alike must worry over wealth, and whether they have it or not, their worry is the same and their anxious thoughts are equal. Harassed and sorrowful, piling up thought upon thought, they run about as its servants, with never a moment of peace. He who has fields worries over fields; he who has a house worries over the house; he who has cattle worries over cattle; he who has horses worries over horses; he who has the six kinds of livestock worries over the six kinds of livestock; he who has servants worries over servants; and clothes, bedding, money, gold, silver, and precious things — he worries over them too, doubling his thoughts and piling up his sighs. He nurses care and sorrow and fear in his heart, and disasters come upon him unlooked for: flood and fire, robbers and thieves, enemies and creditors, washing him away, burning him, binding him, battering him and drowning him; poisoned with grief, dazed and terrified, he has no hour of release. Wrath knotted in his heart, his breath pent up in poison and rage, sickness in his breast and belly, grief in his heart and mind, hard-set and stubborn with never a letting go — or else he sits and is broken down and in the end loses body and life, and when he is cast away and gone, there is none to follow him. The honored and the wealthy have such fears and toil as this, and hard suffering such as this: they bind up all cold and heat and dwell together with pain. The poor of small household, poor and straitened and lacking, with no fields yet worry and wish for fields, with no house yet worry and wish for a house, with no cattle yet worry and wish for cattle, with no horses yet worry and wish for horses, with no livestock yet worry and wish for livestock, with no servants yet worry and wish for servants, with no clothes, bedding, money, goods, or food and drink — they too worry and wish to have them. Having one, they lack another; having this, they lack that; they think of having all alike, and when they have somewhat in small measure, it is spent and gone again. Thus painfully they live, and must seek after more. Their thoughts bring no profit, and they cannot get in time. Body and mind both toil, sitting and rising never at rest; care follows upon care, and hard suffering is like this. Their scorched hearts never leave off hate and anger, and they alone rage; they too bind up all cold and heat and dwell together with pain. Or else they sit and in the end cut short their years and die, and still are unwilling to do good or walk the Way. When their life is spent and they die, all must go far away alone. Whither they go, the way of good and evil, none can know.”

Or again, fathers and sons, brothers, husbands and wives, and the relatives of the household within and without, dwelling between heaven and earth, ought to respect and love one another and not hate one another; where one has and the other lacks, they ought to give to one another and not be greedy; their words and looks ought to be gentle, and they should not oppose one another. Or if their minds contend and they give way to anger, and in this life their resentment makes them hate and envy one another in small measure, in later lives it will grow worse and become a great enmity. Why is this? In this life they wish to hurt one another; though they do not break one another at once in the urgency of the moment, killing each other, the poison of grief and the knot of wrath bind their spirits, and by nature they cannot abide apart from each other, and all must be born facing one another and meet again to repay one another. A person amid the love and desire of the world comes alone and goes alone in death and birth, and must go to the place of suffering or joy where his path leads; he must bear it himself, and there is none to bear it for him. Good and evil bring their changes, and calamity and fault lead to different places; prepared beforehand and sternly awaited, he must rise alone and go far to another place, and none can see where he has gone. Good and evil follow of themselves and draw him to birth, dark and dim, parted for long, their roads different, with no time set for meeting again; most hard, most hard is it to meet once more. Why not cast off all these affairs, each while strong and healthy, and strive with all your might to do good and strive diligently to cross the world? So may one attain the utmost long life. Yet you are utterly unwilling to seek the Way — what else do you wait for, and what pleasure do you seek?”

People such as these do not believe that doing good brings good, do not believe that walking the Way attains the Way, do not believe that after death one is born again into a later life, and do not believe that giving brings merit and blessing; they believe none of it, and they call it untrue, saying there is no such thing. For this reason alone, they see it only for themselves and look on one another, handing it down from one to the next. What a father leaves in his teaching, the commands of ancestors and forebears who never did good and never walked the Way, with body foolish and spirit dark, mind blocked and thoughts shut, not seeing the Way of Heaven — none of them has any capacity at all. When they see people die and the dead are born, and where they go, none can know either. Since they have never seen the way of good and evil, and there is none to tell them of it, they take doing good and evil, merit and blessing, calamity and fault, and punishment, and each competes to do them as he will — and there is nothing strange in it at all. As for the way of birth and death, handed on and continuing, upside down and reversed, above and below, with impermanence as its root — all must pass away and cannot be kept forever. When one teaches and guides them, few believe the Way; all must die and be born, with never a rest. People such as these, dim and unreasoning, do not believe the words of the scripture. Each wishes to please himself, his mind taking no thought; foolish in love and desire, not understanding the Way and its virtue, deluded by anger, greedy and base after wealth and beauty — by this they fail to attain the Way, and must suffer harder still, being born in evil places, and in the end know no rest. Their suffering is most pitiable. Or again, within the household and without, fathers and sons, brothers, husbands and wives — as for the meaning of birth and death, they weep tears over one another and long for one another in turn; care and grief knot up, and love and affection wind on and on; their minds ache and cling, and they look and long for one another, day and night without a moment of release. When one teaches them the Way and its virtue, their minds do not open and clear; love and desire do not leave them, blocked and dim, entangled and covered over, unable to think or plan. If they would rectify their own minds, decide the affairs of the world, and devote themselves single-mindedly to walking the Way, then in a moment they would reach the end; but when their years and life are spent, they cannot attain the Way, and there is nothing to be done. Confused and clamorous all together, all crave love and desire. In matters such as these, those who do not understand the Way are many and those who attain it are few; the world hurries on with nothing to rely on. Noble and base, high and low, honored and wealthy, poor and rich, men and women, old and young, each busy with his own affairs, toiling in body, each cherishing the poison of killing, their evil breath dark and dim, and none but is despondent. They do reckless deeds, going against heaven and earth, not following a kind heart; the Way and its virtue are not evil, and are first given over to them, leaving them free to do as they will; but before their lifespan is up, it is suddenly snatched from them, and they fall into the evil paths, toiling for lifetime after lifetime, turned about in sorrow and poison for many thousands of myriads of millions of years, with no time of escape. Their suffering cannot be told, and they are most pitiable.”

The Buddha told Bodhisattva Ajita and the devas, kings, and people: “I say to you all: it is because people busy themselves with the affairs of the world that they fail to attain the Way. Think it over well: what is evil you should let go and keep far from you; what is good you should hold fast and not recklessly do otherwise. Increase your good deeds, great or small, many or few. The glory of love and desire can never be kept forever; it must part from you, and there is nothing in it to delight in. When the Buddha is in the world, those who have faith and love the Buddha's scripture deeply and practice the Way and its virtue are all my younger brothers. Those who have but now begun to study the Buddha's scripture and precepts are all my disciples. Those who wish to leave their station, leave home and forsake wife and children, cut off wealth and beauty, and come to live as monks and be monks for the Buddha are all my sons and grandsons. My age is most hard to encounter. Those who wish to be born in Amitābha's Buddha-land may attain wisdom and courage and be honored by the multitude. Do not follow the wishes of your own mind and break the scripture and precepts. If afterwards anyone has doubts and does not understand the scripture, let him come forward and ask the Buddha, and the Buddha will explain it for him.”

Bodhisattva Ajita, kneeling long with palms pressed together, said: “The Buddha's awesome spirit is honored and weighty, and the scripture he speaks is excellent. We who hear the Buddha's words all take them into our hearts and ponder them. The people of the world are indeed thus; there is no difference from what the Buddha has said. Now the Buddha in his compassion has opened our eyes to the Way of Heaven and taught us the road of birth; our ears and eyes are clear, and we shall long attain deliverance. As if born again, we who hear the Buddha's words are all kind in heart and joyful, leaping up and opening in understanding. We and all the devas, kings, and people, and the winged and crawling creatures, have all received the Buddha's grace, and there is none who has not been freed from care and suffering. The Buddha's teachings and precepts are most deep, boundless and bottomless. What the Buddha's wisdom sees and knows — the affairs of the eight directions, above and below, past, future, and present — is unsurpassed and without edge or measure. The Buddha is most hard to encounter, the scripture and the Way most hard to hear; we all set our kind hearts upon the Buddha.

That we now have attained deliverance is all because the Buddha, in former lives when he sought the Way, endured bitter hardship in study and questioning and strove diligently. His grace and virtue cover all things; the merit and blessing he carried out are lofty beyond measure, his radiance shines through all, penetrating emptiness without end, opening the way into nirvāṇa. He teaches the scriptures, subdues and transforms by his awesome power, moves all with pity throughout the eight directions, above and below, boundless and limitless. The Buddha is the honored master of the Dharma, transcending all the sages, and there is none who can equal the Buddha. The Buddha is the teacher of all the devas, kings, and people of the eight directions, above and below; according to what their minds wish and long for, great or small, he causes them all to attain the Way. That we now are able to meet the Buddha and to hear the name of Amitābha — we are most glad, and there is none among us who has not opened in bright wisdom.”

The Buddha told Bodhisattva Ajita: “What you say is truly so. If anyone has a kind heart toward the Buddha, he should with great joy truly recollect the Buddha; only after long, long ages does a Buddha again appear in the world. Now I, in this world of suffering, have become a Buddha; the scripture and the Way that I bring forth, teaching and penetrating through, cutting off doubt, rectifying the mind and upright conduct, plucking out all desire, cutting off the root of every evil, roaming unfettered, presiding over wisdom, within and without all the ways, grasping and holding the guiding cords, clear and distinct, opening and showing the five paths, deciding and setting right the way of birth and death and of nirvāṇa.”

The Buddha said: “From countless kalpas past, kalpas beyond all reckoning, you have walked the bodhisattva path, wishing to bring across all devas and humans and the winged and crawling creatures; it is very long, very far, since you began. Countless are the people who have attained the Way and deliverance through you, and countless too are those who have attained the way of nirvāṇa. You, and all the devas, kings, and people of the eight directions, above and below — monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen — by your former lives through countless kalpas past, have been turned about in these five paths, dying and being born, wailing and sighing, weeping tears over one another, longing and craving for one another in turn, care and grief and poisoned sorrow, with pain that cannot be told. Even to this present life, death and birth have not ceased; yet today you meet the Buddha and come together at this time, and so hear the name of Amitābha, which is most excellent. Excellent! I rejoice with you. You may also of yourselves grow weary of the pain of birth and death: birth is most painful, most bitter, most extreme; growing to full years is also painful and extreme; death too is painful and bitter and extreme. Most foul and stinking and impure are its places, with nothing at all to be desired. Therefore the Buddha tells you all: you too may for yourselves cut off the foulness and evil and impurity, and you too may rectify mind and body and increase your good deeds. Then always rectify both within and without, cleanse body and mind, wash away the dirt of the mind, take vows and restrain yourselves, outer and inner answering each other, in word and deed faithful and sincere. A person can deliver himself; helping one another in turn, pluck out all desire, be keen and clear with utmost mind, and let the vow you seek never turn back; bind up the root of the good Way. Though you strive diligently and suffer for one lifetime, it is but a moment. Do good in this life, and in the next you will be born in Amitābha's Buddha-land, with bliss beyond all limit, forever joined with the Way in clarity, and in goodness preserving one another forever; you will long be parted from the pain of the evil paths and the grief of care, pluck out the root of all the suffering of hard toil, and cut off all desire and affection. Born in Amitābha's Buddha-land to long life, you will have no more pain, no more foul stinking places, no more hard toil, no more lust, anger, or folly, and no more care or grief or poisoned sorrow. Being born in Amitābha's Buddha-land, if you wish your life to be one kalpa, ten kalpas, a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, a trillion kalpas, you may freely do as you wish; if you wish to abide for a life of countless kalpas, kalpas beyond all reckoning, you may do as you please and obtain it all. If you wish to eat, or not to eat, freely as you please, all comes naturally and all can be obtained. Next to the way of nirvāṇa, each of you should keenly and clearly seek it out; let there be no doubt in your hearts and no regret. Those who wish to be born there must not, by their own faults, be punished with five hundred years in the natural seven-jeweled city at the edge of Amitābha's Buddha-land.”

Bodhisattva Ajita said: “We receive the Buddha's stern and clear and weighty teaching; we shall all strive diligently and single-mindedly seek it, and we ask to practice it, not daring to doubt or slacken.”

blocks.text: The Sutra of Immeasurable Pure and Equal Enlightenment, Scroll Four

inline.s: The Buddha told Bodhisattva Ajita and the others: “If in this world you can master your own minds and rectify your thoughts, and do no evil in body, that is great virtue and goodness, and throughout the eight directions, above and below, there is nothing to compare with it. Why is this? In the countless Buddha-lands throughout the eight directions, above and below, the devas and humans all naturally do good, they do not greatly do evil, and they are easy to teach and transform. Now I, in this world, am a Buddha amid the five evils, the five pains, and the five burnings, and to be a Buddha here is the most bitter of all. I teach the people, causing them to cut off the five evils, to put away the five pains, to put away the five burnings, to subdue and transform their minds, and to hold the five virtues, so that they obtain merit and blessing, long life in the world, and the way of nirvāṇa.”

The Buddha said: “What are the five evils? What are the five pains? What is it to be amid the five burnings? What is it to melt away the five evils and cause people to hold the five virtues? What is it to hold the five virtues, obtain merit, blessing, and long life, and attain the way of nirvāṇa in the world?”

The Buddha said: “The first evil: the devas and humans, down to the beasts and the winged and crawling creatures, wish to do every evil; the strong overpower the weak, and they destroy and plunder one another, killing and wounding one another, eating one another in turn. They do not know to do good; they are evil and rebellious and against the Way, and they receive its punishment. This is the natural way of things, and so they go on toward it. The gods record and know it, and those who transgress are not forgiven. Handed on and continuing, there are therefore the poor, the lowly, beggars, and the lonely, and there are the deaf, the blind, the mute, the foolish, the wicked, and below them the crippled, the mad, and those who cannot reach their aim. As for those who are honored and wealthy, of high talent and clear understanding, wise and brave — all this is the fate of their former lives, when they did good, were kind and filial, and spread grace and bestowed virtue. Therefore, when there are lawsuits and the king's law and prisons, and they are unwilling to fear and be careful but do evil and fall under the law, they receive their punishment of guilt with heavy penalties brought to extremity, and though they seek and hope for release, it is hard to get free. In this present life these things are before their eyes; at the end of life it is worse still: they enter the dark, and receive a body and are born again. It is like the king's law, with its bitter suffering and extreme punishments; hence there are naturally hells, beasts, and hungry ghosts, and the kinds of winged and crawling creatures. They trade their bodies, change their evil and alter their path; their lifespan is short or long, their soul and spirit, life and essence go naturally into their destination, and receiving a form and lodging in a womb, they must face it alone; born together, following one another, they repay one another in turn, and must return and requite. The punishment of evil and guilt, with its many matters, is not yet finished, and in the end they cannot leave, turned about within it, lifetime after lifetime and kalpa after kalpa, with no time of escape. It is hard to be delivered, and the pain cannot be told. Between heaven and earth this is naturally so; though it does not come suddenly upon them all at once, in time it always takes them by the natural way, and good and evil alike return to them. This is the first great evil, the first pain, the first burning; such is its bitter toil, with sorrow and poison and wailing. It is like a fierce fire that rises and burns a man's body. If a man can, amid it, single-mindedly master his mind, rectify his body and upright his conduct, and alone do every good and do no evil, then his body alone is delivered and he obtains merit and blessing, and may attain long life, pass out of the world, and reach the way of the heavens and nirvāṇa. This is the first great good.”

The Buddha said: “The second evil: the kings and emperors, the senior officials and the people of the world, fathers and sons, brothers, households and husbands and wives, are for the most part without righteousness or principle. They do not follow the government's commands, and turn to lust, extravagance, arrogance, and pride; each wishes to please himself, giving his mind free rein, deceiving and mocking one another, with no fear of death at all. Their minds and mouths are at variance, their words and thoughts insincere; they are flattering and disloyal, fawning with cunning words, their conduct unprincipled, hating and envying one another, slandering one another, and involving one another in evil and wrong. The ruler above is not clear; his mind does not examine and illumine; he employs his ministers, and the ministers, being in place, with shallow measure and ability to act, know the situation and use it. Those in office are not upright, and are mocked by others; they recklessly cast away the loyal and good, and do not accord with the heart of heaven, greatly going against reason. Ministers deceive their lords, sons deceive their fathers, younger brothers deceive their elder brothers, wives deceive their husbands; within and without the household, acquaintances and kin, each cherishes greed and lust, and in his heart alone is angry; blind and deaf and foolish, their desires only increase. High and low, noble and base, man and woman, great and small, their minds are all alike, each wishing to enrich himself. They ruin the household and lose their lives, never thinking of what came before or what comes after; household and kin are brought by it to the destruction of the clan. Or again, within and without the household, acquaintances and friends, the foolish folk of the villages and market-towns, turn to the same pursuits together, profiting and harming one another, fighting over money and goods, their anger turning to enmity and then to contests of victory and defeat. The rich and stingy burn in mind and will not give; they hoard and begrudge, loving treasures and greedy for more, sitting in their thoughts so that mind toils and body suffers. Thus to the very end they have nothing to rely on; they come alone and go alone, with none to follow them. Good and evil, fortune and misfortune, calamity and guilt and punishment, follow where their fate is born — perhaps in a place of joy, perhaps into poisonous suffering — and only then do they repent. What use will it be then? Or again, people of the world with foolish minds and little wisdom, when they see the good, slander them and hate them, unwilling to admire or follow, wishing only to do evil and recklessly do what is unlawful; wishing only to steal and rob, always cherishing a poisonous mind, wishing to get others' goods to supply themselves, and when these are squandered and gone, seeking them again. Crooked in mind and not upright, they are always alone in terror, fearing the looks of others, giving no thought in the moment, and only when the matter comes do they repent. In this present life there are the senior officials and the prisons, and they go naturally toward them and receive their calamity. The poor, the beggars, and the lonely of the world — it is only because in former lives they did not believe in the Way and its virtue and would not do good; and doing evil in this life, the gods keep a separate register, and at the end of life they enter the evil paths. Hence there are naturally hells, beasts, and hungry ghosts, and the winged and crawling creatures, turned about within them, lifetime after lifetime and kalpa after kalpa, with no time of escape. Hard is it to be delivered; the pain cannot be told. This is the second great evil, the second pain, the second burning; such is its bitter toil. It is like a fire rising and burning a man's body. If a man can, amid it, single-mindedly master his mind, rectify his body and upright his conduct, and alone do every good and do no evil, then his body alone is delivered and he obtains merit and blessing, and may attain long life, pass out of the world, and reach the way of the heavens and nirvāṇa. This is the second great good.

The Buddha said: “The third evil: the people of the world, living as parasites on one another, dwell together between heaven and earth, and in the span of their years there is no telling how few their days. There are the honored and wealthy, the wise and good; below them the poor and base, the crippled, the sickly, and the foolish; and among them wicked people who only nurse poison and evil in their thoughts, whose bodies and minds are not upright, who always think of lust and debauchery, whose breasts are full of vexation, whose desires are tangled together, who cannot sit or rise in peace, whose greedy minds are stingy and grudging, and who wish only to get things for nothing. They leer and glance at fine looks; their evil manner is lust and debauchery. They hate and loathe their own wives and slip in and out in secret; they gather what the household has and join together in wrongdoing; they meet to eat and drink and do evil together; they raise troops and become bandits, attack cities and fight and brawl, rob and kill and cut men down, seize by force against the Way, take others' goods, steal and snatch whatever they can get. They will not manage their livelihood; what they ought to seek they will not do. Their evil minds are set outside; they cannot devote themselves to work, but wish to strike and make things happen, threatening and coercing by force; they bring it home to feed the household and live together on it, giving their minds free rein and pleasing themselves, indulging body and taking their pleasure, and violating the wives of others. Or they do not shrink even from their own kin; the noble and base and the elders all hate and loathe them together, and within and without the household all are afflicted and grieved by them. They do not fear the magistrate's laws and ordinances and shrink from nothing; such evil as this is recorded, and there are naturally prisons; the sun and moon shine and know it, the gods note and take it down, the spirits seize and record it. Hence there are naturally hells, beasts, and hungry ghosts, and the winged and crawling creatures, turned about within them, lifetime after lifetime and kalpa after kalpa, with no time of escape. Hard is it to be delivered; the pain cannot be told. This is the third great evil, the third pain, the third burning; such is its bitter toil. It is like a fire rising and burning a man's body.
