If a man can, amid it, single-mindedly master his mind, rectify his body and upright his conduct, and alone do every good and do no evil, then his body alone is delivered and he obtains merit and blessing, and may attain long life, pass out of the world, and reach the way of the heavens and nirvāṇa. This is the third great good.

The Buddha said: “The fourth evil: evil people cannot do good, but ruin and destroy one another, teaching and commanding one another to do every evil together. They make themselves the tellers of tales, wishing only for a double tongue and harsh speech, cursing and lying, envying and striving and throwing one another into confusion; they hate and envy good people and ruin the worthy and good, taking pleasure in evil from the sidelines. They are unfilial and do not support their parents, and they slight their teachers and acquaintances; they are faithless and rarely truthful. They call themselves noble and possessors of the Way, riding roughshod in their might, piling up power and force, encroaching on and bullying others, and they cannot know themselves. Doing evil, they feel no shame; they use themselves and think themselves quite able, and make others serve and revere them. They do not revere heaven and earth, the gods, the sun, and the moon, and they cannot be taught to do good or be subdued and transformed. They use themselves and are arrogant, thinking it should always be so; they have no grieving heart either, and know no fear. Free in their minds and proud as this, the gods note and know them. Relying on their former lives and the fate of their former lives, when they did some merit and virtue, small good deeds propped them up and protected and helped them; but doing evil in this life, when their merit and blessing are utterly spent, the good spirits each depart and leave them, and their bodies stand alone in emptiness with nothing more to rely on, and they receive heavy calamity and punishment. Their lifespan runs its course with evil winding back upon them, and naturally pressed and hurried, it pursues them and they cannot rest. Naturally all their evils run together to their exhaustion. Their name is written where the gods are, and calamity and guilt drag them on; facing what they must meet, they go on toward it and receive the punishment of their guilt, body and mind shattered, spirit and form in utmost suffering, and they cannot get away. They can only go forward, into the cauldron of fire. At that time, what use is repentance? What can reach them then? The way of heaven is natural, and there is no stumbling aside. Hence there are hells, beasts, and hungry ghosts, and the kinds of winged and crawling creatures, turned about within them, lifetime after lifetime and kalpa after kalpa, with no time of escape. Hard is it to be delivered; the pain cannot be told. This is the fourth great evil, the fourth pain, the fourth burning; such is its bitter toil. It is like a fire rising and burning a man's body. If a man can, amid it, single-mindedly master his mind, rectify his body and upright his conduct, and alone do every good and do no evil, then his body alone is delivered and he obtains merit and blessing, and may attain long life, pass out of the world, and reach the way of the heavens and nirvāṇa. This is the fourth great good.”

The Buddha said: “The fifth evil: the people of the world lean and slacken, unwilling to do good, never thinking to make a living, so that wife and children go hungry and cold and the parents likewise. When they wish to scold and teach their son, the son's mind is evil; he glares and answers in anger, his words and commands are ungentle, and he is contrary and rebellious, worse than a savage, like an enemy rather than a son. He borrows and lends recklessly everywhere, and all are afflicted and weary of him; he is utterly without return, with no thought of repaying. Poor and straitened and lacking, he can get no more, and then he turns to tricks and wheedling words, giving himself up to idleness and wandering, a past master at getting things for nothing, and uses them to relieve himself, with no fear of law or prohibition. In eating and drinking he knows no limit, and he drinks wine and craves delicacies; going out and coming in, he keeps no hours. Rough and overbearing, he does not know human feeling, and he leers and forces himself on others. When he sees others happy, he hates and envies and is angry at them. Without righteousness, without courtesy, he uses himself and takes it as his due, and cannot be admonished or made to understand. Nor does he worry about whether his parents and wife and children have anything; nor does he think of repaying his parents' kindness at the last; nor does he think of his teacher's grace. His mind always dwells on evil, his mouth always speaks evil, and day by day he accomplishes nothing. He does not believe in the Way and its virtue; he does not believe that there are wise and good and ancient sages; he does not believe that by doing good and walking the Way one may cross the world; he does not believe that there is a Buddha in the world. He wishes to kill arhats, to set monks at odds, always wishing to kill people, wishing to kill his parents, brothers, wife and children, kinsmen and friends. His parents, brothers, wife and children, kinsmen and friends — he hates and loathes the sight of them and wishes them dead. He does not believe the Buddha's words, does not believe that a person's life ends in death and that afterwards he is born again into a later life, does not believe that doing good brings good and doing evil brings evil. People such as these, men and women, are all alike in mind, contrary and rebellious, foolish and dull, angry and craving, knowing nothing. They use themselves and think themselves excellent and of great wisdom, and do not know whence they came or where birth and death will lead them. They are unwilling to be kind and filial, but go against heaven and earth; and in the meantime they seek for luck and hope to gain long life and to win deathlessness for themselves. Yet they must in the end go to birth and death and bitter toil, to the way of good and evil; the evil their bodies have done, and the calamities and guilt of all their destinations, leave them no deliverance, and they cannot be subdued and transformed to do good either. Though one teaches them with a kind heart, opening and guiding them to the good and evil of birth and death and where they lead, they still do not believe it. Though one speaks to them with bitter earnestness, wishing to bring them to deliverance, it profits such a person nothing. Their minds are blocked, their thoughts do not open and understand; and when the great decree is about to come, at that time they all repent — but repenting afterwards, what use is it? They took no thought beforehand for good; at the extremity, what good can it do them? Between heaven and earth the five paths are clear and distinct. Vast and deep and dim, boundless and shoreless, they receive and hand on to one another; good and evil, poison and pain, each body must bear for itself, and there is none to bear it for another. The way of nature is such that it follows where their conduct goes and pursues their fate to wherever it is born, and they cannot cast it off. The good walk in good, follow good, are kind and filial, and pass from joy into joy, from light into light; the evil walk in evil, and pass from suffering into suffering, from darkness into darkness. Who can know this? The Buddha alone knows and sees it. He teaches the people, but few believe and accept; birth and death are without rest, and the evil paths are never cut off. Of people such as these, one cannot tell it all. Hence there are naturally hells, beasts, and hungry ghosts, and the winged and crawling creatures, turned about within them, lifetime after lifetime and kalpa after kalpa, with no time of escape. Hard is it to be delivered; the pain cannot be told. This is the fifth great evil, the fifth pain, the fifth burning; such is its bitter toil. It is like a fire rising and burning a man's body. If a man can, amid it, single-mindedly master his mind, rectify his body and upright his conduct, make his words and deeds accord, be utterly sincere in what he does, and speak as he speaks, his mind and mouth not turning, and alone do every good and do no evil, then his body alone is delivered and he obtains merit and blessing, and may attain long life, pass out of the world, and reach the way of the heavens and nirvāṇa. This is the fifth great good.”

The Buddha told Bodhisattva Ajita and the others: “I say to you all: the five evils of this world are of such bitter toil; they cause the five pains to arise and the five burnings to arise, giving rise to one another in turn. The people of the world will not do good but wish to do every evil; those who dare to transgress these evil things shall all, of themselves, pass through and enter the evil paths again. Or in this present life they are first struck by sickness and calamity, unable either to die or to live, shown to the multitude to behold. At the end of life they go on into the utmost great suffering, where sorrow and pain and cruel poison consume them, burning one another away; and afterwards they become enemies to one another and wound and kill one another, beginning from something very small and reaching great extremity. All of it comes from greed and lust for wealth and beauty, from being unwilling to bear insult and give in charity, each wishing to please himself, with no thought of right and wrong any more, wishing to win a name for strength, driven by foolish craving, following the thoughts of their minds, and unable to get what they want. Wrath is knotted in their breasts, bound by wealth and beauty, with no deliverance and no knowing when they have enough; enriching themselves and quarreling over desires, taking no thought and keeping no record, utterly without righteousness or principle, not following the right Way. Wealth and honor and glory delight them for a time; they cannot bear insult and do not know to give in charity. Their power is but little, and it scorches along with their evil name; their bodies sit in bitter toil, and after a long while comes great extremity, and it follows them naturally with no release. The king's law spreads its net, and they are naturally seized and bound. Above and below answer to each other, the net and its cords; lonely and afraid, they must enter within it. This has been so in every age, painful and pitiable indeed.”

The Buddha said to Bodhisattva Ajita and the others: “If in this world there is such a Buddha, he pities and grieves for them all; by his awesome spirit he shakes and moves them, and all the many evil things he melts and transforms. He causes them to leave evil and draw near to good, to cast off what they think, to receive and uphold the scripture and precepts, and there is none who does not accept and follow. They carry out the scripture and the Dharma, not daring to transgress or lose the way of crossing the world, of non-action, and of nirvāṇa, which is excellent and good and supremely blissful, most clear and without limit.”

The Buddha said: “You devas, kings, and people, and the people of later ages, having received the Buddha's words, should ponder them well. If you can, amid it, rectify your minds and upright your conduct; and if those above you, being rulers, lead and transform by doing good, restrain and govern those below them, teach and command the people, and cause them to admonish one another in turn, to do good together in turn, and to deliver one another in turn; if each rectifies and keeps himself, is kind and compassionate and pitying, and to the end of life never slackens; if you honor the sages, respect filial piety, penetrate all and love all; and if you dare not break or fail the Buddha's words and commands, but take thought for the way of crossing the world and nirvāṇa, take thought to cut off the pain of birth and death and pluck out the root of evil, take thought to cut off the hells, beasts, and hungry ghosts and the winged and crawling creatures and the way of evil suffering — then you should strive hard while the Buddha is in the world and firmly uphold the scripture and the Way, not daring to lose it.”

The Buddha said: “You who would do good — what is the first and most urgent thing? You should rectify your own body, you should rectify your own mind, you should rectify your own eyes, you should rectify your own ears, you should rectify your own nose, you should rectify your own mouth, you should rectify your own hands, you should rectify your own feet; and being able to restrain yourselves, do not act recklessly. Body and mind pure and clean, both answering to good, restrained within and without, do not follow your cravings and do not transgress any evil. Let your words and looks always be gentle, and let your bodily conduct be single-minded; in walking and standing, sitting and rising, do not be stirred. In whatever you undertake, you should first think it over well and consider it, measure your ability, look all around and lay your plans, and then settle and calmly carry it out. If you undertake a matter in haste, without first thinking it over well, and do it carelessly, you lose your labor, and failure and regret come after, with wasted toil and lost body. Be utterly sincere and faithful, and you will attain the Way and pass beyond.”

The Buddha said: “If you in this world increase your good deeds, spread grace and bestow virtue, and can keep unbroken the prohibitions of the Way, bearing insult, striving diligently, single-minded and wise, and in turn teach and transform one another to do good and be virtuous — if one keeps this scripture and Dharma with a kind and single mind, pure in the fasts and precepts, for one day and one night, it surpasses a hundred years of doing good in Amitābha's Buddha-land. Why is this? In Amitābha's Buddha-land all have gathered merit and every good; there they are non-acting and natural, and whatever they seek they obtain, and there is no evil at all, not so much as a hair's breadth.”

The Buddha said: “If in this world one does good for ten days and ten nights, the blessing obtained surpasses that of the people in Buddha-lands of other directions who do good for a thousand years. Why is this? In Buddha-lands of other directions all do good; those who do good are many and those who do evil are few, and all have natural things, so that without seeking or working they obtain them of themselves. Here the evil are many and the good are few, and without seeking and working one cannot obtain them; it is because a person can rectify and master himself and do good, and seek the Way with all his heart, that he is able to be so. Here there is nothing natural; one cannot supply oneself, but must go out and seek, toiling bitterly to make a living. They deceive and slight one another in turn, tricking and making trouble, and what goods they get they bring home to feed wife and children, drinking bitterness and eating poison, toiling in mind and suffering in body. Thus to the very end their minds are not single, and they turn about without peace. It is because a person can calm himself and do good and strive diligently in virtue that he is able to be so.”

The Buddha said: “I pity you all, and the devas, kings, and people; I teach you all to do every good and not to do any evil, and according to what each is able, I at once give him the Way, teaching, admonishing, opening, and guiding. If all receive and practice it, then rulers lead and transform toward good. They teach and command their ministers below; fathers teach their sons, elder brothers teach their younger brothers, husbands teach their wives; within and without the household, kinsmen and friends teach and speak to one another in turn — doing good and walking the Way, upholding the scripture and keeping the precepts, each rectifying and keeping himself. Above and below restrain one another; with no noble and no base, no man and no woman, pure in the fasts and precepts, none but is glad, harmonious and compliant in righteousness and reason, urging one another to joy and to kindness and filial piety, and restraining one another by vow. Those who obtain the Buddha's words all uphold and ponder them; what ought not to be done — if they transgress and do it, they repent of themselves. They leave evil and draw near to good, cast off the crooked and turn to the upright, hearing it in the morning and mending it by evening; they uphold the scripture and precepts as a poor man who has found treasure. Wherever the Buddha has gone, in whatever commandery or kingdom, they at once bestow the scripture and precepts. The devas, sun and moon, stars and spirits, the kings and their attending ministers, the senior officials and the people, the dragons, ghosts, and spirits, the hells and the beasts — all receive and practice it. Then rulers change and turn to good: pure in the fasts, keen in thought, cleansing and washing themselves, rectifying mind and uprighting conduct, standing in their office in reverence and awe, teaching and commanding and leading the multitude to do good, upholding the prohibitions of the Way, and making their words and commands stand. Ministers serve their lords, loyal and upright, receiving commands and not daring to break or betray them; fathers and sons speak commands, and sons are filial and obedient and receive them; brothers and husbands and wives, kinsmen and friends, above and below give commands to one another, compliant in word and harmonious in reason; noble and base, great and small, respect and serve one another in turn, with courtesy and righteousness, and do not betray one another. None but change their former ways and cultivate what is to come; they wash their minds and alter their conduct, rectify both within and without, and naturally do good, and whatever they wish they obtain. Moved by good, they are subdued and transformed by the natural way; if they seek not to die, they may obtain long life, and if they seek to cross the world, they may attain the way of nirvāṇa.”

The Buddha said: “The Buddha's awesome spirit is honored and weighty: he melts evil and transforms it to good, and there is none who is not delivered. Now I have appeared in the world; amid this evil, in an age of suffering I have become a Buddha, and in pity and compassion and grief I teach and speak and open the Way. The devas and kings, the attending ministers and those about them, the senior officials and the people — according to what their minds wish and long for, I cause them all to attain the Way. Wherever the Buddha has gone, in whatever commandery, kingdom, district, or town, in whatever hamlet or market-town he has passed through in turn, none but is rich and ripe. All the world is at peace; the sun and moon move and shine with doubled brightness and goodness; wind and rain come in season, and the people are at rest. The strong do not oppress the weak, and each finds his place. There are no years of famine or plague, no sick or wasted; weapons do not rise, the kingdom has no robbers or thieves, no wrongs or injustice, no one bound in prison. Rulers and subjects, the people, all are glad; loyal and kind and utterly sincere, each rectifies and keeps himself, and all of themselves keep the kingdom in peace. Concordant and filial, none but is joyful; where one has and another lacks, they give to one another, spreading grace and bestowing virtue. Glad in heart and sharing joy, all respect and love one another, yielding wealth and giving way in righteousness, deferring to one another first and last, serving one another with courtesy as father and son, as elder and younger brother. None but is kind and worthy, harmonious in courtesy and propriety, utterly without dispute; excellent and good beyond all limit.”

The Buddha said: “I pity you, my children, and wish to deliver you, more than parents think of their children. Now all the devas, kings, and people of the eight directions, above and below, and the winged and crawling creatures, having obtained the Buddha's scripture and precepts and practicing the Buddha's Way, all attain bright wisdom, and their minds all open and understand; there are none who are not delivered and freed from care and suffering. Now I have become a Buddha amid the five evils, the five pains, and the five burnings; I subdue and transform the five evils, melt away the five pains, cut off and extinguish the five burnings, attacking evil with good and plucking out the poison and pain, causing them to obtain the five virtues, bright and good, so that the burning evil does not arise. After I have entered parinirvāṇa, the scripture and the Way will gradually be cut off; the people will flatter and fawn and be wholly given to every evil, and will no longer do good. The five burnings will rise again, and the five pains will be bitter in the extreme. Again as before, it will naturally come back, and after a long while grow worse, beyond all telling. I have done but a little for you in the Way.”

The Buddha told Bodhisattva Ajita and the others: “Let each of you think on it and hold it, and teach and admonish one another in turn; according to the Buddha's scripture and Dharma, dare not transgress.”

Bodhisattva Ajita, kneeling long with palms pressed together, said: “What the Buddha has spoken is most painful and bitter. The people of the world do evil, and it is exceedingly harsh, just so, just so. The Buddha in his pity and compassion delivers them all, and we all say that we receive the Buddha's weighty teaching and ask to hand it on in turn, not daring to transgress.”
The Buddha told Ānanda: “I pity you all; I will cause you all to see Amitābha and the bodhisattvas and arhats and the land in which they dwell. Do you wish to see it?”
Then Ānanda was greatly glad, and kneeling long with palms pressed together, he said: “We all wish to see it!”

The Buddha said: “Rise, and put on your robe again; bow toward the west, to where the sun sets, and do reverence to Amitābha, and with your head and face to the ground say: ‘Namo the Immeasurable Purity and Equal Enlightenment.’”

Ānanda said he would, and receiving the teaching, rose, put on his robe again, bowed toward the west, to where the sun sets, did reverence to Amitābha, and with his head to the ground said: “Namo the Immeasurable Purity and Equal Enlightenment.”

Before Ānanda had risen, Amitābha sent forth a great radiance and awesome spirit, which filled the heavens and earth of the countless Buddha-lands throughout the eight directions, above and below, and all was greatly shaken. In the countless heavens and earth of the devas, the jeweled Mount Sumeru, the great jeweled Mount Mahāsumeru, in all the great and small bounds of the heavens and earth, and in all the great hells and small hells, and the dark and hidden places of the mountains, forests, streams, and valleys — all was made greatly bright, and a great rain fell and all was opened wide. Then Ānanda, the bodhisattvas and arhats, the devas, kings, and people, all beheld Amitābha and the seven treasures of the land of the bodhisattvas and arhats; and their hearts were all greatly glad and leaping up, and they all rose and did reverence to Amitābha, with their heads to the ground, and all said: “Namo the Immeasurable Purity Samyaksaṃbuddha.”

When Amitābha, the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity, had released the radiance and authority of his light, all the countless devas and humans, and the winged and crawling creatures as well, beheld that light; and none among them who did not turn toward it in compassion, rejoicing and doing good. In all the hells, among the beasts and hungry ghosts, in every place of torment and bitter toil, the pains ceased and were inflicted no more; none there but found release from grief. The blind regained their sight; the lame and the crippled were able to walk; the sick rose up healed; the feeble grew strong; the foolish became wise; those given to lust and anger were all moved to kind hearts and good deeds; and wherever poison had been taken, the poison worked no more. Bells, drums, lutes and harps, all manner of music that none had sounded, sounded of themselves; the pearls and rings of women rang of themselves; the birds and the many beasts raised their own plaintive cries. In that hour there was none who did not rejoice and attain deliverance. And so, on that very day, all the devas and men throughout the Buddha-lands carried celestial flowers and incense from on high and made offering in the empty sky, scattering them upon all the Buddhas and upon Amitābha; and the devas together wrought ten thousand kinds of spontaneous music, delighting all the Buddhas, the bodhisattvas, and the arhats. At that time the bliss that filled all things could not be spoken.
The Buddha declared: “Ānanda, Ajita the bodhisattva and the rest — the land of Amitābha and of the bodhisattvas and arhats, naturally adorned with the seven treasures: is it not without a peer?”
Ānanda knelt, pressed his palms together, and said: “The Buddha has described the land of Amitābha as excellent and good; there is not a thing in it that differs from what the Buddha has spoken.”
The Buddha said: “Were I to tell of the merit, virtue, and excellence of the land and power of Amitābha, a whole kalpa of days and nights would not yet exhaust it; I have only told you a little.”

Bodhisattva Ajita then knelt, pressed his palms together, and asked the Buddha: “Of the Buddha-lands from here — how many bodhisattvas of the stage of non-retrogression are born in the land of Amitābha? I wish to hear it.”
The Buddha said: “If you wish to know it, listen attentively and hold it in your heart.” Bodhisattva Ajita said: “I receive your instruction.”

The Buddha said: “From this land of mine seventy-two thousand koṭis of bodhisattvas of the stage of non-retrogression are all born in the land of Amitābha. Each such bodhisattva, having gone before and made offerings to countless Buddhas in succession, shall, as Maitreya does, all become Buddhas. And the rest, the lesser bodhisattvas, countless, beyond reckoning, are all likewise to be born in the land of Amitābha.”

The Buddha told Bodhisattva Ajita: “Not only the bodhisattvas of this land shall be born in the land of Amitābha; in other lands of other regions there are also Buddhas, and it is likewise so. The first Buddha is named Light Radiant Far-Reaching; in his land are eighteen koṭis of bodhisattvas, all to be born in the land of Amitābha, in those other lands. The second Buddha is named Jewel-Accumulated; in his land are nine koṭis of bodhisattvas, all to be born in the land of Amitābha, in those other lands. The third Buddha is named Ruless Stain; in his land are twenty-two koṭis of bodhisattvas, all to be born in the land of Amitābha, in those other lands. The fourth Buddha is named Limitless Bright Light; in his land are twenty-five koṭis of bodhisattvas, all to be born in the land of Amitābha, in those other lands. The fifth Buddha is named Supreme in the World; in his land are sixty koṭis of bodhisattvas, all to be born in the land of Amitābha, in those other lands. The sixth Buddha is named Courageous Light; in his land are fourteen thousand bodhisattvas, all to be born in the land of Amitābha, in those other lands. The seventh Buddha is named Perfect Net of Gems; in his land are fourteen koṭis of bodhisattvas, all to be born in the land of Amitābha, in those other lands. The eighth Buddha is named King of Mighty Wisdom; in his land are eight hundred koṭis of bodhisattvas, all to be born in the land of Amitābha, in those other lands. The ninth Buddha is named Might Unsurpassed; in his land are eighty-one koṭis of bodhisattvas, all to be born in the land of Amitābha, in those other lands. The tenth Buddha is named Good Auspice; in his land are a thousand koṭis of bodhisattvas, all to be born in the land of Amitābha, in those other lands. The eleventh Buddha is named Wisdom Eloquent; in his land are twelve thousand bodhisattvas, all to be born in the land of Amitābha, in those other lands. The twelfth Buddha is named Supreme Flower; in his land are bodhisattvas countless and beyond reckoning, all of the stage of non-retrogression, all wise and valiant, each having made offerings to countless Buddhas, and all with one heart all at once wishing to be born — all to be born in the land of Amitābha, in those other lands. The thirteenth Buddha is named Great Wondrous Sound; in his land are seventy-nine koṭis of bodhisattvas, all to be born in the land of Amitābha.”

The Buddha said: “These bodhisattvas are all of the stage of non-retrogression; as for the multitude of monks and the countless lesser bodhisattvas among them, they shall all be born in the land of Amitābha. It is not that the bodhisattvas only of these fourteen Buddha-lands shall be born there — throughout the eight quarters, above and below, in the countless Buddha-lands, bodhisattvas each and all are likewise to be born. The multitudes of the land of Amitābha, gathering from all directions, are so many they cannot be reckoned. Were I but to tell the names of the countless Buddhas of the eight quarters, above and below, a whole kalpa of days and nights would not suffice. Were I but to tell the number of monks and assembled bodhisattvas who are to be born in the land of Amitābha, a kalpa of unceasing speech would not exhaust it; I have only gathered it together and told you a little.”

The Buddha said to Ānanda and to Bodhisattva Ajita and the rest: “Worldly kings and common people, good men and good women, it is by the merit of wholesome deeds done in former lives that they come to hear the name of Amitābha, and with kind hearts rejoice — I rejoice for them.”

The Buddha said: “If there are good men and good women who hear the name of Amitābha and with kind hearts rejoice, leaping up at once, with minds pure and clear, whose hair stands on end as if drawn out — all these practiced the Buddha-way in former lives. If they are from other regions and other Buddhas, as bodhisattvas they are not ordinary beings. And if there are people, men or women, who hear the name of Amitābha and do not believe there is such a Buddha, do not believe the words of the Buddha’s scriptures, do not believe in the order of monks, who harbor doubt in their hearts and put trust in nothing — all these have come from evil paths in the past; born dull and uncomprehending, they do not know their former lives, and their evils are not yet spent. For this reason they have not yet found release, and their hearts are full of doubt and disbelief.”

The Buddha said: “I speak to you, and whatever wholesome Dharma you should practice, you shall practice it fully, with faith; do not because of my parinirvāṇa think otherwise. You, and the people of future ages, must not again say: ‘I do not believe there is a land of Amitābha.’ I have therefore caused you all to see the land of Amitābha. What is to be done, seek it for yourselves; I have set out for you the scriptures, precepts, and the Dharma that accords — hold to it as one holds to the Buddha’s Dharma, and do not let it be lost. I entrust this scripture to you; you shall hold it firmly and not vainly add to or diminish this Dharma of the scriptures. When I have entered parinirvāṇa, this Dharma shall remain in the world a thousand years. A thousand years thereafter, the Dharma-path shall be cut off; yet whatever is wished in the heart may still attain the way.”

The Buddha said: “The teacher opens the eyes and ears of people, makes understanding bright and clear, delivers beings and leads them to what is good, and to the way of nirvāṇa. Always be filial and kind; revere the Buddha as one honors father and mother; always remember the teacher’s kindness, and let that remembrance never be cut off — then the way is quickly attained.”

The Buddha said: “It is very hard for a Buddha to appear in the world; and it is equally hard for a person to believe with trust the deep words of the teacher and the Dharma. If there is a monk, a teacher, who preaches the Buddha’s scriptures to people, this too is very hard to meet with.”

When the Buddha had spoken this scripture, twelve thousand koṭis of devas and humans all obtained the pure heavenly eye that sees all things, and all turned with one heart to the bodhisattva-way. Then twenty-two koṭis of devas and humans all attained the stage of the non-returner. Then eight hundred monks all attained the stage of the arhat. Then forty koṭis of bodhisattvas all attained the stage of non-retrogression.

When the Buddha had finished speaking, all the bodhisattvas, the arhats, and the devas, kings, and common people rejoiced greatly, came forward, bowed to the Buddha, circumambulated him three times, and, touching his feet with their heads, departed.

blocks.text: The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on Amitābha, the Samyaksaṃbuddha of the Tathāgata, Who Ferries Beings Across in the Human Realm

inline.s: Translated by the lay disciple Zhi Qian of the Yue-zhī (Kushan) state in the Wu dynasty.

[Amituofo] Amita — rendered in Chinese as “Immeasurable.” [Sanya sanfo salou fotan] the venerable titles of the Tathāgata. [Crossing over in the human realm] to save and to ferry across; the human realm is one of the six realms (devas, humans, asuras, animals, hungry ghosts, hells), that is, what is commonly called the world of humans. The meaning of “The Sūtra on Amitābha, the Samyaksaṃbuddha of the Tathāgata, Who Ferries Beings Across in the Human Realm” is: the scripture by which the Tathāgata Amitābha ferries across the beings of the human realm.

blocks.text: The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on Amitābha, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, Who Ferries Beings Across in the Human Realm — Scroll One

inline.s: The Buddha dwelt on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa near Rājagṛha. At that time there was a great assembly of twelve thousand monks, all pure and of one kind, all arhats: the Elder Kauṇḍinya, the Elder Padma-vajra, the Elder Mahānāman, the Elder Hasī, the Elder Supūrṇa, the Elder Vimaladī, the Elder Nanda, the Elder Kāśyapa of the fire, the Elder Uruvilvā Kāśyapa, the Elder Nadī Kāśyapa, the Elder Gayā Kāśyapa, the Elder Śāriputra, the Elder Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the Elder Mahākāśyapa, the Elder Mahākātyāyana, the Elder Mahāgaja, the Elder Mahākauṣṭhila, the Elder Mahābhāṇḍa, the Elder Piṇḍapāda, the Elder Aniruddha, the Elder Nandika, the Elder
wa

Pindī, the Elder Xu-feng, the Elder Liyue, the Elder Mahārohiṇa, the Elder Mahāpārayāna, the Elder Pākulala, the Elder Nandas, the Elder Pūrṇa-kula, the Elder Ājita, the Elder Liyue. Thus the assembly of monks was vast beyond measure — many thousands of koṭis.
There were also countless bodhisattvas and arhats, beyond all reckoning, all gathered together in the same assembly — all of them sages.

At that time the Buddha, seated in repose, was pondering the true way. His face shone with a nine-colored radiance, with hundreds and thousands of changing lights, a light surpassing great brightness.

Ānanda then rose, took up his robe, and came forward to touch the Buddha’s feet with his head. Kneeling and pressing his palms together, he asked the Buddha: “The color of the Buddha’s face today — why does it change so from time to time, and glow thus? Now the Buddha’s face is lit with hundreds and thousands of colors, so clear and fine, above and below. Since I have attended the Buddha, I have never seen his face so radiant as today; I have never seen the samyaksaṃbuddha with such luminous authority as this. There must be some intent — I wish to hear it.”
The Buddha said: “Elder Ānanda, is it the devas who have instructed you, or the Buddhas, that you ask me this? Or do you ask the Buddha of your own kind intent?”

Ānanda replied to the Buddha: “No deva has instructed me, nor has any Buddha instructed me to ask. I have of myself, from a kind heart, known the Buddha’s mind and ask him this. Whenever the Buddha sits or rises, comes or goes, enters or departs, whatever he means to do, whatever he commands — I follow the Buddha’s intention. Today the Buddha of himself must be thinking of the Buddhas of the past and of the Buddhas yet to come; or of the Buddha-lands of other regions and the Buddhas now present. It is because the Buddha turns these thoughts over and over that his face shines with this light.”

The Buddha said: “Excellent, excellent. Elder Ānanda, what you have asked is deep and of great joy, and delivers many beings. For asking the Buddha this, it surpasses the offering made to the arhats and pratyekabuddhas of all the world, and the giving to devas, to humans, and to the winged and crawling creatures, by a hundred thousand koṭis of times through many kalpas.”
The Buddha said: “Ānanda, now all the devas and worlds, kings and people, and the winged and crawling creatures — you have delivered them all.”

The Buddha said: “The authority of the Buddha is weighty and hard to bear. What you have asked is deep. You have shown a kind heart toward the Buddha, and pity for the devas, kings, and people — for monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen. This is a great good, and it delivers them all.”

The Buddha said to Ānanda: “Just as in the world there is the udumbara tree, which bears fruit but no flower — when a Buddha appears in the world, then the flower comes forth. It is very hard to meet with a Buddha in the world. Now that I am come into the world to become a Buddha, if a person has great virtue, a clear and bright and kind heart, and knows beforehand the Buddha’s intent, and is not one who idly waits at the Buddha’s side to serve him —”

The Buddha told Ānanda: “Concerning the events of the past, from the time of the great saṃgha onward, the kalpas were countless and beyond reckoning. And so it was, in that age, that there was a Buddha of the past named Dipaṃkara. There came, in turn, a Buddha named Candaka, already past. In turn a Buddha named Suma-kusala-kalpa, already past. In turn a Buddha named Vimala, already past. In turn a Buddha named Ananada, already past. In turn a Buddha named Nāgapī, already past. In turn a Buddha named Ālī, already past. In turn a Buddha named Roṇa-jit, already past. In turn a Buddha named Mililoka, already past. In turn a Buddha named Mathani, already past. In turn a Buddha named Udīpana, already past. In turn a Buddha named Phaladhī, already past. In turn a Buddha named Dūra-laukika, already past. In turn a Buddha named Candra-veśa, already past. In turn a Buddha named Suya-veṣa, already past. In turn a Buddha named Kṣāstrapiṇḍa, already past. In turn a Buddha named Ugrakṣa, already past. In turn a Buddha named Mahānandin, already past. In turn a Buddha named Vicitra-mati, already past. In turn a Buddha named Rājaśri, already past. In turn a Buddha named Yālava, already past. In turn a Buddha named Mañjukukṣa, already past. In turn a Buddha named Pūrṇa-kuṇḍala

, already past. In turn a Buddha named Candana-sūrya-bhāsa, already past. In turn a Buddha named Candana-cāru-kuṇḍa, already past. In turn a Buddha named Prana-da-pīni, already past. In turn a Buddha named Pradhāna-vaśa, already past. In turn a Buddha named Accharā-āyudha, already past. In turn a Buddha named Māyādhīti, already past. In turn a Buddha named Sītavāta, already past. In turn a Buddha named Dharmodgata, already past. In turn a Buddha named Śrīvāsa
, already past. In turn a Buddha named Rūpa-dhāra, already past. In turn a Buddha named Saṃgha-rāja-miloka, already past. In turn a Buddha named Dharmāmṛta-mati-avi-nandi, already past.”

The Buddha told Ānanda: “In turn there was a Buddha named Lokeśvararāja, who taught in the world for forty-two kalpas. And so it was that in that age there was a great king of a great country. When the king heard the Buddha’s scriptures and the way, his heart rejoiced and opened at once. He abandoned his kingdom and his kingship to become a recluse monk, named Dharmākara, and walked the bodhisattva-way. He was of lofty talent, wise and valiant, utterly different from ordinary beings.

He came before the Buddha Lokeśvararāja and bowed, then knelt and pressed his palms together, saying to the Buddha: “I seek Buddhahood, and the bodhisattva-way. When I come to be a Buddha, may I be, in the eight quarters above and below, among the countless Buddhas, the most honored, wise, and valiant. May the radiance of my head-light shine like the Buddha’s light, extending without limit. May the land I dwell in be naturally the seven treasures, and exceedingly soft and good. When I become a Buddha, may my name be heard throughout the eight quarters above and below, in the countless Buddha-lands; may there be none who has not heard my name. May all the countless devas and humans, and the winged and crawling creatures, who come to be born in my land, all be made bodhisattvas; may the arhats be countless, surpassing all Buddha-lands. If it be thus, is it attainable or not?”

The Buddha said to Ānanda: “The Buddha Lokeśvararāja knew his lofty brilliance and the excellence of the vow he sought, and spoke for the bodhisattva Dharmākara this scripture: ‘Consider the great ocean — a single man measures it with a bushel, without ceasing for a kalpa, and still he might exhaust it until it was dry and its bottom mud appeared. When a person seeks the way with an intent heart, how can he not attain it? Seeking with diligence and never resting, he will surely attain what his heart has wished.’ And so Dharmākara the bodhisattva, hearing the Buddha Lokeśvararāja speak the scripture thus, rejoiced greatly and leapt up. The Buddha then chose from the two hundred and ten koṭis of Buddhas’ lands the good and evil of devas and humans in them, and the beauty and the ugliness of those lands, to make the selection his own heart wished for.”

When the Buddha Lokeśvararāja had finished speaking the scripture, Dharmākara then set his heart to one point and obtained the pure heavenly eye that sees all, and beheld in the two hundred and ten koṭis of Buddha-lands the good and evil of the devas and humans, and the beauty and ugliness of the lands, and chose what his heart wished. Then he bound himself into this scripture of twenty-four vows and set about to practice it, valiantly and diligently, earnestly pursuing his quest. And so through countless kalpas he served and made offerings to the Buddhas of the past, who were themselves beyond number. This bodhisattva Dharmākara, having at last, by his own power, become a Buddha, was named Amitābha. Most honored, wise and valiant, his radiance matchless. The land he now dwells in is surpassing good; and in the other lands of other regions he teaches throughout the eight quarters above and below; the countless devas and humans, and the winged and crawling creatures, none but find release from sorrow and deliverance.”

The Buddha said to Ānanda: “When Amitābha was a bodhisattva, he constantly practiced these twenty-four vows. He held them as precious treasure, keeping them with reverence and care, and cultivated the meditations that follow from them; he stood far above the host, extraordinary and singular, so that no one could match him.”
The Buddha said: “What are the twenty-four vows?

“The first vow — that when I come to be a Buddha, in my land let there be none of the hells, none of the animals, none of the hungry ghosts, no flying or crawling creatures. If I attain this vow, then shall I be a Buddha; if I do not attain it, never shall I be a Buddha.”

“The second vow — that when I come to be a Buddha, in my land let there be no women. Whoever of women wishes to be born in my land is at once born a man. All the countless devas and humans, and the winged and crawling creatures, born in my land are transformed and born within the lotus flowers of the seven-treasure pools, and growing up, become bodhisattvas and arhats, all countless. If I attain this vow, then shall I be a Buddha; if not, never.”

“The third vow — that when I come to be a Buddha, my land is by nature the seven treasures, vast and wide, boundless and exceedingly soft and good; the dwellings, the clothes, the food and drink there are all spontaneous, all as in the dwelling of the sixth heaven king. If I attain this vow, then shall I be a Buddha; if not, never.”

“The fourth vow — that when I come to be a Buddha, my name shall be heard throughout the eight quarters above and below in the countless Buddha-lands; and all the Buddhas shall, each in the great assembly of monks, tell of the merit and the excellence of my land. The devas and humans, and the winged and crawling creatures, who hear my name, none but turn toward it with kind hearts and leap for joy — let them all come to be born in my land. If I attain this vow, then shall I be a Buddha; if not, never.”

“The fifth vow — that when I come to be a Buddha, throughout the eight quarters above and below, the countless devas and humans, and the winged and crawling creatures, who in former lives did evil, hearing my name and wishing to be born in my land, shall at once turn back and repent of themselves, practice the way and do good, hold the scriptures and precepts, and keep the wish to be born in my land unbroken. When they come to die, let them none of them again fall into the hells, the animals, or the hungry ghosts, but be born at once in my land, to what their heart desires. If I attain this vow, then shall I be a Buddha; if not, never.”

“The sixth vow — that when I come to be a Buddha, throughout the eight quarters above and below, in the countless Buddha-lands, the devas and humans, if there are good men and good women who wish to be born in my land, let them for my sake do good all the more, whether they give alms and offerings, or circumambulate the stūpas and burn incense and scatter flowers and light lamps, or hang many colored banners, or give food to monks, or raise stūpas and build temples, and cut off love and desire — let them come to be born in my land as bodhisattvas. If I attain this vow, then shall I be a Buddha; if not, never.”

“The seventh vow — that when I come to be a Buddha, throughout the eight quarters above and below, in the countless Buddha-lands, the devas and humans, if there are good men and good women who walk the bodhisattva-way and practice the scripture of the six pāramitās, or who become monks without destroying the scriptures and precepts, who cut off love and desire, keep the fasts and are pure, and with one heart yearn to be born in my land, day and night without break — when the measure of that person’s life is spent, I shall myself with the bodhisattvas and arhats fly to meet him, and he shall be born in my land, and become a bodhisattva of the stage of non-retrogression, wise and valiant. If I attain this vow, then shall I be a Buddha; if not, never.”

“The eighth vow — that when I come to be a Buddha, the bodhisattvas of my land who wish to be born in the Buddha-lands of other regions, let them never again fall into the hells, the animals, or the hungry ghosts; let them all attain Buddhahood. If I attain this vow, then shall I be a Buddha; if not, never.”

“The ninth vow — that when I come to be a Buddha, the bodhisattvas and arhats of my land shall all have features upright and noble, pure and fine, all of one color, all of one kind, all as the devas of the sixth heaven. If I attain this vow, then shall I be a Buddha; if not, never.”

“The tenth vow — that when I come to be a Buddha, the bodhisattvas and arhats of my land shall all be of one heart, so that what one thinks and wishes and would say the other knows beforehand. If I attain this vow, then shall I be a Buddha; if not, never.”

“The eleventh vow — that when I come to be a Buddha, the bodhisattvas and arhats of my land shall none of them have lustful hearts, never shall they think of women, and never shall they be given to anger or folly. If I attain this vow, then shall I be a Buddha; if not, never.”

“The twelfth vow — that when I come to be a Buddha, the bodhisattvas and arhats of my land shall all revere and love one another, and never envy or hate. If I attain this vow, then shall I be a Buddha; if not, never.”

“The thirteenth vow — that when I come to be a Buddha, the bodhisattvas of my land, wishing to make offerings together to the countless Buddhas of the eight quarters above and below, shall all fly, and arriving at once, whatever of the ten thousand kinds of things they desire, shall find it present before them; and after making offerings to all the Buddhas, before the sun reaches the middle of the day, they shall fly back to my land. If I attain this vow, then shall I be a Buddha; if not, never.”

“The fourteenth vow — that when I come to be a Buddha, the bodhisattvas and arhats of my land, when they wish to eat, shall find naturally in the seven-treasure bowls a hundred flavors of food set before them; and when they have eaten, it passes away of itself. If I attain this vow, then shall I be a Buddha; if not, never.”

“The fifteenth vow — that when I come to be a Buddha, the bodies of the bodhisattvas of my land shall all be of the color of refined gold, with the thirty-two marks and the eighty lesser marks, all as the Buddha. If I attain this vow, then shall I be a Buddha; if not, never.”

“The sixteenth vow — that when I come to be a Buddha, the bodhisattvas and arhats of my land, when they speak, shall sound like three hundred bells, and when they preach the scriptures and walk the way, all as the Buddha. If I attain this vow, then shall I be a Buddha; if not, never.”

“The seventeenth vow — that when I come to be a Buddha, may my seeing pierce through and my hearing pass all bounds, and my flying be tenfold that of all the Buddhas. If I attain this vow, then shall I be a Buddha; if not, never.”

“The eighteenth vow — that when I come to be a Buddha, may my wisdom in preaching the scriptures and walking the way be tenfold that of all the Buddhas. If I attain this vow, then shall I be a Buddha; if not, never.”

“The nineteenth vow — that when I come to be a Buddha, throughout the eight quarters above and below, the countless devas, humans, and the winged and crawling creatures, let them all attain the human realm, and all become pratyekabuddhas and arhats; let them all sit in meditation with one heart and together try to reckon my age, how many thousands, tens of thousands of koṭis of kalpas — let them all be unable to find the end of my life. If I attain this vow, then shall I be a Buddha; if not, never.”

“The twentieth vow — that when I come to be a Buddha, throughout the eight quarters above and below, in each of a thousand koṭis of Buddha-lands, the devas, humans, and the winged and crawling creatures, let them all become pratyekabuddhas and arhats, and sit in meditation with one heart and together try to reckon the bodhisattvas and arhats of my land, knowing them to be so many thousands of koṭis — let them all be unable to know the number. If I attain this vow, then shall I be a Buddha; if not, never.”
“The twenty-first vow — that when I come to be a Buddha, the bodhisattvas and arhats of my land shall have a life of countless kalpas. If I attain this vow, then shall I be a Buddha; if not, never.”

“The twenty-second vow — that when I come to be a Buddha, the bodhisattvas and arhats of my land shall all be wise and valiant, knowing of themselves the deeds of former lives through hundreds of thousands of koṭis of kalpas, discerning what was good and evil, and, without limit, seeing through all things with the clear eye and knowing the affairs of the past, the future, and the present in the ten directions. If I attain this vow, then shall I be a Buddha; if not, never.”

“The twenty-third vow — that when I come to be a Buddha, the bodhisattvas and arhats of my land shall all be wise and valiant, and on the crown of their heads shall have radiance. If I attain this vow, then shall I be a Buddha; if not, never.”

“The twenty-fourth vow — that when I come to be a Buddha, may the radiance on the crown of my head be surpassing fine, exceeding the brightness of the sun and the moon a hundred thousand koṭis of times, and surpassing all the Buddhas. Let my light shine forth on all the countless worlds, and all the places of darkness be made bright. The devas, humans, and the winged and crawling creatures who see my light, none but are moved to kind hearts and do good — let them all come to be born in my land. If I attain this vow, then shall I be a Buddha; if not, never.”

The Buddha told Ānanda: “When Amitābha was a bodhisattva, he constantly practiced these twenty-four vows: giving alms and offerings, never violating the precepts of the way, patient and diligent, of one mind and wisdom, his vow ever valiant, never destroying the scriptures of the Dharma, seeking without rest. Alone he cast off his kingdom and his kingship, renouncing wealth and passion; with pure intent he sought the vow, without partiality. He accumulated merit and virtue through countless kalpas, and now of himself has attained Buddhahood, and has gained all of it, without losing the fruit of his work.”

The Buddha said: “The light of Amitābha is the most honored, first and without peer. The lights of all the Buddhas cannot reach it. Among the countless Buddhas of the eight quarters above and below — there is a Buddha whose headlight shines seven zhangs; a Buddha whose headlight shines one li; a Buddha whose headlight shines two li; a Buddha whose headlight shines five li; a Buddha whose headlight shines ten li; a Buddha whose headlight shines twenty li; a Buddha whose headlight shines forty li; a Buddha whose headlight shines eighty li; a Buddha whose headlight shines one hundred and sixty li; a Buddha whose headlight shines three hundred and twenty li; a Buddha whose headlight shines six hundred and forty li; a Buddha whose headlight shines thirteen hundred li; a Buddha whose headlight shines twenty-six hundred li; a Buddha whose headlight shines fifty-two hundred li; a Buddha whose headlight shines ten thousand four hundred li; a Buddha whose headlight shines twenty-one thousand li; a Buddha whose headlight shines forty-two thousand li; a Buddha whose headlight shines eighty-four thousand li; a Buddha whose headlight shines one hundred seventy thousand li; a Buddha whose headlight shines three hundred fifty thousand li; a Buddha whose headlight shines seven hundred thousand li; a Buddha whose headlight shines fifteen hundred thousand li; a Buddha whose headlight shines three million li; a Buddha whose headlight shines six million li; a Buddha whose headlight shines one Buddha-land; a Buddha whose headlight shines two Buddha-lands; a Buddha whose headlight shines four Buddha-lands; a Buddha whose headlight shines eight Buddha-lands; a Buddha whose headlight shines fifteen Buddha-lands; a Buddha whose headlight shines thirty Buddha-lands; a Buddha whose headlight shines sixty Buddha-lands; a Buddha whose headlight shines one hundred and twenty Buddha-lands; a Buddha whose headlight shines two hundred and forty Buddha-lands; a Buddha whose headlight shines five hundred Buddha-lands; a Buddha whose headlight shines a thousand Buddha-lands; a Buddha whose headlight shines two thousand Buddha-lands; a Buddha whose headlight shines four thousand Buddha-lands; a Buddha whose headlight shines eight thousand Buddha-lands; a Buddha whose headlight shines sixteen thousand Buddha-lands; a Buddha whose headlight shines thirty-two thousand Buddha-lands; a Buddha whose headlight shines sixty-four thousand Buddha-lands; a Buddha whose headlight shines one hundred thirty thousand Buddha-lands; a Buddha whose headlight shines two hundred sixty thousand Buddha-lands; a Buddha whose headlight shines five hundred thousand Buddha-lands; a Buddha whose headlight shines a million Buddha-lands; a Buddha whose headlight shines two million Buddha-lands.”

The Buddha said: “The lights radiating from the crowns of the countless Buddhas of the eight quarters above and below are all as I have told. The light shining from the crown of Amitābha reaches ten million Buddha-lands. Why is it that the lights of the Buddhas shine near and far, differently? In former lives, when they sought the way, they were bodhisattvas, and the merit they vowed, each was greater or lesser; when they at last became Buddhas, each received it as it was. Therefore it is that the lights turn out not all alike — the authority of all Buddhas is equal, but each wills and does what he does not reckon beforehand. The light of Amitābha shines the farthest; the lights of all the Buddhas cannot reach it.”

The Buddha praised Amitābha, saying his light is supremely good. The light of Amitābha is supremely good, bright and beautiful among the good, surpassing and without compare, extraordinary and without limit. The light of Amitābha is pure, without stain or flaw, without diminishment. The light of Amitābha is beautiful and fine, surpassing the brightness of the sun and moon a hundred thousand koṭis of times. It is the brightest of all Buddha-lights, the best of all lights, the most brilliant of all lights, the most excellent of all lights, the king of all Buddhas, the most honored of all lights, the brightest of all, without limit. Its radiance shines upon all countless worlds, and the places of darkness are made ever bright. All the people, and the winged and crawling creatures, see the light of Amitābha. Whoever sees it is moved to kind hearts and rejoices. All in the world who are given to lust, anger, and folly, who see the light of Amitābha, do good. Those in the hells, among the animals and hungry ghosts, in the places of torment and bitter toil, when the light of Amitābha reaches them, the torments cease and are no more inflicted; and after death none fails to find release from sorrow. The name of the light of Amitābha is heard throughout the eight quarters above and below, endless and without limit, in the countless Buddha-lands; the devas and humans, none but have heard it, and hearing it, none but are delivered.”

The Buddha said: “It is not I alone who praise the light of Amitābha; the countless Buddhas of the eight quarters above and below, the pratyekabuddhas, the bodhisattvas, and the arhats, all praise it as I have done.”

The Buddha said: “If there are people, good men and good women, who hear the name of Amitābha and praise his light, morning and evening, always praising the goodness of that light, with an intent heart and never ceasing, and who wish in their hearts to be born in the land of Amitābha, they may be honored by the host of bodhisattvas and arhats. And if they in turn become Buddhas, they too shall be praised for their light by the countless Buddhas of the eight quarters above and below, by the pratyekabuddhas, the bodhisattvas, and the arhats, even so. Thereupon the assembly of monks, the bodhisattvas and arhats, and the devas, kings, and people, hearing this, all rejoiced and leapt up, and none failed to praise.”

The Buddha said: “Were I to tell of the light of Amitābha — its beauty, its loftiness, and its praise as supremely good — a whole kalpa of days and nights would not yet be done; I have only told you a little.”

The Buddha told how Amitābha, as a bodhisattva, sought and attained these twenty-four vows. At that time the crown prince Ajātaśatru, with five hundred sons of elders and noble householders, each bearing a golden flower canopy, came together to the place of the Buddha, and bowing before the Buddha, touched his feet with their heads, each offered his golden flower canopy, and all sat to one side to hear the scripture. The crown prince Ajātaśatru and the five hundred sons of elders, hearing the twenty-four vows of Amitābha, all rejoiced greatly and leapt up, and in their hearts all wished aloud: “May we, when we come to be Buddhas, be even as Amitābha.”
The Buddha knew this, and told the assembly of monks: “The crown prince Ajātaśatru and the five hundred sons of elders, in a time beyond counting kalpas, shall all become Buddhas as Amitābha is.”

The Buddha said: “The crown prince Ajātaśatru and the five hundred sons of elders, since they entered the bodhisattva-way, have passed through countless kalpas, and have each made offerings to four hundred koṭis of Buddhas; now they come again to make offerings to me. The crown prince Ajātaśatru and the five hundred sons of elders, in the age of the Buddha Kāśyapa in a former life, were my disciples; now they gather again, and this is their meeting together.”
Then the assembly of monks, hearing the Buddha’s words, all leapt up, and none failed to rejoice on their behalf.

The Buddha said to Ānanda: “Since Amitābha became a Buddha, ten small kalpas have passed. The land in which he dwells is named Sumati; it lies directly in the west, beyond a thousand billion Buddha-lands of Mount Sumeru from this Jambudvipa. The ground of that land is naturally of the seven treasures. The first treasure is silver; the second, gold; the third, crystal; the fourth, lapis lazuli; the fifth, red coral; the sixth, amber; the seventh, giant clam. These are the seven treasures. All of them together make up the ground, vast and boundless beyond measure, each set within the others and passing into one another, each blazing with light and shining into the rest — exceedingly soft and fair, beautiful beyond compare. That ground of seven treasures, throughout the eight quarters above and below, is the essence and savor of all treasures, naturally gathered and born by transformation. Those treasures all equal the seven treasures of the sixth heaven.

In that land there is no Mount Sumeru. Its sun, moon, and stars, the first heaven of the Four Heavenly Kings, and the second heaven of Trayastrimsa, all dwell in the empty air. In that land there is no great ocean, nor any small sea, nor rivers and the waters of the Ganges, nor mountains and forests, streams and valleys, nor any place of darkness. The ground of seven treasures in that land is everywhere level and even; there are no hells, no beasts, no hungry ghosts, no winged or crawling creatures. There are no asuras, no nagas, no ghosts or spirits; there is never a time of rain from the sky, nor spring, summer, autumn, or winter, neither great cold nor great heat, but always harmonious, temperate, and evenly attempered — blissful and good beyond compare.

All things of ten thousand kinds come into being of themselves; food of a hundred flavors — when the mind wishes to obtain it, it is at once naturally before one, and what is not wanted at once naturally departs. It is like the things that come of themselves in the sixth heaven: freely, as one pleases, all according to one's thought. In that land all are bodhisattvas and arhats; there are no women, and their lives last countless kalpas. A woman who is reborn there is at once transformed into a man. There are only bodhisattvas and arhats beyond number, all of them with celestial sight and celestial hearing, all seeing one another from afar, gazing upon one another from afar, hearing one another's voices from afar. All are seekers of the way and doers of good, of one single kind; there are no beings of a different sort. Those bodhisattvas and arhats are all of upright face and form, pure and incomparably fair, all of one color; there is none among them crooked or ugly. The bodhisattvas and arhats are all keen and wise. All wear garments that come of themselves; the virtue they hold in mind and the words they wish to speak are all foreknown to one another in thought. They always speak of right matters; whatever they say is always the scriptures and the way, and they do not speak of the faults of others. The sound of their speech is like three hundred bells. All love and respect one another; there is none who envies or hates. All speak according to elder and younger, higher and lower, in due order. In righteousness and according to propriety they serve one another as elder brother serves, as younger brother serves. In benevolence they tread the path of righteousness, never acting or speaking rashly. Admonishing one another, they teach one another, and let none fall into contention. Receiving one another in turn, all are pure in heart. They covet nothing, and never harbor anger, lust, or folly. They have no crooked thoughts, no thoughts of women. All are wise and valiant, harmonious and joyful in heart, delighting in the scriptures and the way. They know of themselves the lives from which they came in former ages, through billions of kalpas — the good and evil of former destinies, of what has passed and what now is — knowing it without limit through what Amitābha Buddha has taught. The lecture halls and monasteries are likewise naturally of the seven treasures: gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, white jade, amber, and giant clam, each wrought together with the rest, exceedingly fair and bright, beautiful beyond compare. There is no maker of them, and none knows whence they come; there is none who brings them, and none knows where they go.

So weighty is the virtue of Amitābha Buddha's vows, and so good the deeds of those who dwell there. They discuss the meaning of the scriptures, expound the scriptures and walk the way. Assembled in the lecture halls, they are born by transformation. Those lecture halls and monasteries all have their seven-treasure towers, galleries, and railings. Again, gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, white jade, amber, and giant clam are made into strings of jewels. Again, white pearls, moon-bright pearls, and mani pearls are made into the netted canopies spread above them, and all of themselves give forth the five tones, fair beyond compare. The dwelling places of the bodhisattvas and arhats are likewise born by transformation from the seven treasures — gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, red coral, amber, giant clam, and agate — wrought together to form their dwellings. Each has its seven-treasure towers, galleries, and railings. Again, gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, white jade, amber, and giant clam are made into strings of jewels. Again, white pearls, moon-bright pearls, and mani pearls are made into netted canopies. Spread above them, each again of itself gives forth the five tones. In the lecture halls and monasteries of Amitābha Buddha, and in the dwelling places of the bodhisattvas and arhats, within and without, in every place, there are again natural flowing springs and bathing pools, all born together with the natural seven treasures — gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, amber, and giant clam — wrought together with one another. In a pool of pure gold, the sand at the bottom is silver. In a pool of pure silver, the sand at the bottom is gold. In a pool of pure crystal, the sand at the bottom is lapis lazuli. In a pool of pure lapis lazuli, the sand at the bottom is crystal. In a pool of pure red coral, the sand at the bottom is amber. In a pool of pure amber, the sand at the bottom is red coral. In a pool of pure giant clam, the sand at the bottom is agate. In a pool of pure agate, the sand at the bottom is giant clam. In a pool of pure white jade, the sand at the bottom is purple burnished gold. In a pool of pure purple burnished gold, the sand at the bottom is white jade. There are also pools made of two treasures together, whose bottom sand is gold and silver. There are also pools made of three treasures together, whose bottom sand is gold, silver, and crystal. There are also pools made of four treasures together, whose bottom sand is gold, silver, crystal, and lapis lazuli. There are pools made of five treasures together, whose bottom sand is gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, and red coral. There are pools made of six treasures together, whose bottom sand is gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, red coral, and amber. There are pools made of seven treasures together, whose bottom sand is gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, red coral, amber, and giant clam. Among the bathing pools, some are forty li long, some eighty li, some a hundred and sixty li, some three hundred and twenty li, some six hundred and forty li, some a thousand two hundred and eighty li, some two thousand five hundred and sixty li, some five thousand one hundred and twenty li, some ten thousand two hundred and forty li, some twenty thousand four hundred and eighty li; and these pools are equal in length and breadth. Such pools are the bathing places where the bodhisattvas and arhats always bathe.”

The Buddha said: “The bathing pool of Amitābha Buddha is forty-eight thousand li long and forty-eight thousand li broad. The pool is wrought altogether of the seven treasures, and the sand at its bottom is white pearl, moon-bright pearl, and mani pearl. The water in the bathing pools of Amitābha Buddha and of the bodhisattvas and arhats is all pure, fragrant, and clean. In the pools there are fragrant flowers: a hundred kinds of flowers all born of themselves, each kind of a different color, each color of a different fragrance. Every branch has a thousand petals, fragrant beyond compare; their fragrance cannot be told in words. Those flowers are not flowers of the world, nor yet flowers of the heavens. The fragrance of these flowers, throughout the eight quarters above and below, is the essence among the fragrances of all flowers, born of itself by transformation. The water in those pools flows onward, pouring one into another. That flowing water is neither slow nor swift, and all of it again gives forth the five tones.”

The Buddha said: “Throughout the eight quarters above and below, in countless Buddha-lands, the devas and humans and the winged and crawling creatures who are born in the land of Amitābha Buddha are all born by transformation in the lotus flowers of the pools of seven treasures. They at once grow up of themselves, and there is none to suckle them; all eat the food that comes of itself. Their bodies are neither the bodies of humans of the world nor the bodies of devas of the heavens. All have accumulated the virtue of a multitude of good deeds, and all receive a body of natural emptiness, a substance without limit, beautiful beyond compare.”
The Buddha said to Ānanda: “Suppose a poor beggar in the world were made to stand beside a king — would his face and form, his features and color, be like the king's?”

Ānanda said: “If a prince were to stand beside a king, his face and form would be very ugly and uncomely, not equal to the king's by a hundred thousand billion times. Why is this? The beggar is poor and utterly destitute; his food and drink are always vile. He has never known a time of good food, and since his food is vile he cannot eat his fill. What he eats barely sustains his life; his joints prop one another up, and he has nothing with which to support himself. He is always lacking, with no store laid by, hungry and cold, fearful and wretched. This is only because in a former life, as a man, he was foolish. Lacking wisdom, stingy and greedy, he would not show compassion. He would not do good, love widely, or give in charity, but wished only to gain without labor, hoarding food and drink, eating delicacies alone, not believing that giving in charity would later bring its recompense; and he did not believe that by doing good he would in a later life obtain its blessing. Covered in ignorance and stubborn, he did ever more evil. When his life ended thus, his goods were all gone, and having never shown kindness or virtue he had nothing to rely on. He fell into the evil paths, and suffered there accordingly. Only afterward did he win release and gain birth as a man. He was born lowly, made the child of a poor family. Barely in human shape, his appearance is very ugly. His clothing is worn and torn; alone and empty he stands, unable to cover his body — a beggar born to it. Hungry and cold, in want and bitterness, his face is gaunt and mean, not the color of a man. Because of what he himself did in former lives, he receives this retribution. He is shown to the multitude, and there is none to pity him. Cast out upon the market road, exposed and wasted, black and ugly and utterly vile, he is not the equal of a man.

Why then is the king alone among men honored and excellent? Because in a former life, when he was a man, he did good and faithfully received the scriptures and the way. He bestowed kindness and practiced virtue, loved widely and followed righteousness. Compassionate and kind, he delighted to give; he did not hoard food and drink but shared them with all. He kept back nothing and was never contentious. Having gained such good blessing, when his life ended his virtue followed him, and he did not pass again into the evil paths. Now born as a man, he is born into a royal house. Naturally honored and noble, he alone rules as king, governing and commanding the people, and is their hero and champion. His face is fair and white, his countenance mild and handsome. His body is upright, and all revere and serve him. Fine food and good clothing follow his heart and will. Whatever he desires is naturally before him, and there is no contention at all. Thus is he beautiful among men, free of care and happy, his face radiant and bright — and for this reason, and no other.”

The Buddha said to Ānanda: “Suppose it be so. Though the king is matchless in beauty among men, if he were made to stand beside a Cakravartin king, his face and form would be very ugly and uncomely, just as a beggar standing beside a king. The king's own face and form are not the equal of the Cakravartin king's fair color by a hundred thousand billion times. And as the Cakravartin king is matchless in beauty in the world, if he were made to stand beside the king of the second heaven, his face would be very ugly and uncomely, not the equal of Sakra's upright and beautiful countenance by a hundred thousand billion times. And as Sakra, lord of devas, if made to stand beside the king of the sixth heaven, his face would be very ugly and uncomely, not the equal of the sixth heaven's king's upright and beautiful countenance by a hundred thousand billion times. And as the king of the sixth heaven, if made to stand beside the bodhisattvas and arhats in the land of Amitābha Buddha, his face would be very ugly, not the equal of the upright and beautiful countenances of the bodhisattvas and arhats in the land of Amitābha Buddha by a hundred thousand billion times.”

The Buddha said: “The countenances of the bodhisattvas and arhats in the land of Amitābha Buddha are all upright, incomparably fair, next only to the way of nirvāṇa. In the lecture halls and monasteries of Amitābha Buddha and of the bodhisattvas and arhats, in the dwelling places where they abide, and above the bathing pools within and without, there are seven-treasure trees. Among them are trees of pure gold, pure silver, pure crystal, pure lapis lazuli, pure white jade, pure red coral, pure amber, and pure giant clam, each kind growing in its own separate row. There are also trees made of two treasures together. A silver tree has silver roots and golden stems, silver branches and golden leaves, silver flowers and golden fruit. A gold tree has golden roots and silver stems, golden branches and silver leaves, golden flowers and silver fruit. A crystal tree has crystal roots and lapis lazuli stems, crystal branches and lapis lazuli leaves, crystal flowers and lapis lazuli fruit. A lapis lazuli tree has lapis lazuli roots and crystal stems, lapis lazuli branches and crystal leaves, lapis lazuli flowers and crystal fruit. Thus two treasures together make one tree. There are also trees made of four treasures together. A crystal tree has crystal roots and lapis lazuli stems, golden branches and silver leaves, crystal flowers and lapis lazuli fruit. A lapis lazuli tree has lapis lazuli roots and crystal stems, golden branches and silver leaves, crystal flowers and lapis lazuli fruit. Thus the trees of four treasures are wrought together, each in its own separate row. There are also trees made of five treasures together. A silver tree has silver roots and golden stems, crystal branches and lapis lazuli leaves, silver flowers and golden fruit. A gold tree has golden roots and silver stems, crystal branches and lapis lazuli leaves, red coral flowers and silver fruit. A crystal tree has crystal roots and lapis lazuli stems, red coral branches and silver leaves, golden flowers and lapis lazuli fruit. A lapis lazuli tree has lapis lazuli roots and red coral stems, crystal branches and golden leaves, silver flowers and red coral fruit. A red coral tree has red coral roots and lapis lazuli stems, crystal branches and golden leaves, silver flowers and lapis lazuli fruit. Thus five treasures together make one tree, each in its own separate row. There are also trees made of six treasures together. A silver tree has silver roots and golden stems, crystal branches and lapis lazuli leaves, red coral flowers and amber fruit. A gold tree has golden roots and silver stems, crystal branches and lapis lazuli leaves, amber flowers and red coral fruit. A crystal tree has crystal roots and lapis lazuli stems, red coral branches and amber leaves, silver flowers and golden fruit. A lapis lazuli tree has lapis lazuli roots and red coral stems, amber branches and crystal leaves, golden flowers and silver fruit. Thus the trees of six treasures are wrought together, each in its own separate row. There are also trees made of seven treasures together. A silver tree has silver roots and golden stems, crystal branches and lapis lazuli leaves, red coral flowers and amber fruit. A gold tree has golden roots and crystal stems, lapis lazuli branches and red coral leaves, amber flowers and silver fruit. A crystal tree has crystal roots and lapis lazuli stems, red coral branches and amber leaves, giant clam flowers and white jade fruit. A red coral tree has red coral roots and amber stems, white jade branches and lapis lazuli leaves, giant clam flowers and moon-bright pearl fruit. An amber tree has amber roots and white jade stems, red coral branches and lapis lazuli leaves, crystal flowers and golden fruit. A white jade tree has white jade roots and giant clam stems, red coral branches and amber leaves, golden flowers and mani pearl fruit. Thus the trees of seven treasures are wrought together, each kind distinct, row matching row, stem matching stem, branch matching branch, leaf facing leaf, flower gazing upon flower, fruit answering fruit.”

The Buddha said: “In the lecture halls and monasteries of Amitābha Buddha, within and without, the seven treasures and the bathing pools encircle the edges. Above are all the seven-treasure trees, and there are the bodhisattvas and arhats. In the seven-treasure dwelling places, with seven-treasure bathing pools within and without, the seven-treasure trees around the pool edges stand in many hundreds of thousands of rows, all of them thus, each of itself giving forth the five tones — tones fair beyond compare.”

The Buddha said to Ānanda: “As a king in the world has a hundred kinds of instrumental music, it is not the equal of the music of a Cakravartin king by a hundred thousand billion times. As the Cakravartin king's ten thousand kinds of music are not the equal of a single tone of the music in the second heaven of Trayastrimsa by a hundred thousand billion times. As the ten thousand kinds of music in the heaven of Trayastrimsa are not the equal of a single tone in the sixth heaven by a hundred thousand billion times. As the ten thousand kinds of music in the sixth heaven are not the equal of a single tone of the seven-treasure trees in the land of Amitābha Buddha by a hundred thousand billion times.
