In the land of Amitābha Buddha there are also ten thousand kinds of music that come of themselves, delightful beyond measure. When Amitābha Buddha and the bodhisattvas and arhats wish to bathe, each may enter the pool of seven treasures and bathe. When the bodhisattvas and arhats wish the water to cover their feet, the water at once covers their feet. When they wish the water to reach their knees, the water at once reaches their knees. When they wish the water to reach their waists, the water at once reaches their waists. When they wish the water to reach their armpits, the water at once reaches their armpits. When they wish the water to reach their necks, the water at once reaches their necks. When they wish the water to pour over their bodies, the water at once pours over their bodies. When they wish the water to return to what it was, the water at once returns to what it was. Freely, as they please, according to what they delight in.”

The Buddha said: “When Amitābha and the bodhisattvas and arhats have all bathed, each sits upon a great lotus flower, and at once a natural swirling wind rises from the four quarters. That swirling wind is neither the wind of the world nor the wind of the heavens. Throughout the eight quarters above and below, it is the essence among all winds, naturally gathered together and born by transformation. It is neither cold nor hot, always harmonious, temperate, and evenly attempered, exceedingly cool and refreshing, fair beyond compare. It rises gently, neither slow nor swift, just right and well measured. It blows upon the seven-treasure trees, and all give forth the five tones. With the flowers of the seven-treasure trees it covers the whole land. They scatter upon the Buddha and upon the bodhisattvas and arhats, and as the flowers fall to the ground they lie four inches deep, exceedingly soft and fair beyond compare; and then the natural swirling wind blows the withered flowers, and they all naturally depart. Then again the natural swirling wind of the four quarters blows upon the seven-treasure trees, and the trees all again give forth the five tones, and the tree flowers all of themselves scatter upon the Buddha and upon the bodhisattvas and arhats. When the flowers have slightly withered and fallen to the ground, they at once naturally depart; and again the swirling wind of the four quarters rises and blows upon the seven-treasure trees. Thus it is four times over. Among the bodhisattvas and arhats, some wish only to hear the scriptures, some wish only to hear music, some wish only to smell the fragrance of flowers; and there are some who do not wish to hear the scriptures, some who do not wish to hear music, some who do not wish to smell the fragrance of flowers. Whatever they wish to hear, that alone they hear; what they do not wish to hear, that alone they do not hear. Freely, according to what they wish and delight in, their vows are not opposed; and when they have bathed, each goes his own way.

As they walk the way, there are those on the ground expounding the scriptures, reciting the scriptures, preaching the scriptures, receiving the scriptures by mouth, hearing the scriptures, recalling the scriptures, contemplating the way, sitting in meditation, and walking in meditation. There are those in the empty air expounding the scriptures, reciting the scriptures, preaching the scriptures, receiving the scriptures by mouth, hearing the scriptures, recalling the scriptures, contemplating the way, sitting in single-minded meditation, and walking in meditation. Those who had not attained the way of the stream-winner at once attain the way of the stream-winner. Those who had not attained the way of the once-returner at once attain the way of the once-returner. Those who had not attained the way of the non-returner at once attain the way of the non-returner. Those who had not attained the way of the arhat at once attain the way of the arhat. Those who had not attained the stage of non-retrogression at once attain non-retrogression. Each expounds the scriptures and walks the way. All attain the way, and there is none who does not rejoice and leap up.

Among the bodhisattvas there are those who wish to make offerings to the countless Buddhas throughout the eight quarters above and below. At once they all come forward, bow to the Buddha, take leave of the Buddha, and go to make offerings to the countless Buddhas throughout the eight quarters above and below. The Buddha at once consents. Then those bodhisattvas all rejoice greatly. Many thousands of hundreds of billions of people, countless and beyond reckoning, all wise and valiant, each in his own company flying in pursuit of one another, all together scatter and fly. They reach the places of the countless Buddhas throughout the eight quarters above and below. All come forward, bow to the Buddhas, and at once make offerings. When they wish to have ten thousand kinds of natural things, they are at once naturally before them: a hundred kinds of flowers of varied colors, a hundred kinds of variegated silk and brocade, a hundred kinds of kalpavrksa garments, seven-treasure lamps and torches, ten thousand kinds of music — all are before them. The fragrances of those flowers and the ten thousand kinds of natural things are neither things of the world nor things of the heavens; these ten thousand kinds of things are throughout the eight quarters above and below the essence of all that is natural, gathered and born by transformation. What they wish to have is at once born by transformation; what they do not use at once passes away. The bodhisattvas then hold these together and make offering to the Buddhas and to the bodhisattvas and arhats, on every side, before and behind, encircling them round about. Whatever they wish in mind at once all arrives. At that time the bliss cannot be told in words. When the bodhisattvas each wish to have flowers forty li across, they are at once naturally before them. Then in the empty air they hold them together and scatter them upon the Buddhas and upon the bodhisattvas and arhats. All come down from the empty air; the flowers are exceedingly fragrant and fair, and when they have slightly withered and fallen to the ground, the natural swirling wind at once blows the withered flowers, and they all naturally depart. When the bodhisattvas each again wish to have flowers eighty li across, they are at once naturally before them, and they hold them together and scatter them upon the Buddhas and upon the bodhisattvas and arhats. The flowers all again come down from the empty air, and when they have slightly withered and fallen to the ground, the natural swirling wind at once blows the withered flowers, and they all naturally depart. When the bodhisattvas each again wish to have flowers a hundred and sixty li across, they are at once naturally before them, and in the empty air they hold them together and scatter them upon the Buddhas and upon the bodhisattvas and arhats; the flowers all again come down from the empty air, and when they have slightly withered and fallen to the ground, the natural swirling wind at once blows the withered flowers, and they all naturally depart. When the bodhisattvas each again wish to have flowers three hundred and twenty li across, they are at once naturally before them. Again in the empty air they hold them and scatter them upon the Buddhas and upon the bodhisattvas and arhats. The flowers come down from the empty air, and when they have slightly withered and fallen to the ground, the natural swirling wind at once blows the withered flowers, and they all naturally depart. When the bodhisattvas each again wish to have flowers six hundred and forty li across, they are at once naturally before them. Again they scatter them upon the Buddhas and upon the bodhisattvas and arhats; all come down from the empty air, and when they have slightly withered and fallen to the ground, the swirling wind naturally blows the withered flowers away. When the bodhisattvas each again wish to have flowers a thousand two hundred and eighty li across, they are at once naturally before them. Again in the empty air they hold them together and scatter them upon the Buddhas and upon the bodhisattvas and arhats. All come down from the empty air, and when they have slightly withered and fallen to the ground, the swirling wind naturally blows, and the withered flowers all naturally depart. When the bodhisattvas each again wish to have flowers two thousand five hundred and sixty li across, they are at once naturally before them. Again in the empty air they hold them together and scatter them upon the Buddhas and upon the bodhisattvas and arhats. All come down from the empty air, and when they have slightly withered and fallen to the ground, the swirling wind blows the withered flowers, and they all naturally depart. When the bodhisattvas each again wish to have flowers five thousand one hundred and twenty li across, they are at once naturally before them. Again in the empty air they hold them together and scatter them upon the Buddhas and upon the bodhisattvas and arhats. All come down from the empty air, and when they have slightly withered and fallen to the ground, the swirling wind blows the withered flowers, and they all naturally depart. When the bodhisattvas each again wish to have flowers ten thousand two hundred and forty li across, they are all at once naturally before them. Again in the empty air they hold them together and scatter them upon the Buddhas and upon the bodhisattvas and arhats; when they have slightly withered and fallen to the ground, the swirling wind blows the withered flowers, and they all naturally depart. When the bodhisattvas each again wish to have flowers twenty thousand four hundred and eighty li across, they are all at once before them. Again in the empty air they hold them together and scatter them upon the Buddhas and upon the bodhisattvas and arhats. All come down from the empty air, and when they have slightly withered and fallen to the ground, the swirling wind blows the withered flowers, and they all naturally depart. When the bodhisattvas each again wish to have flowers fifty thousand li across, they are all at once before them. Again in the empty air they hold them together and scatter them upon the Buddhas and upon the bodhisattvas and arhats. All come down from the empty air, and when they have slightly withered and fallen to the ground, the swirling wind blows the withered flowers, and they all naturally depart. When the bodhisattvas each again wish to have flowers a hundred thousand li across, they are all at once before them. Again in the empty air the bodhisattvas hold them together and scatter them upon the Buddhas and upon the bodhisattvas and arhats. All come down from the empty air, and when they have slightly withered and fallen to the ground, the swirling wind blows the withered flowers, and they all naturally depart. When the bodhisattvas each again wish to have flowers two hundred thousand li across, they are all at once before them. Again in the empty air they hold them together and scatter them upon the Buddhas and upon the bodhisattvas and arhats; when they have slightly withered and fallen to the ground, the swirling wind blows the withered flowers, and they all naturally depart. When the bodhisattvas each again wish to have flowers four hundred thousand li across, they are all at once before them. Again in the empty air they hold them together and scatter them upon the Buddhas and upon the bodhisattvas and arhats. All come down from the empty air, and when they have slightly withered and fallen to the ground, the swirling wind blows the withered flowers, and they all naturally depart. When the bodhisattvas each again wish to have flowers eight hundred thousand li across, they are all at once before them. Again in the empty air they hold them together and scatter them upon the Buddhas and upon the bodhisattvas and arhats. All come down from the empty air, and when they have slightly withered and fallen to the ground, the swirling wind blows the withered flowers, and they all naturally depart. When the bodhisattvas each wish to have flowers one million six hundred thousand li across, they are all at once before them; they hold them together and scatter them upon the Buddhas and upon the bodhisattvas and arhats, and when they have slightly withered and fallen to the ground, the swirling wind blows the withered flowers, and they all naturally depart. When the bodhisattvas each wish to have flowers three million li across, they are all at once before them; they hold them together and scatter them upon the Buddhas and upon the bodhisattvas and arhats, and when they have slightly withered and fallen to the ground, the swirling wind blows the withered flowers, and they naturally depart. When the bodhisattvas each wish to have flowers six million li across, they are all at once before them; they hold them together and scatter them upon the Buddhas and upon the bodhisattvas and arhats, and the flowers all of themselves become one flower. The flower is upright, straight, and round, equal on every side, and flower upon flower doubles what went before. The flowers are exceedingly soft and fair, surpassing the former flowers by many thousands of hundreds of times. Color differs from color, and fragrance from fragrance beyond words. The bodhisattvas all rejoice greatly, and together in the empty air make a great chorus of sound, music that comes of itself. They delight the Buddhas and the bodhisattvas and arhats, and at that time the bliss cannot be told in words.

The bodhisattvas all withdraw and sit to hear the scriptures; when they have heard the scriptures they all recite them through and master them. They know the scriptures and the way anew, and their wisdom grows brighter. Then throughout those Buddha-lands, from the first heaven of the Four Heavenly Kings up to the heaven of the Thirty-three, the devas and humans all bring down ten thousand kinds of natural things from the heavens and make offering to the bodhisattvas and arhats. The devas and humans all again, in the empty air, make a great chorus of music. The devas and humans who came first withdraw to make way for those who come after. Those who come after again make offering as before, giving way to one another. The devas and humans joyfully hear the scriptures and make music together. At that time the bliss is beyond measure. When the bodhisattvas have finished making offering and hearing the scriptures, they all rise, bow to the Buddha, and depart. They at once fly again to the places of the countless Buddhas throughout the eight quarters above and below, to make offering and hear the scriptures. Each is as before, and when all is done everywhere, before the sun has reached midday each flies back to his own land. They bow to Amitābha Buddha, all withdraw and sit to hear the scriptures, and when it is done they rejoice greatly.”

The Buddha said: “When Amitābha Buddha and the bodhisattvas and arhats wish to eat, there are at once natural seven-treasure tables, and kalpavrksa woolen cloth is spread as seats. The Buddha and the bodhisattvas all sit before them, and all have natural seven treasures. In their bowls is food and drink of a hundred flavors, and that food and drink is like neither the world's nor the heavens'. This food and drink of a hundred flavors, throughout the eight quarters above and below, is the essence among all natural food and drink, exceedingly fragrant and fair beyond compare, born of itself by transformation. If they wish it sweet or sour, they have whatever they wish. Among the bodhisattvas and arhats, some wish for a golden bowl, some for a silver bowl, some for a crystal bowl, some for a red coral bowl, some for an amber bowl, some for a white jade bowl, some for a giant clam bowl, some for an agate bowl, some for a moon-bright pearl bowl, some for a mani pearl bowl, some for a purple burnished gold bowl — according to their wish it at once arrives. It comes from nowhere, and there is none who offers it; it is born of itself by transformation. The bodhisattvas and arhats all eat, and they eat neither much nor little, all equally. They do not speak of what is fine or vile, nor are they glad because it is fine. When the meal is done, the food, vessels, tables, and seats all naturally pass away by transformation. When they wish to eat again, these are again born by transformation. The bodhisattvas and arhats are all pure in heart. What they eat and drink serves only for strength; it all naturally disperses, dissolves, and passes away.”

The Buddha said to Ānanda: “When Amitābha Buddha expounds the scriptures for the bodhisattvas and arhats, they all assemble in the lecture hall. The bodhisattvas and arhats, with the devas and humans, countless and beyond reckoning, all fly to where Amitābha Buddha is, bow to the Buddha, and withdraw to sit and hear the scriptures. That Buddha broadly expounds the great scripture of the wisdom of the way, and all hear and know it; there is none who does not rejoice and leap up, whose heart does not open and understand. Then a natural swirling wind rises from the four quarters and blows upon the seven-treasure trees, and all give forth the five tones. The flowers of the seven-treasure trees cover that land. All come down from the empty air, and the fragrance of those flowers fills the whole land, scattering upon Amitābha Buddha and upon the bodhisattvas and arhats. The flowers fall to the ground four inches deep, and when they have slightly withered the swirling wind at once blows, and the withered flowers naturally depart. Four times the swirling wind of the four quarters blows upon the flowers of the seven-treasure trees. Then from the first heaven of the Four Heavenly Kings, from the second heaven of Trayastrimsa up to the heaven of the Thirty-three, the devas and humans all bring ten thousand kinds of natural things from the heavens: a hundred kinds of flowers of varied colors, a hundred kinds of varied incense, a hundred kinds of variegated silk and brocade, a hundred kinds of kalpavrksa cloth garments, and ten thousand kinds of music, each surpassing the last in excellence. Each brings them down, bows to Amitābha Buddha, and makes offering to the Buddha and to the bodhisattvas and arhats. The devas and humans all again make great music, delighting Amitābha Buddha and the bodhisattvas and arhats. At that time the bliss cannot be told in words. The devas again give way to one another for those who come after, and those who come after again make offering as before. Then from the countless Buddha-lands of the east, their number beyond reckoning — like the flowing sands of the Ganges, one grain of sand for each Buddha, such is their number — each of those Buddhas sends bodhisattvas, countless and beyond reckoning. All fly to where Amitābha Buddha is, bow, and hear the scriptures, all rejoicing greatly. All rise, bow, and depart in like manner. The Buddhas of the west, north, and south, and of the four corners, are each in number like the flowing sands of the Ganges. Each sends countless bodhisattvas, who fly to where Amitābha Buddha is, bow, and hear the scriptures, and likewise again. Then the Buddhas below and above are each in number like the flowing sands of the Ganges. All send bodhisattvas, beyond reckoning, who fly to where Amitābha Buddha is, bow, and hear the scriptures, giving way to one another. Thus it is, and never is there a time when it ceases.”

The Buddha said: “The reason the Buddhas are numbered by the flowing sands of the Ganges is that the countless Buddhas throughout the eight quarters above and below are so greatly numerous, each beyond reckoning, that they are numbered by the flowing sands of the Ganges.

The Buddha said to Ānanda: “When Amitābha Buddha has finished expounding the scriptures for the bodhisattvas and arhats, among the devas and humans there are those who had not attained the way, and they at once attain the way. Those who had not attained stream-winner at once attain stream-winner. Those who had not attained once-returner at once attain once-returner. Those who had not attained non-returner at once attain non-returner. Those who had not attained arhat at once attain arhat. Those who had not attained the stage of non-retrogression at once attain the stage of non-retrogression.

Amitābha Buddha, according to the vows and delights of their seeking hearts in their former destinies, great or small as they wish, expounds the scriptures and imparts them, and at once causes them to open and understand swiftly. All are bright and wise, each delighting in what he wishes; the scriptures and the way they desire — is there any who does not rejoice in them? Those who recite and practice them recite and master them fluently, never wearied, beyond measure. Among the bodhisattvas and arhats, some recite the scriptures, and their sound is like three hundred bells. Some expound the scriptures, like a swift wind and violent rain. Thus for a whole kalpa through, never is there a time of sloth or weariness. All are wise and valiant, their bodies light and nimble, never any pain or itch. At all times, walking, standing, sitting, or rising, all are able, strong, and valiant. Like the king among lions in the deep mountains, wherever he turns there is none who dares withstand him, and no thought of doubt or difficulty. What he does in his heart cannot be foreknown — by a hundred thousand billion times. And yet that fierce king among lions, by a hundred thousand billion times, is not the equal in valor of my second disciple Mahamaudgalyayana by a hundred thousand billion times. As Mahamaudgalyayana is matchless among the bodhisattvas and arhats of all those lands, flying and advancing or halting, wise and valiant, with celestial sight and celestial hearing, knowing the affairs of the eight quarters above and below, of past, future, and present, by a hundred thousand billion times — all that wisdom joined into one — if he were made to stand beside the arhats in the land of Amitābha Buddha, his virtue would still not equal theirs by a hundred thousand billion times.”

Bodhisattva Ajita then rose, came forward, knelt long, pressed his palms together, and asked the Buddha: “Among the arhats in the land of Amitābha Buddha, are there any who have passed into parinirvāṇa? I wish to hear it.”
The Buddha said: “If you wish to know, the stars of these four continents — do you see them?”
Bodhisattva Ajita said: “Yes, I see them.”

The Buddha said: “My second disciple Mahamaudgalyayana, flying up into the heavens for a single day and night, counts and knows every one of the stars. The stars of these four continents are so many that they cannot be reckoned, and yet that is a hundred thousand billion times more than the stars. If from the great ocean of the world a single drop were taken away, could it make the ocean water less, so that one knew it had diminished?”
He answered: “Take away a hundred thousand billion bushels and pecks, and still one could not know the ocean to have diminished.”

The Buddha said: “In the land of Amitābha Buddha, though there be arhats who have passed into parinirvāṇa, it is as when a single drop of water is taken from the great ocean: one cannot know the arhats to have diminished.”
The Buddha said: “If a single stream of water were taken from the great ocean, would it make the ocean less?”
He answered: “Take away a hundred thousand billion streams of water, and still one could not know it to have diminished.”
The Buddha said: “If a single Ganges were taken from the great ocean, could it make the ocean less?”
He answered: “Take away a hundred thousand billion Ganges, and still one could not know it to have diminished.”

The Buddha said: “Of the arhats in the land of Amitābha Buddha, those who have passed into parinirvāṇa are countless, and those who remain, newly attaining the way, are also countless; there is neither increase nor decrease at all.”
The Buddha said: “If all the waters of the world flowed together into the great ocean, could they make the ocean water increase?”
He answered: “They could not make it increase. Why is this? Because the great ocean is for all the waters of the world the king among all that is good, and so it is thus.”

The Buddha said: “The land of Amitābha Buddha is likewise. Though all the countless devas and humans and the winged and crawling creatures of the countless Buddha-lands throughout the eight quarters above and below go there to be born — greatly numerous, beyond reckoning — the bodhisattvas, arhats, and company of monks in the land of Amitābha Buddha remain as ever, one dharma, no different, in no way increased. Why is this? Because the land of Amitābha Buddha is the most blissful. Throughout the eight quarters above and below, in the countless Buddha-lands, it is the king among all that is good. It is the hero among Buddha-lands, the treasure among Buddha-lands; among Buddha-lands its life is the longest; it is the champion among Buddha-lands, the vastness among Buddha-lands, the capital among Buddha-lands — natural and unconditioned, most blissful, bright, and fair, a delight beyond measure. Why is this? Because when Amitābha Buddha was a bodhisattva, his vows were valiant, his striving unremitting, and this is what the piling up of virtue brought about. And so it is thus.”

Bodhisattva Ajita rejoiced greatly, knelt long, pressed his palms together, and said: “The Buddha has proclaimed the land of Amitābha Buddha — blissful, good, bright, and fair, most beautiful beyond compare — is it alone thus?”

The Buddha said: “In the land of Amitābha Buddha, among the seven-treasure dwelling places where the bodhisattvas and arhats abide, some are in the empty air and some on the ground. Some wish their dwelling to be the tallest, and their dwelling is at once tall. Some wish their dwelling to be the largest, and their dwelling is at once large. Some wish their dwelling to be in the empty air, and their dwelling is at once in the empty air — all naturally according to their thought, doing as they will. Some there are who cannot make their dwellings follow their wish. Why is this? Those who can make their dwellings follow their wish are all those who, when they sought the way in former lives and destinies, were compassionate in heart, strove diligently, and did ever more good, and this came of the weight of their virtue. Those who cannot are all those who, when they sought the way in former lives and destinies, were not compassionate in heart, did not strive diligently, and did not do ever more good, and this came of the thinness of their virtue. The clothing and food they receive is all alike, natural and equal. But their virtue is great or small, and so their valor is known apart, and this is shown to the multitude.”
The Buddha said: “Do you see the dwelling place of the king of the sixth heaven?”
Yes, I see it.”

The Buddha said: “The lecture halls and dwelling places in the land of Amitābha Buddha all surpass the dwelling place of the king of the sixth heaven by a hundred thousand billion times. The bodhisattvas and arhats all have celestial sight and celestial hearing, and see and know the affairs of the eight quarters above and below, of past, future, and present. And the minds and thoughts of numberless devas and humans above and below, and of the winged and crawling creatures — the good and evil they think, the words they wish to speak — they know in what year and in what kalpa each shall win deliverance and attain the human way, and be born in the land of Amitābha Buddha. They know who shall become bodhisattvas and arhats, and all this they foreknow. The crowns of the bodhisattvas and arhats all have light of their own. The extent of what they illumine differs; among the bodhisattvas there are two most honored, who always stand at the Buddha's right and left, seated in attendance upon the true teaching. The Buddha always sits face to face with these two bodhisattvas, deliberating the affairs of the eight quarters above and below, of past, future, and present. If he wishes to send these two bodhisattvas to the places of the countless Buddhas throughout the eight quarters above and below, they at once fly, going wherever they wish; their flight is as swift as the Buddha's, valiant beyond compare. One of these bodhisattvas is named Galevaja, and the other is named Mahasthamaprapta; in light and wisdom they are foremost. The light from their crowns blazes upon other quarters. In a thousand Buddha-lands of Mount Sumeru there is always great brightness. The light from the crowns of those bodhisattvas each illumines a thousand billion myriad li. The light from the crowns of the arhats each illumines seven zhang.”

The Buddha said: “If among the people of the world there be a good man or good woman who is in urgent fear or trouble with the authorities, let him but take refuge with these bodhisattvas Galevaja and Mahasthamaprapta, and there is none who shall not be freed.”

The Buddha said to Bodhisattva Ajita: “The light from the crown of Amitābha Buddha is a light of utmost greatness. The sun, moon, and stars all dwell in the empty air and can no longer turn and move; they have no brilliance, and their light is wholly hidden and seen no more. The Buddha's light illumines the whole land, and its blaze shines upon the Buddha-lands of other quarters, always greatly bright. Never is there a time of darkness. In that land there is no first day or second day, nor five days or ten days, nor a fifteenth day or a month, nor five months or ten months, five years or ten years, nor a hundred years or a thousand years, nor ten thousand years or a hundred million years, nor a hundred thousand million years; there is no one kalpa, ten kalpas, a hundred kalpas, a thousand kalpas, ten thousand kalpas, a million kalpas, ten million kalpas, or a hundred billion myriad kalpas. The light of Amitābha Buddha is bright beyond measure; after countless kalpas, and countless kalpas repeated upon countless kalpas, and countless kalpas beyond number, never shall there be a time of darkness. The land and all the heavens never decay. Why is this? Because the life of Amitābha Buddha is exceedingly long and the land exceedingly good, and so it is thus. The honored life of that Buddha — after countless kalpas, and countless kalpas repeated, he has not yet come to the end of parinirvāṇa. In the world he teaches, wishing to deliver the countless devas and humans and the winged and crawling creatures of the countless Buddha-lands throughout the eight quarters above and below, he wishes them all to be born in his land and all to attain the way of nirvāṇa. Those who become bodhisattvas he wishes all to become Buddhas. When they have become Buddhas, they in turn teach the devas and humans and the winged and crawling creatures throughout the eight quarters above and below, and wish them all in turn to become Buddhas. When they have become Buddhas, they in turn teach the countless devas and humans and the winged and crawling creatures, and cause them all to attain the way of nirvāṇa and depart. All who can be taught as disciples, in turn teach one another and deliver one another, until they attain the ways of stream-winner, once-returner, non-returner, arhat, and pratyekabuddha, delivering one another in turn. All attain the way of nirvāṇa, all thus. And he himself does not yet wish to enter parinirvāṇa; those delivered by Amitābha Buddha are thus in turn. He abides again through countless kalpas, through kalpas beyond reckoning, and never is there a time of parinirvāṇa. Throughout the eight quarters above and below, of the countless devas and humans and winged and crawling creatures born in the land of Amitābha Buddha, those who shall become Buddhas cannot be numbered; and those who become arhats and attain the way of nirvāṇa are also countless, wholly beyond reckoning.

The kindness and virtue of Amitābha Buddha, and all that he bestows, throughout the eight quarters above and below, are without end or limit, most deep and immeasurable, blissful and good beyond words. The scriptures and the way that issue from his wisdom and teaching are proclaimed throughout the countless heavens and earths of the eight quarters above and below, most inexhaustible. The number of his scripture scrolls is exceedingly great, beyond reckoning, wholly without limit.”
The Buddha said to Bodhisattva Ajita: “Do you wish to know the time of Amitābha Buddha's life without limit?”
He answered: “I wish to hear and know it.”

The Buddha said: “Listen well. Suppose all the devas and humans and winged and crawling creatures in the countless Buddha-lands throughout the eight quarters above and below were all brought to enter the way, all made pratyekabuddhas and arhats, all seated in single-minded meditation, their wisdom joined into one valor, and together they wished to reckon and know the life of Amitābha Buddha — how many thousands of billions of myriads of kalpas and years it is — none could reckon or know it. And suppose again in each of a thousand Buddha-lands of Mount Sumeru in the other quarters, all the devas and humans and winged and crawling creatures were all brought to enter the way, all made pratyekabuddhas and arhats, all made to sit in single-minded meditation, their wisdom joined into one valor, and together they wished to count the bodhisattvas and arhats in the land of Amitābha Buddha, to know how many thousands of billions of myriads there are — none could know the number. The years and life of Amitābha are exceedingly long, vast and luminous, his bright goodness most deep, without limit or bottom. Who could know it and believe in it? Only the Buddha himself believes and knows it.”

Bodhisattva Ajita, hearing the Buddha's words, rejoiced greatly, knelt long, pressed his palms together, and said: “The Buddha has proclaimed that the life of Amitābha Buddha is exceedingly long, his awesome spirit honored and great, his wisdom and light towering, blissful and good — is it alone thus.”

The Buddha said: “When Amitābha Buddha at last enters parinirvāṇa, then Bodhisattva Galevaja shall become a Buddha. He shall lead the wisdom of the way and preside over teaching. The devas and humans of the world and of the eight quarters above and below, and the winged and crawling creatures whom he delivers, shall all attain the Buddha's way of nirvāṇa. His goodness and merit shall again be as those of the great teacher Amitābha Buddha. He shall abide through countless kalpas, through kalpas beyond reckoning. Following the great teacher as his model, he shall then enter parinirvāṇa. After him, Bodhisattva Mahasthamaprapta shall in turn become a Buddha. He shall preside over wisdom and lead in teaching. The merit of what he delivers shall again be as that of the great teacher Amitābha Buddha. He shall abide through countless kalpas and shall still not enter parinirvāṇa. Handing on the scriptures and the way in turn, most clear; the land most good — thus is the dharma. Never shall there be an end to it. It cannot be exhausted.”

Ānanda knelt long, pressed his palms together, and asked the Buddha: “In the land of Amitābha Buddha there is no Mount Sumeru. On what then do the first heaven of the Four Heavenly Kings and the second heaven of Trayastrimsa rest and abide? I wish to hear it.”

The Buddha said to Ānanda: “Have you any doubt concerning the Buddha? Throughout the eight quarters above and below, without end or limit, boundless and immeasurable, if all the great ocean waters of the world were measured out by one man, bushel by bushel, they could yet be dried up and their bottom mud reached — can the Buddha's wisdom be other than this?”

The Buddha said: “What I see and know of all the Buddhas of the past who bore my name, Śākyamuni — they are again like the flowing sands of the Ganges, one grain of sand for each Buddha. The Buddhas to come who shall bear my name are likewise like the flowing sands of the Ganges. Those who are only now first seeking to become Buddhas and shall bear my name are likewise like the flowing sands of the Ganges. The Buddha sits facing directly south and sees the south. The Buddhas now present who bear my name are again like the flowing sands of the Ganges. The Buddhas of the eight quarters above and below, past, future, and present, who bear my name, are each like ten Ganges' flowing sands, one grain of sand for each Buddha — such is their number. The Buddha foreknows them all.”

The Buddha said: “From ages past, through numberless kalpas, in one kalpa, ten kalpas, a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, a hundred million, a hundred billion myriad kalpas, there are Buddhas. Of all the Buddhas past — one Buddha, ten, a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, a hundred million, a hundred billion myriad Buddhas — each has a different name, and there is none who bears my name. In the kalpas just now to come, in one kalpa, ten, a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, a hundred million, a hundred billion myriad kalpas, there are Buddhas: one, ten, a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, a hundred million, a hundred billion myriad Buddhas, each with a different name, and only now and then is there one Buddha who bears my name. Throughout the countless Buddha-lands of the eight quarters above and below, the Buddhas now present — in this other land and that, in one Buddha-land, ten, a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, a hundred million, a hundred billion myriad Buddha-lands there are Buddhas, each with his own name, many and all different; there is none who bears my name. Among the countless Buddhas of the eight quarters above and below, only now and then is there one who bears my name. Throughout the eight quarters above and below, past, future, and present, the space between them is vast and far, distant and remote, without end or limit; the Buddha's wisdom is broad and most clear, searching out antiquity and knowing the present, knowing what is past beyond limit and beholding what is not yet, foreknowing beyond measure, wholly beyond reckoning. The countless Buddhas, their awesome spirit, honor, and brightness — he knows them all. The Buddha's wisdom and virtue are one light; there is none who can ask the Buddha to the limit of the scriptures and the way, and the Buddha's wisdom can never be measured to its end.”
Ānanda heard the Buddha's words and was greatly afraid, and the hair on his body stood on end.

He said to the Buddha: “I dare not have doubt concerning the Buddha. The reason I asked the Buddha is that in the Buddha-lands of other quarters there is everywhere a Mount Sumeru, and the first heaven of the Four Heavenly Kings and the second heaven of Trayastrimsa all rest and abide upon it. I feared that after the Buddha enters parinirvāṇa, there might be devas and humans, or monks, nuns, laymen, or laywomen, who would come and ask me: In the land of Amitābha Buddha, why alone is there no Mount Sumeru? On what do the first heaven of the Four Heavenly Kings and the second heaven of Trayastrimsa rest and abide? I should have to answer them. If I do not ask the Buddha now, after the Buddha has gone, with what words shall I reply? Only the Buddha himself knows this; no other can explain it for me. For this reason I asked the Buddha.”
The Buddha said to Ānanda: “The third heaven of Yama, the fourth heaven of Tusita, up to the seventh heaven of Brahma — on what do they all rest and abide?”

Ānanda said: “All those heavens naturally dwell in the empty air. They abide in the empty air, resting on nothing. The Buddha's awesome spirit is most weighty: whatever he wishes to do, he does without forethought. If all those heavens still abide in the empty air, how much more the Buddha, whose awesome spirit is honored and weighty, in whatever he wishes to do?”

Ānanda heard the Buddha's words and rejoiced greatly, knelt long, pressed his palms together, and said: “The Buddha's wisdom knows the affairs of the eight quarters above and below, of past, future, and present, without end or limit, without bound or edge, most lofty, great, wonderful, and utterly blissful, most bright and fair beyond compare. His awesome spirit is honored and weighty, not to be withstood.”

blocks.text: Sutra of Amitābha, the Truly Enlightened One of the Sagely Lineage, Delivering Beings of the Human Path, Scroll the Lower

inline.s: The Buddha said to Bodhisattva Ajita: “Among the people of the world, good men and good women who wish to be born in the land of Amitābha Buddha are of three grades, and the virtue they do is great or small, so that they do not reach one another.”

The Buddha said: “What are the three grades? The foremost, the first grade: one should leave home, forsake wife and children, and cut off the desires of love. One should live as a renunciant and enter the way of non-doing. One should walk the bodhisattva-way and practice the scriptures of the six paramitas. As a renunciant one should not fail in the precepts; compassionate in heart, one should strive diligently and not give way to anger. One should not have dealings with women; one should observe the fasts purely and cleanly, with a heart that covets nothing. With utmost sincerity one should wish to be born in the land of Amitābha Buddha. If one thinks of it constantly with a whole heart, never breaking it off, then in this present life, while seeking the way, one will naturally see Amitābha Buddha and the bodhisattvas and arhats in one's sleep and dreams. When such a person's life is about to end, Amitābha Buddha himself, with the bodhisattvas and arhats, will fly together to welcome him, and he will be born in the land of Amitābha Buddha. There, in a pool of seven treasures, he will be born by transformation in a lotus flower, and will at once naturally receive a body that grows up. He will become a bodhisattva of non-retrogression, and with the bodhisattvas will fly in company and make offering to the countless Buddhas throughout the eight quarters above and below. He will at once attain wisdom and valor, delight in hearing the scriptures and the way, and his heart will rejoice. The seven-treasure dwelling he inhabits is in the empty air, and he does as he wills and wishes, near to Amitābha Buddha.”

The Buddha said: “Those who wish to be born in the land of Amitābha Buddha should strive diligently, keep the scriptures and precepts, and practice the excellent dharma as above. Then they shall be born in the land of Amitābha Buddha, and shall be honored by the multitude. This is the foremost, the first grade.”

The Buddha said: “The middle grade: one who wishes to be born in the land of Amitābha Buddha, though he cannot leave home, forsake wife and children, cut off the desires of love, and live as a renunciant, should yet hold the scriptures and precepts without failing in them. He should give more in charity and generosity, always faithfully receive the Buddha's words, and with deep sincerity hold to genuine faith. He should feed renunciants, build temples and raise stupas, scatter flowers, burn incense, light lamps, and hang variegated silk and brocade. In such dharmas he should have no preference or aversion. He should not give way to anger; he should observe the fasts purely and cleanly. Compassionate in heart, he should strive diligently and cut off the thoughts of desire. If, wishing to be born in the land of Amitābha Buddha, he does not break it off for a day and a night, then in this present life, too, he will see Amitābha Buddha in his sleep and dreams. When his life is about to end, Amitābha Buddha will manifest a transformation, causing him to see Amitābha Buddha and his land with his own eyes. Being born in the land of Amitābha Buddha, he may attain wisdom and valor.”

The Buddha said: “One who practices giving and charity thus, if afterward he should regret it in mid-course and doubt in his heart, not believing that giving in charity and doing good will bring blessing in a later life, not believing that there is a land of Amitābha Buddha, not believing that one may be born in that land — yet even so, if he continues to think of it without breaking off, now believing and now not believing, his will wavering with nothing to rest on, still, because he continues his good vow as his foundation, he shall be born there. When his life is about to end in sickness, Amitābha Buddha himself manifests a transformed image and causes him to see it with his own eyes. He can no longer speak, but in his heart he rejoices and leaps up, thinking: “I repent that I did not know to observe the fasts more and do good; now I shall be born in the land of Amitābha Buddha.” Such a person at once repents in his heart, and by his repentance his fault is somewhat lessened, though there is much he can no longer make up for. When his life comes to its end, he is at once born in the land of Amitābha Buddha. He cannot come before Amitābha Buddha, but on the way he sees, at the border of the land of Amitābha Buddha, a natural city of seven treasures, and his heart rejoices greatly, and he stops within that city. There, in a pool of seven treasures, he is born by transformation in a lotus flower, and receives a body that naturally grows up within the city. There he remains five hundred years. The city is two thousand li in length and breadth, and within the city there are also seven-treasure dwelling places, with seven-treasure bathing pools within and without. In the bathing pools there is also natural flower fragrance encircling them, and above the bathing pools there are also seven-treasure trees in many rows, all again giving forth the five tones. When he wishes to eat, natural food is before him, furnished with food of a hundred flavors, and whatever he wishes for comes according to his thought. Such a person is happy in the city as well, for within that city it is like the natural things of the second heaven of Trayastrimsa. Yet even so, he cannot get out of that city, and cannot see Amitābha Buddha. He sees only his light, and in his heart reproaches himself and repents, rejoicing and glad. Nor can he hear the scriptures, nor see the company of monks, nor see and know what the bodhisattvas and arhats in the land of Amitābha Buddha are like in appearance. Such a person is grieved, and this is but a small comfort to him. The Buddha does not cause such a one to obtain by his own bodily deeds what comes naturally; it is all the heart's own turning toward the way that brings him into that city. When this person sought the way in his former destiny, his heart and mouth were at variance, and his words and thoughts had no sincerity or trust. He doubted the Buddha's scriptures and did not believe in them, and so he naturally entered the evil paths; Amitābha Buddha, in pity, drew him out by his awesome spirit. Such a person must remain in that city five hundred years before he can come out. When he comes before Amitābha Buddha and hears the scriptures, his heart does not open and understand, and he is not permitted to hear the scriptures among the bodhisattvas, arhats, and company of monks. Because the dwelling he inhabits is on the ground, he cannot make his dwelling tall and lofty in the empty air at will. And he is very far from Amitābha Buddha, and cannot come near to him. His wisdom is not bright, and he knows few scriptures; his heart is not glad, and his mind does not open and understand. Yet in time he too shall of himself open and understand in wisdom and know the scriptures. Bright, strong, and valiant, his heart shall rejoice, and he shall next become as the first grade above. Why is this? Because when he sought the way in former lives and destinies, he did not much observe the fasts and precepts, and destroyed and lost the scriptures and the dharma. His will doubted, he did not believe the Buddha's words, did not deeply believe the Buddha's scriptures, did not believe that giving in charity and doing good would bring blessing in a later life. And again he regretted it in mid-course, not believing that he would be born in the land of Amitābha Buddha, and his virtue was not done with a whole heart. For this reason it is thus. This is the second, the middle grade.”

The Buddha said: “The third grade: one who wishes to be born in the land of Amitābha Buddha, though he has no means for charity and generosity, and cannot burn incense, scatter flowers, light lamps, hang variegated silk and brocade, build temples, raise stupas, or feed renunciants, should yet cut off the desires of love, covet nothing, take up the scriptures swiftly, be compassionate in heart and strive diligently, not give way to anger, and observe the fasts purely and cleanly. In such dharmas he should single-mindedly think and wish to be born in the land of Amitābha Buddha, and if for ten days and nights he does not break it off, then when his life ends he shall at once be born in the land of Amitābha Buddha. He may attain honor, wisdom, and valor.”

The Buddha said: “After one has done thus, if he again regrets it in mid-course and his heart doubts, not believing that doing good will bring blessing in a later life, not believing that he will be born in the land of Amitābha Buddha — yet even so, he shall still be born there. When his life is about to end in sickness, Amitābha Buddha causes him, in his sleep and dreams, to see the land of Amitābha Buddha. His heart rejoices greatly, and he thinks within himself: “I repent that I did not know to do more good; now I shall be born in the land of Amitābha Buddha.” This alone he thinks; he can no longer speak, and at once repents. By his repentance his fault is lessened, though there is much he can no longer make up for. When his life ends, he is at once born in the land of Amitābha Buddha. He cannot come before it, but on the way he sees a city of seven treasures two thousand li across, and his heart alone rejoices, and he stops within it. There, too, in a seven-treasure bathing pool, he is born by transformation in a lotus flower, and at once naturally receives a body that grows up. That city is also as the former city was, like the natural things of the second heaven of Trayastrimsa; and this person, too, must remain in the city until five hundred years are done before he can come out. When he comes to where Amitābha Buddha is, his heart rejoices greatly; but when he hears the scriptures, his heart does not open and understand, his mind is not glad, his wisdom is not bright, and he knows few scriptures. The dwelling he inhabits is on the ground, and he cannot make his dwelling tall and lofty in the empty air at will. And he is very far from Amitābha Buddha, and cannot come near to him. Thus it is again. This is the doubter of the second, middle grade: in time he too shall open and understand in wisdom, know the scriptures, be valiant, and have a joyful heart, and shall next become as the first grade above. Why is this? It is all because when he sought the way in former lives and destinies he regretted it in mid-course and doubted, believing and not believing by turns. Not believing that doing good brings merit and blessing, he nonetheless obtains it all naturally. According to his merit and virtue, whether he grasps it or not, each naturally turns to his own course. In expounding the scriptures and walking the way, they are a myriad billion times apart and do not reach one another.”

The Buddha said: “Those who wish to seek the bodhisattva-way and be born in the land of Amitābha Buddha shall all afterward attain to bodhisattvahood of non-retrogression. Bodhisattvas of non-retrogression shall all have the thirty-two marks, a purple burnished golden color, and the eighty minor marks. They shall all become Buddhas, according to their vows and wherever they wish. They shall become Buddhas in the Buddha-lands of other quarters, and never again pass through hell, the animal realm, or the realm of hungry ghosts. According to their diligence in seeking the way, whether sooner or later, the matter is the same for all. If they seek the way without rest, they shall surely attain it, and shall not lose what they have vowed and wished.”

The Buddha said to Bodhisattva Ajita and the rest: “Devas, kings, and people, I tell you all: those who wish to be born in the land of Amitābha Buddha, though they cannot greatly strive in meditation and hold the scriptures and precepts, must in sum do good:

First, one must not take life. Second, one must not steal. Third, one must not commit lewdness or lust after the wives of others. Fourth, one must not deceive. Fifth, one must not drink wine. Sixth, one must not speak with a double tongue. Seventh, one must not speak harshly. Eighth, one must not speak falsely. Ninth, one must not envy. Tenth, one must not be greedy and gluttonous. One must not be stingy in heart, must not give way to anger, must not be foolish, must not indulge the appetites at will, must not regret in heart, must not doubt. One should be filial and obedient, should be utterly sincere and faithful, should faithfully receive the Buddha's words, and should deeply believe that doing good brings blessing in a later life. Those who uphold and practice this and do not fail in the dharma may, according to the wish of their hearts, be born in the land of Amitābha Buddha. Above all one should keep the fasts and be single-minded and pure. Thinking of it day and night, wishing to be born in the land of Amitābha Buddha, for ten days and ten nights without breaking it off — I in my compassion pity them all, and cause them all to be born in the land of Amitābha Buddha.”

The Buddha said: “People of the world who by their wishes aspire to worth and wisdom, and who live at home practicing good and walking the way, dwelling together with wife and children amid the bonds of affection and desire, are beset by many cares and household affairs in confusion, and have no leisure for great fasts and single-minded purity. Though they cannot leave home and cast off desire, yet when they have leisure they should order their own hearts and minds, think on the good their bodies may do, and single-mindedly and earnestly walk the way. If ten days and ten nights are quite impossible, let them think and weigh the matter carefully for themselves, if they wish to deliver their bodies. At the least they should cut off thought and put away care, not think on household affairs, and not share a bed with a woman. Let them order body and mind aright and cut off the desires of love. Single-mindedly keeping the fasts in purity, with utmost thought wishing to be born in the land of Amitābha Buddha, if for a day and a night they do not break it off, then when their lives end they shall all be born in that land. Born by transformation in a lotus flower in a seven-treasure bathing pool, they may attain wisdom and valor. The seven-treasure dwelling they inhabit, they do with as they will at ease, and they may become as the first grade above.”

The Buddha said to Bodhisattva Ajita: “The countless devas and humans throughout the eight quarters above and below — monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen — who are born in the land of Amitābha Buddha: this great assembly all together in the waters of the seven-treasure bathing pools, every one of them seated upon a great lotus flower, all declare their own virtue and good deeds, each telling of his former destiny when he sought the way, the precepts he kept and the good dharmas he did, the beginning and end of the life he came from, the scriptures and way he delighted in, the wisdom he has of the scriptures, and the merit he has practiced. From highest to lowest, all in turn are told through. Thus one knows whether one's knowledge of the scriptures is bright or dim, one's wisdom deep or shallow, great or small, one's virtue excellent or poor, thick or thin; by the natural way one knows them apart. Talent, wisdom, vigor, and valor — the multitude look upon one another, in propriety and harmony, all rejoicing and leaping up; yet in wisdom and valor none reaches another.”

The Buddha said: “One who has done no virtue beforehand, who takes good lightly and makes sport of it, who does not believe it is so, who idles and is indolent, thinking it will serve — when the time comes and all are gathered to expound the scriptures and the way, he is naturally pressed and hard put, and his answers come late. The wisdom of the way stands out supreme and transcendent, in talent and strength most lofty; and he alone is at the margin, weak, repenting only when the matter is at hand. But when the repentance is already out, what good can come of it afterward? Only bitterness in his heart. Such is the one who envies and aspires to be their equal.”

The Buddha said: “The bodhisattvas and arhats of the land of Amitābha Buddha, and all that great assembly, naturally gather in a great meeting. They restrain their hearts and govern their minds, order their bodies and walk uprightly, sport and penetrate everywhere, follow one another in flight, going out and in company after company, making offerings without limit, joyful in heart and glad, together contemplating the scriptures and the way of practice, harmonious and long accustomed, keen and wise. Their will is like the empty air; they strive and seek their vows, and their hearts never again turn aside midway, their minds never again turn back, and never is there a time of sloth or weariness. Though they seek the way, outwardly they seem slow; inwardly they alone are swift. Vast and empty, they hit the mean exactly; within and without answering each other, naturally well ordered, restrained and upright, body and mind clean and pure, with no desire of love, nothing whatsoever coveted, no evil or blemish at all. Their vows and wishes are each settled and excellent, neither added to nor diminished. They seek the way in harmony and uprightness, not erring into crookedness, measuring themselves against the dharma of the way, following the scriptures and the rules, not daring to transgress or stumble. Throughout the eight quarters above and below, without bound or edge, at ease as they wish, they reach to the endless and limitless, all of them thus for the way — broad and vast, thinking of the way with no other thought, free of care and grief, natural and unconditioned, empty and still, at peace and without desire. Fulfilling good vows, they exhaust their hearts in seeking, holding pity and compassion, striving within and without, in full accord with propriety and righteousness, penetrating and unobstructed, harmonious and fitting, embracing within and without, delivering and liberating, able to ascend into nirvāṇa, forever one light with virtue and the way, naturally preserving one another, the taste of delight most true, truly pure and white, their vow supreme, the stillness of purity, the joy of quiet without end, good and fair beyond compare, towering radiance, radiance shining through, open, reaching, bright, and clear. Within the natural, the marks of the natural; what is so has its root; naturally they accomplish five lights; the five lights reach to nine colors; the nine colors interweave and turn; many hundreds of thousands of changes. The naturalness of Uttarakuru naturally accomplishes the seven treasures, and gathering them across makes the ten thousand things; the essence of light, interwoven and bright, all issues fair, most beautiful beyond measure. If that land is thus, why not strive to do good, and think on the naturalness of the way? Fix your will above and below, penetrate without bound or edge, cast your aim into the empty air. Why does each not strive, and exert himself to seek? You may attain transcendence and depart. Be born in the land of Amitābha Buddha, cut across the five evil paths; naturally they are closed, and you ascend the way without limit — easy to go, yet there is none who goes. That land does not oppose or defy; it naturally draws one along. Why not cast off the affairs of the world, practice and seek the way of virtue, and attain utmost long life, a life without end? Why cling to the affairs of the world, and with endless chatter share in anxious thoughts of impermanence? The people of the world are shallow and common; they contend together over matters that are not urgent, together here amid the utmost evil and bitterest suffering. They toil body and mind to make a living, to keep one another alive. No honored, no lowly; no rich, no poor; no old, no young; no man, no woman — all must worry together over wealth, and whether they have it or not, it is the same: their anxious thoughts are exactly equal. Distressed and wretched, piling up thoughts and cares. Driven by the mind, they never have a time of rest. He who has fields worries over fields; he who has a house worries over the house. He who has oxen worries over oxen; he who has horses worries over horses. He who has the six kinds of livestock worries over them. He who has servants worries over servants. He who has clothing, wealth, gold, silver, and treasures worries over them too. Thoughts heaped up, breath upon breath, worry, care, grief, and fear. Suddenly come the unforeseen: flood and fire, robbers and thieves, creditors and debtors, drowning and burning and binding, sudden assault and sinking. The poison of care is dull and heavy, and never is there a time of release. Wrath knotted in the breast, breath stored up in anger. Sickness in chest and belly, and sorrow that never leaves. The heart hard and the will firm, and no letting go at all. Some are broken and laid low, and lose their lives for good. They cast all away and go; there is none who follows them. Honored and lowly, noble and rich, poor and humble — all have these fears. Toiling thus, they bind up all manner of chills and fevers and dwell together with pain. The poor of small households, in want and hardship, lacking. He who has no fields worries and wishes for fields; he who has no house worries and wishes for a house; he who has no oxen worries and wishes for oxen; he who has no horses worries and wishes for horses; he who has none of the six livestock worries and wishes for them; he who has no servants worries and wishes for servants; he who has no clothing, wealth, goods, food and drink and the like worries and wishes to have them. No sooner has he one thing than he lacks another; having this and lacking that, he thinks to have them all equal. No sooner has he a little than it is all taken away again. Thus he lives in bitterness and must seek again. His thoughts profit him nothing, and he cannot get what he wants in time. Body and mind both toil, and sitting or rising he has no peace. Care follows upon care, and his toil is thus. Scorched heart that never leaves him, and wrath and hate and solitary rage. He too binds up all manner of chills and fevers and dwells together with pain. Sometimes for this he loses his life early, and still he will not do good or walk the way. When his life is ended and he dies, he must go far away alone. Whither he goes, and whether the path be good or evil, none can know. Sometimes people of the world, fathers and sons, brothers, husbands and wives, households and kin within and without, dwelling between heaven and earth, ought to respect and love one another, and not hate one another; in having or lacking they ought to give to one another, and not be greedy and grudging; in word and countenance they ought to be harmonious, and not contend. If perchance their hearts contend and anger arises, the hatred of this life, the small envies and hates, in later lives grow worse and become great enmity. Why is this? As matters stand now, they wish to harm one another; though they do not at the moment break one another in sudden anger, yet the poison of grief and the wrath knotted in the spirit are naturally marked and known, and cannot be parted. Each must be born facing the other, and meet and take revenge in turn. A person in the world, amid the desires of love, goes alone and comes alone, dies alone and is born alone. When he comes to a place of suffering or of joy, he must bear it himself; there is none to take his place. Good and evil change, and calamity and evil places await him, prepared long beforehand; he must ascend alone and go far to another place, and none can see where he has gone. Good and evil naturally follow him as he goes and is born. Dark and obscure, the parting is long. The roads differ, and there is no time of meeting. It is very hard to meet again. Why not cast off household affairs, each while strong and well, strive to do good, and with all your strength seek deliverance from the world, and attain utmost long life? Yet you will not seek the way; what delight do you wait for and desire?”

People such as these do not believe that doing good brings good, do not believe that walking the way attains the way, do not believe that after death one is born again in a later world, do not believe that giving in charity brings merit and blessing; they believe none of it. They say it is not so, that there is no such thing at all; and so they see only for themselves, and pass the word from one to another, one after another, receiving it in turn. The father's leftover teaching: the ancestors and grandfathers did no good and never walked the way. Dull in body and dark in spirit, their hearts stopped up and their minds closed, they did not see the great way, and had no ability at all. Seeing people die and be born and go to some place, they could not know it either. Since they had not seen the way of good and evil, and had none to tell them, how could they do good or evil, merit or blessing, receive calamity or punishment? Each contended to do as he pleased, and none found it strange at all. And so the way of death and birth is handed on and stands from one to another. Sometimes a child weeps for a father, sometimes a father weeps for a child; sometimes a younger brother weeps for an elder, sometimes an elder weeps for a younger; sometimes a wife weeps for a husband, sometimes a husband weeps for a wife. Upside down and topsy-turvy, impermanence is the root of it, and all must pass away and cannot be kept forever. Teaching and guiding them, few believe the way. All must die and be born, and there is no rest. People such as these are dim and dull and obstinate. They do not believe the words of the scriptures, and each wishes to please himself. Their hearts take no thought. They are foolish in the desires of love and do not understand virtue and the way. They are deluded by anger and ravenous for wealth and beauty. For this they do not attain the way, and must toil more bitterly. Born at the utmost in evil places, they never find rest or cease; their suffering is most pitiable. Sometimes within a household and kin, fathers and sons, brothers, husbands and wives, at the meaning of death and birth weep over one another and long for one another in turn. Care and grief knit together, and the bonds of affection wind on and on. Heart and mind cling to pain, and they look upon one another with longing. Day and night they are bound and obstructed, and never is there a time of release. Taught to look to virtue and the way, their hearts do not open and brighten. They think on affection and fondness, and the desires of love do not leave them. Closed and blinded, crossed and covered over. They cannot think or reckon. If the heart would order itself aright and cut through the affairs of the world, and single-mindedly and earnestly walk the way, turning at once to the very end — when life ends and the breath is gone, they cannot attain the way. What is to be done? All in a muddle and clamor, all greedy for the desires of love. In such a dharma as this, those who do not understand the way are many and those who attain it are few. The world hurries on, and there is nothing to rely on. Honored and lowly, high and low, noble and rich, poor and humble, men and women, great and small, each hurries about his own affairs, toiling and bowing his body, cherishing the poison of killing. Evil breath dark and dim, and none but is sorrowful. They do things recklessly and defy heaven and earth. They do not follow the human heart, and virtue is not evil. First it is granted them, and they are let do as they will. Before their time of life has come, it is snatched from them at a stroke. They go down into the evil paths and toil through life after life. Turning and turning in the poison of grief for many thousands of myriads of billions of years, with no time of rest — a pain beyond words, most pitiable.”

The Buddha said to Bodhisattva Ajita and the devas, kings, and people: “I tell you all: people who do the affairs of the world — for this reason they do not attain the way. Think it over well, all of you: what is evil you should let go, abandon, and turn away from. What is good you should firmly hold, and not recklessly do what is not right. Do ever more good, great or small, much or little; the glory of the desires of love can never be kept forever. It must part, and there is nothing to delight in. While the Buddha is in the world, those who faithfully receive the Buddha's words deeply and practice virtue and the way are all my younger brothers. Those who wish to begin learning the Buddha's scriptures and precepts are all my disciples. Those who wish to leave their station, go from home, forsake wife and children, cut off wealth and beauty, and become renunciants and monks for the Buddha are all my children and grandchildren. My age is very hard to meet with. Those who wish to be born in the land of Amitābha Buddha may attain wisdom and valor and be honored by the multitude. Do not follow the wishes of your heart and fail the scriptures and precepts, falling behind others. If you have any doubt and do not understand the scriptures, come forward again and ask the Buddha, and I will explain them for you.”

Bodhisattva Ajita knelt long, pressed his palms together, and said: “The Buddha's awesome spirit is honored and weighty, and the scriptures he speaks are blissful and good. Hearing the words of the scriptures, we all take them to heart. The people of the world are truly so; there is no difference from what the Buddha has said. Now the Buddha in his compassion pities us, opens and shows the great way, and teaches the words of the living path. Ears and eyes made keen, we shall long attain deliverance, and now seem to be born anew. Hearing the Buddha's words of scripture, there is none of us who is not compassionate in heart and glad, who does not leap up and open in understanding; and the devas, kings, and people, and the winged and crawling creatures, all receive the grace, and there is none who is not freed from grief. The Buddha's words of teaching and admonition are most deep and good, without limit or bottom. What the Buddha's wisdom sees and knows — the affairs of the eight quarters above and below, of past, future, and present — has no above and no below, no bound and no edge. The Buddha is very hard to hear. We have set our compassionate hearts upon the Buddha. That we have been able to win deliverance is all because the Buddha, when he sought the way in former lives, studied and questioned with diligence and pain, and attained to clarity — the grace of his virtue covering all. The merit he practiced and the blessings of his marks tower on high; his light shines through, penetrating the void without limit, entering into nirvāṇa, teaching and gathering the scriptures, establishing his awe and melting away all things. He moves and changes the eight quarters above and below, without end or limit. The Buddha is the teacher of dharma, honored above all the sages, and there is none who can equal the Buddha. The Buddha is the teacher of the devas, kings, and people throughout the eight quarters above and below; according to the wishes of their hearts, great or small, he causes them all to attain the way. Now that we have been able to see the Buddha and to hear the name of Amitābha Buddha, we rejoice greatly, and there is none of us who has not attained keen wisdom and understanding.”

The Buddha said to Bodhisattva Ajita: “If what you say is true and it is so, then those who have a compassionate heart toward the Buddha rejoice greatly, and should truly think on the Buddha. Only after long ages does a Buddha again appear in the world. Now I have become a Buddha in an age of suffering; the scriptures and the way I set forth teach and penetrate everywhere. They cut off doubt and set the heart upright and the conduct straight. They pull out all desires of love and cut off the root of every evil. Walking at liberty and unconstrained, I govern and gather up wisdom. The ways within and without all dharmas I grasp and hold by the guiding cords. Brightly and clearly I open and show the five paths, and decide and set right the ways of birth and death and of nirvāṇa.”

The Buddha said: “From numberless kalpas past, through kalpas beyond reckoning, you have walked the bodhisattva-way, wishing to deliver the devas and humans and the winged and crawling creatures. It is very long since you began. Those who have won the way through you are countless, and those who have reached the way of nirvāṇa are also countless. You, and the devas, kings, and people throughout the eight quarters above and below, monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen — your former destinies, through numberless kalpas past, have turned and turned within these five paths, dying and being born with wailing and lamentation. Weeping over one another, longing for one another in turn, care and grief and the poison of sorrow — a pain beyond words. To this present life, death and birth have not ceased. Only today have you met the Buddha and come together with him, and now you hear the name of Amitābha Buddha, most blissful and good. I share your joy; and you may also grow weary of the pain of birth and death. Birth is most painful, most bitter, most extreme. Growing up in years is also bitter and extreme. At death, too, there is pain and bitterness and extremity; the place of evil stench and impurity is foul, and there is nothing clean or good in it. Therefore the Buddha tells you all: you too may cut off the foul place and the evil dew. You too may set your hearts upright and your bodies straight, and do ever more good. Thus always keep within and without upright, make body and mind clean. Wash away the stains of the heart, and bind and restrain yourselves. Let within and without answer each other, in word and deed faithful and true. A person can deliver himself and, in turn, support and receive others. Pull out all desires of love, be clear and bright with a whole heart. Let your vow not turn back, and bind fast the root of the good way. Though you strive and suffer for one lifetime, it is but a moment; doing good in this life, in the next you shall be born in the land of Amitābha Buddha, and your bliss shall be beyond measure. Forever one light with virtue and the way, in goodness you shall preserve one another. Forever apart from the evil paths, from the pain and itch of grief and affliction, pulling out the bitter root of all evil and toil, cutting off the desires of love and fond affection. Long living in the land of Amitābha Buddha, there is no pain or itch, no evil foul place, no toil or bitterness, no lust, anger, or folly, no care or grief or poison of sorrow. Born in the land of Amitābha Buddha, you may wish for a life of one kalpa, ten kalpas, a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, a hundred million kalpas. At your own will and pleasure, you may abide with a life of countless kalpas, of kalpas beyond reckoning. As you will and wish, you may have it all. To eat or not to eat, as you please. All things are natural, and you may have them all. Next to the way of nirvāṇa, let each of you be clear and bright and seek it out. Whatever your heart wishes, do not doubt or regret in your heart. Those who wish to be born there must not, by their own fault, be set down for five hundred years in a natural city of seven treasures at the border of the land of Amitābha Buddha.”
Bodhisattva Ajita said: “We receive the Buddha's stern and lucid and weighty teaching; we shall all strive diligently and single-mindedly seek. We beg to practice it, and dare not doubt or slacken.”

The Buddha said to Bodhisattva Ajita and the rest: “If in this world you can govern your own hearts and set your minds upright, and your bodies do no evil, this is great virtue and goodness. This is a whole grade of its own, matchless throughout the eight quarters above and below. Why is this? Throughout the eight quarters above and below, in the countless Buddha-lands, the devas and humans all naturally do good and do not greatly do evil, and are easy to teach and transform. Now I have become a Buddha in this world, become a Buddha amid the five evils, the five pains, and the five burnings. I teach and speak to the people in the sharpest extremity, causing them to let go the five evils, to put away the five pains, and to put away the five burnings, subduing and transforming their hearts. I cause them to hold the five goods, and to attain the merit and blessing of deliverance from the world, long life, and the way of nirvāṇa.”

The Buddha said: “What are the five evils? What are the five pains? What are the five burnings? What is the melting away of the five evils? What is it to attain the five goods? What is it to hold the five goods, and to attain the merit and blessing of long life, and the way of deliverance from the world and nirvāṇa?”

The Buddha said: “The first evil: devas and humans, and down to the beasts and the winged and crawling creatures, wish to do all manner of evil. The strong overpower the weak, and they plunder one another in turn. They wound and kill one another, and eat one another in turn. They do not know to do good, and are evil and defiant and without the way. They receive their calamity and punishment, for such is the natural way of things. Where they are bound, the spirits mark and know it. Those who transgress are not forgiven, and the debt is handed on and on. Hence there are poverty and lowliness, begging and loneliness. Hence there are deafness and blindness, dumbness and folly, sullenness and evil. Below there are the crooked and the mad, and those who cannot reach what they seek. Hence there are the honored and lowly, the noble and rich, the highly gifted and clear-minded, the wise and valiant — all by their former destinies of doing good, being compassionate and filial, and bestowing kindness and virtue. Hence there are lawsuits, the king's law, and prisons. Those who will not fear and take care, who do evil and fall under the law, receive their fault and punishment, and heavy fines bring extremity. They seek release and deliverance, but it is hard to win free. In this life there is this, present before your eyes. When life ends there is a place; they enter its darkness and receive a body and are born again. It is like the king's law, with bitter suffering and utmost punishment. Hence there are the natural hells, the beasts, the hungry ghosts, and the winged and crawling creatures. Their bodies change in trade, they alter their evil and change their path. Life short or long, the spirit and subtle consciousness naturally enter their course and receive a body and lodge in a womb. Each must meet what faces him, and they follow one another and are born together. They repay one another in turn, and must give back in turn. Calamity and evil, disaster and punishment — the many matters are not yet done. They can never be free, but turn and turn within them.
