Life after life, kalpa piled on kalpa, there is no time of escape. Deliverance is hard to win, and the pain is beyond words. Between heaven and earth this is naturally so. Though it is not at the moment, it comes suddenly in its season. One has only to take the natural way; good and evil both return to it. This is the first great evil, the first pain, the first burning. Toil and bitterness such as this, the poison of sorrow and wailing. It is like a fierce fire rising to burn a man's body. If a person can within this single-mindedly govern his mind, set his body upright and walk straight, and alone do all good and do no evil, then he alone is delivered and wins merit and blessing. He may attain long life, deliverance from the world, ascent to the heavens, and the way of nirvāṇa. This is the first great good.”

The Buddha said: “The second evil: the kings of the world, the officials and the people, fathers and sons, brothers, households, husbands and wives, are almost wholly without propriety or reason. They do not follow the upright commands, but are extravagant, lewd, and arrogant. Each wishes to please himself and do as his heart pleases. They cheat and mock one another, and have no fear of death at all. Heart and mouth differ, and their words and thoughts are untrue. Flattering and fawning, disloyal, wheedling and cunning in speech. Their conduct has no order; they envy and hate one another, slander and speak evil of one another in turn, and ensnare people in false charges. The ruler is not clear-minded, his heart does not examine and illumine, and he employs his ministers. The ministers, being in place, tread and measure what they can do. Knowing how to shape and apply things, they sit in their seats without uprightness. Being mocked by them, he recklessly damages the loyal and good and worthy and virtuous. This does not accord with the heart of heaven, and greatly violates reason. The minister cheats his lord, the son cheats his father. The younger brother cheats the elder, the wife cheats the husband. Within the household and without, friends and acquaintances sue one another. Each harbors greed and lust, a heart of poison and anger, and in blind folly and ignorance wishes to increase himself. There is no honored or lowly, high or low; no man, no woman; no great, no small. Their hearts are all alike, each wishing to enrich himself. They ruin their households and destroy themselves, with no thought of those before or after. Household and kin are broken and their clan destroyed by it. Sometimes within the household and without, friends and acquaintances, the village and the marketplace, foolish folk and rustics, turn to one another's affairs, each seeking his own gain and harm. They contend over wealth and fight lawsuits, and wrath and rage become enmity, and they contend in turn for victory and defeat. The rich and stingy scorch their hearts and will not give in charity. Grudging and guarding what they love, clinging to it and hoarding it. For this they brood, and their hearts toil and their bodies suffer. Thus to the very end, with nothing to rely on. They come alone and go alone, and not one follows them. Good and evil, merit and blessing, calamity and punishment follow the life they go to; some are in a place of bliss, some enter poison and suffering. Only then do they repent — but what use is that? Sometimes people of the world, foolish in heart and scant of wisdom, seeing the good, slander and hate them, and will not aspire to follow. They wish only to do reckless and wayless things, wish only to steal, always harboring a poisonous heart. They wish to get the wealth of others to supply themselves. When it is scattered and spent, they seek it again. Their crooked hearts are not upright, and they are always alone in terror, fearing the countenance of others. At the moment they take no thought, and only when the matter comes do they repent. In this present life, the officials and the prisons — they naturally turn their course and receive their calamity. The poverty, begging, and loneliness of the world come only from former destinies. Not believing in virtue and the way, unwilling to do good, doing evil in this life, the devas record them in a separate register. When life ends they enter the evil paths; hence there are the natural hells, the beasts, the hungry ghosts, and the winged and crawling creatures. They turn and turn within them. Life after life, kalpa piled on kalpa, there is no time of escape. Deliverance is hard to win, and the pain is beyond words. This is the second great evil. The second pain, the second burning — toil and bitterness such as this. It is like a fire rising, fiercer than burning a man's body. If a person can within this single-mindedly govern his mind, set his body upright and walk straight, and alone do all good and do no evil, then he alone is delivered and wins merit and blessing. He may attain long life, deliverance from the world, ascent to the heavens, and the way of nirvāṇa. This is the second great good.”

The Buddha said: “The third evil: the people of the world, dwelling as parasites upon one another, live together between heaven and earth, and the years of their lives — how many can there be? There are the noble and rich and elders, the wise and good; below them the poor and lowly, the crooked and weak, the foolish. Among them are wicked people who only harbor poison and evil in their thoughts, whose bodies and minds are not upright. They always think on lust, and their breasts are full and troubled. Desires of love cross and tangle, and sitting or rising they have no peace. Their greedy minds are stingy, and they wish to seize and get by force. They leer at fine forms, with evil manner and lust. Hating and loathing their own wives, they go secretly in and out on their own. They take what the household has and give it to wrongdoing. They gather to eat and drink, and together devote themselves to evil. They raise troops and turn bandit, attack cities and fight duels. They rob and kill and cut off, and seize by force without the way. Taking the wealth of others, stealing to get what they want, unwilling to make an honest living. What they ought to seek, they will not do. Their evil minds are set abroad and cannot be single in their work. Wishing to bind things into accomplishment, they use threats and force. They bring it home to supply the household, to live on together. They give their hearts free rein and take their pleasure, going to the utmost in revelry. They violate the wives of others, and do not shrink even from their own kin; the honored and lowly and the elders all hate and loathe them. Within the household and without, they are afflicted and angered by them. Nor do they fear the officials and the law, and there is nothing they avoid or take account of. For evil such as this, naturally there are prisons. Sun and moon shine and know it, the spirits mark and take it down, the gods seize and record it; hence there are the natural hells, the beasts, the hungry ghosts, and the winged and crawling creatures. They turn and turn within them, life after life, kalpa piled on kalpa, with no time of escape. Deliverance is hard to win, and the pain is beyond words. This is the third great evil, the third pain, the third burning. Toil and bitterness such as this are like a fire rising to burn a man's body. If a person can within this single-mindedly govern his mind, set his body upright and walk straight, and alone do all good and do no evil, then he alone is delivered and wins merit and blessing. He may attain long life, deliverance from the world, ascent to the heavens, and the way of nirvāṇa. This is the third great good.”

The Buddha said: “The fourth evil: people cannot do good, and ruin one another. They teach and command one another, and together do all manner of evil. Their chief business is to carry tales; they wish only for a double tongue, harsh speech, abuse, and lies. They envy and stir up strife against one another. They hate and envy the good, and ruin the worthy and virtuous. They take pleasure in it on the side, and are not filial or dutiful, nor do they support their parents. They make light of teachers, friends, and acquaintances, and are without trust and hard to make honest. They think themselves great and honored; they have a way of going about in force and might, adding power and authority. They encroach upon and mistreat others, and cannot know themselves; doing evil, they are not ashamed, but rely on their own stubborn strength. They wish people to serve and fear and respect them. Yet they do not fear or respect heaven and earth, the spirits, the sun and moon. Nor can they be taught or commanded to do good, nor be subdued and transformed; they rely on themselves and are proud, and think it must always be so. Nor have they any heart of grief or pity, nor know the meaning of fear. Arrogant as they are, the devas mark them. Relying on their former destinies, they have done some merit and virtue. A little good supports and receives them, guards and helps them. Doing evil in this life, they exhaust all their good, and day by day it departs. They see evil and go after it; they stand alone and empty, with nothing more to rely on, and receive heavy calamity and punishment. When life ends, all evils gather around them. Naturally pressed and hard put, they must go in pursuit, and cannot rest. Naturally all evils together drive them to exhaustion. Their names are recorded in the register of the spirits. Calamity draws and pulls them, and they must meet what they have earned. Naturally they turn their course, and receive their punishment. Body and mind are shattered, spirit and form in utmost suffering, and they cannot get away. They can only go forward, and enter the cauldron of fire. At that time, what use is repentance? What can they do? The way of heaven is natural, and none can stumble aside. Hence there are the natural hells, the beasts, the hungry ghosts, and the winged and crawling creatures; they turn and turn within them, life after life, kalpa piled on kalpa, with no time of escape. Deliverance is hard to win, and the pain is beyond words. This is the fourth great evil, the fourth pain, the fourth burning. Toil and bitterness such as this are like a fire rising to burn a man's body. If a person can within this single-mindedly govern his mind, set his body upright and walk straight, and alone do all good and do no evil, then he alone is delivered and wins merit and blessing. He may attain long life, deliverance from the world, ascent to the heavens, and the way of nirvāṇa. This is the fourth great good.”

The Buddha said: “The fifth evil: people of the world idle and are lazy, unwilling to do good, and do not think to make a living. Their wives and children go hungry and cold, and their parents likewise. When they wish to scold and teach their children, their children's hearts are evil. They glare and answer in anger, and will not obey their words. Defiant and rebellious, worse than the wild folk. Like enemies, better to have had no children at all. They borrow and lend recklessly, and all are afflicted and sick of it. There is especially no thought of repaying. Impoverished and in want, they cannot get again. They lay snares and make fair sounds, give themselves up to wandering and scattering. Habitually they get things for nothing, and use them to relieve themselves, with no fear of the prohibitions. In food and drink they know no limit, drinking wine and craving delicacies. Their coming and going has no set time; rude and reckless, they knock against everything. They do not know human feeling, and force and compel with shouts. Seeing others happy, they hate and envy and rage at them. Without righteousness or propriety, self-willed in judging what is right, past all remonstrance. They do not grieve over whether their parents, wives, and children have anything or not, nor think to repay their parents' kindness, nor think on the goodness of their teachers. Their hearts always think evil, their mouths always speak evil, their bodies always do evil, and day by day they accomplish nothing. They do not believe in virtue and the way, do not believe there are wise and worthy sages of old, do not believe that doing good and walking the way can deliver one from the world, do not believe that there is a Buddha in the world. They wish to kill arhats, to set the company of monks at odds, always to kill people, to kill their parents, brothers, wives, children, kin, and friends. Their parents, brothers, wives, children, kin, and friends hate and loathe the sight of them, and wish them dead. They do not believe the Buddha's words of scripture, do not believe that a person's life comes to an end, that after death one is born again in a later world. They do not believe that doing good brings good, nor that doing evil brings evil. Men and women such as these, their hearts all alike, defiant and rebellious. Foolish and blind, angry and craving, knowing nothing at all. They think themselves happy and good, and greatly wise. They do not know whence they come, nor where birth and death are bound. They will not be kind or filial, and defy heaven and earth. In the meantime they hope for luck. They wish for long life, and call upon death not to come. But they must go to it at last — the toil and bitterness of birth and death, the ways of good and evil. The evil their bodies have done, the calamities and all their courses, they cannot win free of. Nor can they be subdued and transformed and made to do good. With a compassionate heart one teaches and speaks, opening and guiding them through the suffering of death. Whither good and evil lead — they do not believe even this. Yet with bitter heart one speaks to them, wishing to deliver them, and it profits them nothing. Their hearts are closed up and their minds do not open and understand. The great command is about to come, and at that time they all repent. Repenting afterward — what can they do? Not having planned beforehand to do good, what use is it in extremity? Between heaven and earth the five paths are each distinct. Vast and deep, wide and boundless. They receive in turn, good and evil, poison and pain. Each must bear it himself, and there is none to take his place. The way is natural, and follows what one has done. It pursues the life one goes to, and one cannot let it go. The good do good, are compassionate and filial, and go from bliss into bliss, from light into light. The evil do evil, and go from suffering to darkness; who can know them? Only the Buddha sees and knows. Teaching and speaking to the people, few believe and accept. Birth and death do not cease, and the evil paths are not cut off. People such as these cannot all be told of. Hence there are the natural hells, the beasts, the hungry ghosts, and the winged and crawling creatures. They turn and turn within them, life after life, kalpa piled on kalpa, with no time of escape. Deliverance is hard to win, and the pain is beyond words. This is the fifth great evil, the five pains, the five burnings; toil and bitterness such as this are like a fire rising to burn a man's body. If a person can within this single-mindedly govern his mind, set his body upright and walk straight, let word and deed answer each other, and make all he does utterly sincere. Let his words be as they are, his heart and mouth not turning. Alone doing all good and doing no evil, then he alone is delivered and wins merit and blessing. He may attain long life, deliverance from the world, ascent to the heavens, and the way of nirvāṇa. This is the fifth great good.”

The Buddha said to Bodhisattva Ajita and the rest: “I tell you all: the five evils of this world, and the toil and bitterness that are thus. They give rise to the five pains, give rise to the five burnings, and beget one another in turn. The people of the world will not do good. Those who wish to do all manner of evil and dare to commit these evil things shall all naturally pass through and enter the evil paths. Some in this life first suffer sickness and calamity, and in death and birth find no relief; they are shown to the multitude. When life ends they go to the utmost suffering, grief, and cruel poison. They scorch one another and burn one another away. After that they become enemies together and wound and kill one another. From the smallest beginning it grows to great extremity. It all comes of greed and lust for wealth and beauty, of unwillingness to bear insult, and of each wishing to please himself in what he gives. There is no more right or wrong, only the wish for a strong name. Driven by foolish craving and following the thoughts of the heart, they cannot get what they want, and wrath is knotted in their breasts. Bound by wealth and beauty, with no release, knowing no contentment. Enriching themselves and contending in desire, taking no account of anything. Wealth and honor and glory — if at the time one could bear insult and did not know to do good in charity. Power lasts but a little, and one is scorched along with an evil name. The body sits in toil and bitterness, and after a long time comes great extremity. Naturally it follows and pursues, and there is no release. The king's law is spread abroad, and naturally impeaches and seizes them. Above and below answer one another, a net of rule and order. Alone and afraid, they must enter it. From ancient times to now this has been so — how pitiable and grievous. Wholly without reason or propriety, not knowing the upright way.”

The Buddha said to Bodhisattva Ajita and the rest: “When a Buddha such as this is in the world, in his compassion and pity, the awe of his spirit shakes and moves them. All evil things are melted away and transformed. He causes them to leave evil and draw near to good, and to cast off what they think. Upholding the scriptures and precepts, there is none who does not receive them. They practice the scriptures and the dharma, and dare not transgress or lose them. The way of deliverance from the world, of non-doing and nirvāṇa, is blissful and good and of utmost joy.”

The Buddha said: “You devas, kings, and people, and the people of later ages: when you have obtained the Buddha's words of scripture, think them over well. If you can within this set your hearts upright and walk straight, and those above you do good and lead and transform and restrain those below, teaching the multitude and commanding one another in turn, together doing good and delivering one another in turn, each ordering and keeping himself, compassionate and kind and pitying, never slackening to the end of life, honoring the sages and reverencing filial piety, penetrating and loving widely — the Buddha's words and commands, let none dare fail. You should grieve for the way of deliverance from the world and nirvāṇa; you should grieve to cut off the pain and itch of birth and death and pull out the root of evil. You should grieve to cut off the evil and bitter paths of the hells, the beasts, the hungry ghosts, and the winged and crawling creatures. While the Buddha is in the world, hold firmly to the scriptures and the way, and dare not transgress or lose them.”

The Buddha said: “If you would believe, what is the first urgency? You should order your own body, order your own mind, order your own eyes, order your own ears, order your own nose, order your own mouth, order your own hands, order your own feet. If you can restrain yourselves and not act recklessly. Let body and mind be pure and clean, and both answer to good. Restrain within and without, and do not follow the appetites. Transgress no evil; let word and countenance be harmonious, and the body's conduct single. In walking, standing, sitting, or rising, let all you do be at peace. In whatever you do, first think it over carefully and reckon it. Measure your ability, look all around, and settle it calmly before you act. To act in haste, without forethought and careful reckoning, is to do it without truth, and you lose your labor. Failure and regret come after, and you toil in vain and lose yourself. Utterly sincere and faithful, you attain the way and depart.”

The Buddha said: “If you thus do ever more good, bestowing kindness and practicing virtue, and can avoid transgressing the prohibitions of the way, bearing insult and striving diligently, single-minded in wisdom, teaching one another in turn and doing good and virtue — then in such a dharma as this, with a compassionate heart and single-mindedness, keeping the fasts purely and cleanly for a day and a night, you surpass a hundred years of doing good in the land of Amitābha Buddha. Why is this? In the land of Amitābha Buddha all is accumulated virtue and a multitude of good. Unconditioned and natural, whatever one seeks is there. There is no evil at all, great as a hair.

The Buddha said: “Here, one who does good for ten days and ten nights surpasses in virtue the people of the Buddha-lands of other quarters who do good for a thousand years. Why is this? In the Buddha-lands of other quarters all do good. Those who do good are many and those who do evil are few, and all have natural things. They do not go seeking and doing, but get them of themselves. Here those who do evil are many and those who do good are few, and if one does not go seeking and doing, one cannot get them. The people of the world can order and govern themselves and do good, and with a whole heart seek the way, and so it is thus. Here there is nothing natural; one cannot supply oneself. One must go seeking, toiling bitterly to make a living. Cheating and deceiving one another in turn, tricking and feigning good and evil. Getting wealth and goods, one brings them home to wife and children. Food and drink poison the mind and weary the body with suffering. Thus to the very end. The heart and mind are not single
yi
tai
gong
xin
— that is, confused and ill at ease. If a person can quiet himself and do good and strive in virtue, then it is thus.”

The Buddha said: “I pity you all, and the devas, kings, and people. I teach and command you all to do every good and not to do any evil. According to what each can do, I at once impart the way. Teaching and admonishing and opening and guiding — all of you, practice them. Then the ruler leads and transforms to good and teaches and commands his ministers; the father teaches his son, the elder brother his younger, the husband his wife; within the household and without, kin and friends teach and speak to one another in turn. Doing good and walking the way, upholding the scriptures and keeping the precepts. Each orders and keeps himself; above and below restrain one another. No honored, no lowly; no man, no woman. Pure in the fasts, there is none who is not glad. Harmonious and reasonable, joyful and compassionate and filial, they bind and restrain one another. Those who obtain the Buddha's words of scripture all hold and think on them. What they ought not to do, if they transgress and do it, they at once repent and turn from evil and draw near to good. They cast off the crooked and make it upright, hearing in the morning and mending by evening. Upholding the scriptures and precepts, the foolish obtain a treasure. Wherever the Buddha has been, in whatever province or kingdom, he at once imparts the scriptures and precepts: to the devas, sun, moon, stars, and gods; to kings, ministers, officials, and people; to nagas, ghosts, and spirits, the hells, the beasts, the hungry ghosts, and the winged and crawling creatures — there is none who does not open in a compassionate heart. All revere and serve, and receive the scriptures and the way from the Buddha with bowed head. They receive and practice them, and the ruler at once changes and is transformed to good. Keeping the fasts, thinking with purity, washing himself clean, ordering his heart and walking straight, he sits in his place in reverence and awe. He teaches and commands and leads the multitude to good. He practices the prohibitions of the way, and makes his commands and words upright. The minister is filial to his lord, loyal and upright, receiving his commands and daring not to defy them. Father and son in their commands are dutiful and obedient. Brothers, husbands and wives, kin and friends. Above and below they command one another, obeying in harmonious reason. Honored and lowly, great and small, serve one another with respect in turn. In propriety and righteousness they do not betray one another, and all change what is past and cultivate what is to come, washing the heart and altering conduct, upright within and without. Naturally doing good, whatever they wish they at once obtain. All good subdues and transforms by the natural way. If one seeks not to die, one may obtain long life; if one seeks deliverance from the world, one may obtain the way of nirvāṇa.”

The Buddha said: “The Buddha's awesome spirit is honored and his virtue weighty; he melts evil into good, and there is none who is not delivered. Now I have come forth into the world, here amid evil, become a Buddha in an age of suffering, in compassion and pity and grief, teaching and speaking and opening and guiding. The devas, kings, ministers and attendants about them, officials and people — according to what their hearts wish and delight in, I cause them all to attain the way. Wherever the Buddha has been, through whatever provinces, counties, towns, hamlets, and marketplaces he has passed, there is nothing that is not abundant and ripe. The world is at great peace; sun and moon move and shine, doubling their brightness and beauty. Wind and rain come in season, and the people are at rest. The strong do not oppress the weak, and each finds his place. There are no bad years or plagues, no sick or wasted folk. Weapons are not raised, and in the land there are no robbers or thieves. There are no grievances
da
ding
wang

; none are imprisoned. Rulers and ministers and people, there is none who does not rejoice and leap up. Loyal and compassionate and utterly sincere, each orders and keeps himself, and each keeps his own land. Harmonious and filial, there is none who is not glad. In having and lacking they give to one another, bestowing kindness and practicing virtue. Their hearts are glad and joyful, and all respect and love. They yield and defer in righteousness and modesty. Before and after, they serve one another with propriety. As father and son, as elder brother and younger brother, there is none who is not benevolent and worthy. Harmonious in propriety and measure, wholly without contention. Blissful and good beyond measure.”

The Buddha said: “I pity you as my children, and wish to deliver you, more than a father and mother think on their child. Now the devas, kings, and people throughout the eight quarters above and below, and the winged and crawling creatures, who obtain the Buddha's scriptures and precepts and practice the Buddha-way, all attain bright wisdom, and their hearts all open and understand; there is none who does not win deliverance from grief. Now that I have become a Buddha amid the five evils, the five pains, and the five burnings, I subdue and transform the five evils, melt away the five pains, and utterly extinguish the five burnings. With good I attack evil and pull out the poison and suffering. I cause them to attain the five paths, to attain the five goods, bright and fair, so that the burning evil does not arise. After I enter parinirvāṇa, the scriptures and the way will gradually be cut off. The people will be flattering and fawning, and gradually do all manner of evil again, and no more do good. The five burnings will rise again. The five pains will be bitter in the extreme. It will be as before. Naturally it will come back again. After a long time it will grow worse, beyond all telling. I have told you only a little of the way.”

The Buddha said to Bodhisattva Ajita and the rest: “Let each of you think on this and hold it, and teach and admonish one another in turn. According to the Buddha's scriptures and dharma, let none dare transgress.”

Bodhisattva Ajita knelt long, pressed his palms together, and said: “The Buddha's record of the way is most bitter and painful, and the people of the world do evil so greatly. The Buddha in his compassion pities them all and delivers them all. We all say that we receive the Buddha's weighty teaching. We beg to teach one another in turn. We dare not transgress.”
The Buddha said to Ānanda: “In my pity for you all, I cause you all to see Amitābha Buddha and the land where the bodhisattvas and arhats dwell. Do you wish to see it?”
Ānanda at once rejoiced greatly, knelt long, pressed his palms together, and said: “I wish to see it all.”
The Buddha said: “Rise, and put on your robe again, and bow toward the west. Where the sun sets, bow to Amitābha Buddha. With your head to the ground, say: Namo Amitābha Samyak-saṃbuddha.”

Ānanda said: “Yes, I receive your teaching. Then he rose, put on his robe again, and bowed toward the west. Where the sun sets, he bowed to Amitābha Buddha. With his head to the ground, he said: Namo Amitābha Samyak-saṃbuddha.”

Before Ānanda had risen, Amitābha Buddha at once sent forth the radiance and awe of his great light. It filled the eight quarters above and below, the countless Buddha-lands; and all the countless heavens and earths were at once greatly shaken. In all the countless heavens and earths, the precious Mount Sumeru and the precious Great Mount Sumeru, and the great and small boundaries of all the heavens and earths — within them the great hells and small hells, and the dark places of the mountains, forests, streams, and valleys — were at once greatly bright, all widely opened and made plain.

Then Ānanda, the bodhisattvas, the arhats, and the devas, kings, and people all saw Amitābha Buddha and the seven treasures of the land of the bodhisattvas and arhats, and their hearts rejoiced and leaped up greatly. All rose and bowed to Amitābha Buddha. With their heads to the ground, they all said: Namo Amitābha Samyak-saṃbuddha.

When the land of Amitābha Buddha sent forth the radiance and awe of its light, all the countless devas and humans and the winged and crawling creatures saw the light of Amitābha Buddha, and there was none whose heart was not compassionate and glad. In all the hells, among the beasts and hungry ghosts, in every place of torment and bitter toil, all at once ceased and tormented no more, and there was none who was not freed from grief. All who were blind at once received sight. All who were deaf at once received hearing. All who were mute at once could speak. All who were bent at once were straightened. The lame, the crippled, and the halt all at once walked and ran. All who were sick at once rose healed. All who were weak at once grew strong. All who were foolish at once became wise. All who were given to lust all practiced the pure life. All who were angry all became compassionate in heart and did good. In all who had taken poison, the poison did not work. Bells and chimes, lutes and zithers, harps and konghous, instruments and all manner of music, sounded of themselves without being struck. The pearls and rings of women gave forth sound of themselves. The hundred birds and the beasts all raised their own plaintive cries. At that time there was none who did not rejoice in good bliss and win deliverance. And at that very time, all the devas and humans throughout the Buddha-lands brought down celestial flowers and incense, and in the empty air made offering to all, scattering them upon all the Buddhas and upon Amitābha Buddha. The devas each together made ten thousand kinds of spontaneous music, delighting all the Buddhas and the bodhisattvas and arhats. At that time the bliss could not be told in words.

The Buddha said to Ānanda: “Ajita the bodhisattva and the rest — when I speak of Amitābha Buddha and of the bodhisattvas and arhats and the land naturally adorned with the seven treasures, is there anything that differs?”

Ānanda knelt long, pressed his palms together, and said: “The Buddha has proclaimed the land of Amitābha Buddha as blissful and good; there is not one thing that differs from what the Buddha has spoken.”
The Buddha said: “Were I to tell of the merit, virtue, and excellence of the land of Amitābha Buddha, a whole kalpa of days and nights would not yet exhaust it; I have told you only a little.”

Bodhisattva Ajita at once knelt long, pressed his palms together, and asked the Buddha: “From this land of the Buddha, how many bodhisattvas of non-retrogression shall there be who are born in the land of Amitābha Buddha? I wish to hear it.”
The Buddha said: “If you wish to know, listen clearly and hold it in your heart.”
Bodhisattva Ajita said: “I receive your teaching.”

The Buddha said: “From this land of mine there shall be seven hundred and twenty koṭis of bodhisattvas of non-retrogression, all to be born in the land of Amitābha Buddha. Each such bodhisattva of non-retrogression, having gone before and made offering to countless Buddhas in succession, shall in turn, as Maitreya does, all become Buddhas; and the rest, the lesser bodhisattvas, countless and beyond reckoning, shall all be born in the land of Amitābha Buddha.”

The Buddha said to Bodhisattva Ajita: “Not only the bodhisattvas in my own land shall be born in the land of Amitābha Buddha. In the Buddha-lands of other quarters there are also Buddhas, and it is likewise with them. The first Buddha is named Surupa; in his land there are a hundred and eighty koṭis of bodhisattvas, all to be born in the land of Amitābha Buddha, in the Buddha-lands of other quarters. The second Buddha is named Ratnakara; in his land there are ninety koṭis of bodhisattvas, all to be born in the land of Amitābha Buddha, in the Buddha-lands of other quarters. The third Buddha is named Suruci; in his land there are two hundred and twenty koṭis of bodhisattvas, all to be born in the land of Amitābha Buddha, in the Buddha-lands of other quarters. The fourth Buddha is named Amṛtarāja; in his land there are two hundred and fifty koṭis of bodhisattvas, all to be born in the land of Amitābha Buddha, in the Buddha-lands of other quarters. The fifth Buddha is named Lobhapravaracai
tiao
zhao
cai

, and in his land there are six hundred koṭis of bodhisattvas, all to be born in the land of Amitābha Buddha, in the Buddha-lands of other quarters. The sixth Buddha is named Nandivicai; in his land there are ten thousand four hundred bodhisattvas, all to be born in the land of Amitābha Buddha, in the Buddha-lands of other quarters. The seventh Buddha is named Vīraprapaṇḍacai
tiao
zhao
cai

, and in his land there are fifteen bodhisattvas, all to be born in the land of Amitābha Buddha, in the Buddha-lands of other quarters. The eighth Buddha is named Ahacai; in his land there are eight bodhisattvas, all to be born in the land of Amitābha Buddha, in the Buddha-lands of other quarters. The ninth Buddha is named Śrīgaṇacai; in his land there are eight hundred and ten koṭis of bodhisattvas, all to be born in the land of Amitābha Buddha, in the Buddha-lands of other quarters. The tenth Buddha is named Nandacai; in his land there are ten thousand koṭis of bodhisattvas, all to be born in the land of Amitābha Buddha, in the Buddha-lands of other quarters. The eleventh Buddha is named Haranavīyuhaicai
tiao
zhao
cai

, and in his land there are twelve thousand bodhisattvas, all to be born in the land of Amitābha Buddha, in the Buddha-lands of other quarters. The twelfth Buddha is named Vipulayanacai; in his land the bodhisattvas are countless and beyond reckoning, all of them of non-retrogression, all wise and valiant, each having made offering to countless Buddhas, and with one mind at one time all wishing to go, they shall all be born in the land of Amitābha Buddha, in the Buddha-lands of other quarters. The thirteenth Buddha is named Svākṣarāvarta; in his land there are seven hundred and ninety koṭis of bodhisattvas, all to be born in the land of Amitābha Buddha.”

The Buddha said: “These bodhisattvas are all of non-retrogression; and among the company of monks, and the lesser bodhisattvas, countless in number, all shall be born in the land of Amitābha Buddha. Not only the bodhisattvas of these fourteen Buddha-lands shall be born there. Throughout the eight quarters above and below, the bodhisattvas of the countless Buddha-lands, each and every one, shall all be born in the land of Amitābha Buddha. Countless beyond number, they shall all go together to the assembly in the land of Amitābha Buddha. The great multitude cannot be reckoned. Were I to tell only the names of the countless Buddhas of the eight quarters above and below, for a whole kalpa of days and nights it would not yet be done. Were I again to tell only the number of the monks and bodhisattvas in the Buddha-lands who shall be born in the land of Amitābha Buddha, telling it for a kalpa without rest, it would not yet be done. I have told you only the whole of it gathered up in little.”

The Buddha said to Ānanda: “Ajita the bodhisattva and the rest — the kings and people of the world, good men and good women, who by good done in former destinies have won towering blessings and honor, so that they may hear the name of Amitābha Buddha — how blissful and good; I rejoice for them.”

The Buddha said: “Those good men and good women who hear the name of Amitābha Buddha, and with a compassionate heart rejoice, leaping up at once; whose hearts and minds are pure and clean, the hair on whose bodies stands on end, and whose tears at once flow — all these have in former destinies walked the Buddha-way. Or they are bodhisattvas from other quarters, come for the sake of the Buddha, and are no ordinary people. And those people, men and women, who hear the name of Amitābha Buddha and do not believe it, who do not believe the scriptures and the Buddha's words, who do not believe there is a company of monks, whose hearts doubt and who believe nothing at all — all these have come from the evil paths to be born here. Foolish and not understanding their former destinies, their calamity and evil are not yet exhausted. Because they are not yet to be delivered, their hearts doubt and they do not believe.”

The Buddha said: “I tell you all: whatever good dharmas you ought to do, you should all practice and believe, and not doubt. After I enter parinirvāṇa, you and the people of later ages must not again say, I do not believe there is a land of Amitābha Buddha. I have caused you all to see the land of Amitābha Buddha, and what should be done, each should seek for himself. I have fully told you the scriptures, the precepts, and the dharma of care, and you should hold them as the Buddha's dharma, and not destroy or lose them. I entrust this scripture to you all; you should firmly hold it, and not deal with it falsely, adding to or taking from this dharma of scripture. After I enter parinirvāṇa, the scriptures and the way will remain for a thousand years. After a thousand years the scriptures and the way will be cut off; in my compassion I will keep this dharma of scripture and let it remain a hundred years. When the hundred years are done, then it will cease and be cut off. According to the wish of the heart, all may attain the way.”

The Buddha said: “A teacher opens and guides people's ears and eyes, and by wisdom and clear understanding delivers them, causing them to attain good and join the way of nirvāṇa. One should always be filial and kind toward the Buddha and one's parents, always think on the teacher's kindness, and think of it without cease — and one shall swiftly attain the way.”
The Buddha said: “A Buddha appearing in the world is very hard to meet with. And if there be a renunciant, or a teacher who expounds the scriptures for others, he is very hard to meet with.”

When the Buddha spoke this scripture, twelve thousand koṭis of devas and humans all attained celestial sight and celestial vision, and all with one mind set out on the bodhisattva-way. Two hundred koṭis of devas and humans all attained the way of the non-returner. Eight hundred renunciants all attained the way of the arhat. Forty koṭis of bodhisattvas all attained non-retrogression.

When the Buddha had spoken the scripture, the bodhisattvas and arhats, the devas, kings, and people all rejoiced greatly, rose, bowed to the Buddha, walked around him three times, and went their way, bowing their heads to the Buddha's feet.

blocks.text: The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on Immeasurable Pure and Equal Enlightenment, Scroll Five

inline.s: Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Saṃghavarman of Tianzhu, in the Cao Wei dynasty.

Thus have I heard. At one time the Buddha dwelt on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa near Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of twelve thousand bhikṣus. All were great saints whose spiritual powers were fully attained. Their names were: the Venerable Kauṇḍinya, the Venerable True Vow, the Venerable True Speech, the Venerable Great Renown, the Venerable Benevolent and Worthy, the Venerable Free of Stain, the Venerable Renowned, the Venerable Noble Lineage, the Venerable Perfect in All, the Venerable Ox King, the Venerable Uruvilvā Kāśyapa, the Venerable Gayā Kāśyapa, the Venerable Nadī Kāśyapa, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, the Venerable Śāriputra, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the Venerable Kalpika, the Venerable Mahāvāsin, the Venerable Mahāvīrya, the Venerable Mahācunda, the Venerable Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, the Venerable Free of Hindrance, the Venerable Abundant Wealth, the Venerable Firmly Subdued, the Venerable King of Countenance, the Venerable Fruit of the Vehicle, the Venerable Benevolent Nature, the Venerable Joy and Bliss, the Venerable Well Come, the Venerable Rāhula, the Venerable Ānanda — all of them foremost men of this kind. And with them were bodhisattvas of the Great Vehicle: the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, the Bodhisattva Maitreya, and all the bodhisattvas of this present Bhadra kalpa; and the sixteen worthies, Bhadrapāla and the rest; the Bodhisattva Well Reasoned, the Bodhisattva Faith and Wisdom, the Bodhisattva Emptiness, the Bodhisattva Spiritual Power and Splendor, the Bodhisattva Light of Splendor, the Bodhisattva Supreme Wisdom, the Bodhisattva Banner of Wisdom, the Bodhisattva Root of Stillness, the Bodhisattva Vow and Wisdom, the Bodhisattva Elephant of Incense, the Bodhisattva Jewel of Splendor, the Bodhisattva Dwelling in the Mean, the Bodhisattva Subdued Conduct, the Bodhisattva Liberation. All of them followed the virtue of the great being Samantabhadra, and were complete in the boundless vows and practices of all bodhisattvas; they dwelt peacefully in the dharma of all merits and virtues, walked through the ten directions, practiced skillful means, entered the treasury of the Buddha-dharma and reached the farther shore, and in countless worlds manifested the attainment of perfect enlightenment.

Dwelling in the Tuṣita heaven, he proclaimed the true Dharma far and wide. Leaving that heavenly palace, he descended in spirit into a mother’s womb; he came forth from her right side, and at once walked seven steps. Light shone forth and blazed, illumining the ten directions; in countless Buddha-lands the earth quaked in six ways, and he raised his voice and declared: “In the world I shall be the Supreme Honored One; Brahmā and Indra shall attend me, and devas and humans shall look up to me in faith!” He displayed his mastery of reckoning, letters and arts, archery and chariot-driving; he was thoroughly versed in the ways and arts, and practiced all the classics. He strolled in the garden, and gave proof of his skill at arms; he dwelt in the palace, amid color and taste. Seeing old age, sickness, and death, he awakened to the impermanence of the world. Renouncing his kingdom, wealth, and throne, he entered the mountains to learn the Way. He sent back his white horse, his jeweled crown, and his necklaces, and dismissed them to return; he put off his precious and wondrous garments and clothed himself in the Dharma robe. He shaved off beard and hair, sat upright beneath the tree, and for six years labored and practiced, doing all that was fitting to do. He appeared in a land of five turbidities and complied with the capacities of living beings. Showing that he had dust and defilement, he bathed in the golden stream; the devas bent down the branches of a tree, and he climbed out of the pool. Winging birds attended him, and he went toward the seat of the Way. Auspicious signs answered his coming and proclaimed the merit of his deeds. In pity he accepted the grass that was offered, spread it beneath the Buddha-tree, and sat down cross-legged. He sent forth a great radiance and let Māra know of it; Māra led his officers and hosts and came to press and test him, but he subdued them all by the power of wisdom. He attained the subtle and wondrous Dharma and accomplished the most perfect enlightenment. Brahmā and Indra prayed and urged him, and begged him to turn the wheel of the Dharma; he walked in the Buddha’s stride, and the Buddha’s roar he roared. He beat the Dharma drum, blew the Dharma conch, held the Dharma sword, raised the Dharma banner, shook the Dharma thunder, flashed the Dharma lightning, poured the Dharma rain, and bestowed the Dharma gift, ever awakening all the world with the voice of Dharma. His light shone everywhere over countless Buddha-lands, and in every world the earth quaked in six ways. He gathered in all the realms of Māra, shook the palaces of Māra, and the hosts of Māra were seized with terror, and none failed to submit. He shattered the net of false views, extinguished all wrong opinions, scattered every dust of affliction, and broke down every moat of desire. He strictly guarded the citadel of Dharma and opened wide the gates of Dharma. He washed away all filth and defilement, made clear and bright what was pure and white, made the Buddha-dharma shine and blend as one, and proclaimed and spread the true transformation.

He entered the towns to receive alms and protected the abundant offerings. He stored up merit and showed the field of blessing. When he wished to proclaim the Dharma, he showed a joyful smile. With the medicine of all dharmas he healed the three sufferings, and revealed the mind of the Way and its boundless merit. He bestowed the prediction of bodhisattvahood and brought beings to perfect enlightenment. He showed his entry into parinirvāṇa and rescued beings without limit. He wiped away all the outflows and planted the roots of every virtue. Complete in merit and virtue, subtle and beyond measure, he walked through all Buddha-lands and everywhere revealed the teaching of the Way. All that he practiced was pure and without stain. He was like a master of illusions who shows a host of strange forms: now a man, now a woman, nothing that he does not become, for his own study is clear and bright and all is as he intends it. So too are all these bodhisattvas. They study all dharmas and master them through and through; where they dwell is peaceful and true, and none they meet but are transformed. In countless Buddha-lands they all appear everywhere, never arrogant or self-indulgent, but grieving in pity for living beings. In this way they are complete in all dharmas.

In the bodhisattva scriptures they fathomed and unfolded the essential and wondrous; their fame reached everywhere, and they guided the ten directions by the Way. Countless Buddhas all protected and remembered them. Where the Buddha dwells, they had all attained to dwell; what the great saints established, they had all established. The Tathāgata’s teaching and transformation each of them could proclaim. For all bodhisattvas they acted as great teachers. With profound meditative wisdom they guided living beings. They penetrated the nature of all dharmas and understood the marks of living beings. They clearly knew all lands and made offerings to all Buddhas. Their transformations appeared like lightning; they skillfully learned the net of fearlessness and understood clearly the dharma of illusion. They broke and tore the net of Māra and loosed all bonds. They transcended the grounds of the hearers and the solitary Buddhas and attained the samādhi of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness. Skillfully establishing skillful means, they revealed the three vehicles. When their transformation here was ended, they showed parinirvāṇa. Yet they did nothing at all, and possessed nothing at all. Neither arising nor ceasing, they attained the dharma of equality. They were complete in accomplishing countless dhāraṇīs and a hundred thousand samādhis.

Their faculties were wise and far-reaching, broad and universally still. They entered deeply into the treasury of the bodhisattva dharmas and attained the Buddha’s flower-adornment samādhi, proclaiming and expounding all the scriptures. Dwelling at the gate of profound meditation, they beheld with one thought all the countless Buddhas of the present, and in a single moment of thought there was nowhere they did not reach. They rescued beings from every grievous peril, whether at leisure or in want of leisure, and distinguished and revealed the true and ultimate; they attained the eloquence and wisdom of all the Tathāgatas. They entered into all the sounds of speech and opened and transformed all beings. They surpassed all dharmas of the world, and their minds ever dwelt truly in the way of delivering the world. Toward all things whatsoever they were free and at ease as they wished. For all the multitudes of beings they were friends who were never asked; they bore the heavy burden of living beings. They received and upheld the Tathāgata’s profound treasury of Dharma and guarded the Buddha-seed, ever keeping it unbroken. They roused great compassion and pitied living beings. They unfolded compassionate eloquence and bestowed the eye of Dharma. They closed the three evil paths and opened the gate of goodness. With the Dharma that is given unasked they benefited all the common folk. Like a child of pure filial piety who loves and reveres his father and mother, so they looked upon all living beings as themselves, and all roots of goodness crossed over to the farther shore. They all obtained the Buddhas’ boundless merit and virtue; their wisdom and sagely clarity were inconceivable. Bodhisattvas and great beings such as these, beyond reckoning, assembled together at that time.

Then the World-Honored One’s faculties were serene and joyful; his bearing and countenance were pure, his radiant face majestic. The Venerable Ānanda, receiving the Buddha’s holy intention, rose from his seat, uncovered his right shoulder, knelt long with palms pressed together, and said to the Buddha: “Today the World-Honored One’s faculties are serene and joyful, his bearing and countenance pure, his radiant face majestic. Like a bright mirror made clean, whose reflections shine through and through within and without, his dignified countenance is bright and shining, surpassing the boundless; never before have I beheld such wondrous excellence as today! And yet, Great Saint, my mind says within me: Today the World-Honored One dwells in a rare and marvelous Dharma; today the World Hero dwells where all Buddhas dwell; today the World Eye walks in the conduct of a guide; today the World’s Chief walks the most victorious way; today the Heaven-Honored One practices the Tathāgata’s virtue. Buddhas past, future, and present are mindful of one another. Might it be that the Buddha of today is mindful of the Buddhas? Why else should his authority and radiance shine so brightly?” Then the World-Honored One said to Ānanda: “How is it, Ānanda? Do the devas send you to question the Buddha, or do you ask about this majestic countenance out of your own wisdom and insight?” Ānanda said to the Buddha: “No devas have come to instruct me; I ask this meaning out of what I myself have seen.”

The Buddha said: “Excellent, Ānanda! Your question is most welcome. You have brought forth profound wisdom and truly wondrous eloquence, and in pity for living beings you ask this meaning of wisdom. With inexhaustible great compassion the Tathāgata takes pity on the three realms; therefore he appears in the world and makes the teaching of the Way shine. He wishes to rescue the multitudes of living beings and give them the benefit of what is true

. Through countless koṭis of kalpas he is hard to meet and hard to see, like the udumbara flower that appears only from time to time. What you have asked now brings benefit to many, and opens and transforms all the devas and people. Ānanda, know that the Tathāgata’s perfect enlightenment — his wisdom is hard to measure and guides and governs many. His wisdom and insight are unobstructed, and none can hold them back. By the power of a single meal he can abide in life for a hundred thousand kalpas, and countless and immeasurable beyond that; his faculties remain serene and joyful and are not worn away, his bearing and countenance do not change, his radiant face is without difference. Why is this? The Tathāgata’s samādhi and wisdom are utterly penetrating and boundless, and in all dharmas he has attained freedom. Ānanda, listen well! Now I shall speak for you!” He answered: “Yes, indeed. Gladly would I hear it!”
The Text on the Original Vow

The Buddha said to Ānanda: “In ages past, long ago, through immeasurable, inconceivable, countless kalpas, the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara appeared in the world. He taught and delivered immeasurable living beings, bringing them all to attain the Way, and then entered parinirvāṇa. Next there was a Tathāgata named Light Afar; next, Moonlight; next, Sandalwood Fragrance; next, Good Mountain King; next, Sumeru Crown of Heaven; next, Sumeru Equal Radiance; next, Moon’s Hue; next, Right Mindfulness; next, Free of Stain; next, Without Attachment; next, Dragon Heaven; next, Night Light; next, Peaceful Bright Summit; next, Immovable Ground; next, Wondrous Flower of Lapis Lazuli; next, Golden Hue of Lapis Lazuli; next, Golden Treasury; next, Blazing Light; next, Blazing Root; next, Seed of Earth; next, Moon’s Image; next, Sun’s Sound; next, Flower of Liberation; next, Adorned Radiance; next, Awakening of the Ocean’s Spiritual Power; next, Water Light; next, Great Fragrance; next, Free of Dust and Stain; next, Abandoning Weariness of Mind; next, Jewel Blaze; next, Wondrous Summit; next, Brave and Steadfast; next, Virtue That Holds Wisdom; next, Sun-and-Moon-Hiding Light; next, Sun-and-Moon Lapis Lazuli Light; next, Supreme Lapis Lazuli Light; next, Highest Foremost; next, Flower of Bodhi; next, Moon Brightness; next, Sunlight; next, King of Flower Hue; next, Water and Moon Light; next, Remover of Deluded Darkness; next, Crosser of the Covered; next, Pure Faith; next, Good Dwelling; next, Awe-Inspiring Spirit; next, Wisdom of Dharma; next, Phoenix Voice; next, Lion’s Voice; next, Dragon’s Voice; next, Dwelling in the World. Tathāgatas such as these have all passed away.”

Then there appeared a Buddha named World Sovereign King, the Tathāgata, the Worthy of Offerings, the Perfectly Enlightened One, the Perfect in Wisdom and Conduct, the Well Gone, the Knower of the World, the Peerless One, the Tamer of Men, the Teacher of Devas and Humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One. At that time there was a king who, hearing the Buddha teach the Dharma, was filled with joy and delight. He straightway brought forth the mind of supreme, true enlightenment, renounced his kingdom and gave up his throne, and went forth as a śramaṇa under the name Dharmākara — a man of lofty ability, brave and wise, surpassing the world. He came to where the Tathāgata World Sovereign King was, bowed his head at the Buddha’s feet, walked around him three times to the right, knelt long with palms pressed together, and praised him in verse:
Majestic is your radiant face, your awesome power without bound. Such blazing brightness as is here has nowhere been equaled found.
The sun and moon, the maṇi gem, the flame and splendor of every pearl — all are hidden quite away, like ink that into one is rolled.
The Tathāgata’s countenance surpasses the world, without a peer. The great sound of perfect enlightenment rings out through the ten directions here.
In discipline, learning, and effort, in samādhi and in wisdom’s store, in awe and virtue without match, supremely rare forevermore.
In profound truth and excellent thought, the ocean of all Buddhas’ dharma, you have fathomed depth and hidden subtlety and reached its very bottom-most.
Of ignorance, desire, and wrath the World-Honored One is forever free. Lion among men, teacher of gods, of boundless spirit and virtue is he.
Vast and great are his merits, deep and wondrous his wisdom’s light; his radiance and his awesome marks shake the great thousand worlds with might.
May I become a Buddha, equal to the sage, the Dharma King, and cross beyond birth and death, till all attain deliverance.
In giving and in taming the mind, in discipline, patience, and effort, in samādhi such as this, and in wisdom that has no support.
I vow that I shall win Buddhahood and carry out this vow for all; for every being in every fear I shall make a great peace to fall.
Suppose there were Buddhas, hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, a hundred million more, great saints beyond all measure, countless as the Ganges’ sand upon the shore.
To make offering to all of them, to every one of these Buddhas, is not to equal seeking the Way with a firm and upright heart that does not pause.
Suppose the Buddha-worlds were as many as the Ganges’ sands, and again beyond all reckoning, lands beyond number in all lands.
My light shall shine upon them all and reach throughout those many lands. Such is my effort, and my awesome spirit none can understand.
Let me become a Buddha, and let my land be the foremost one, its people wondrous, its seat of enlightenment beyond compare.
Let my land be like nirvāṇa, with nothing that can equal it. In pity I shall deliver all; my heart is set on saving it.
Beings from the ten directions who are reborn, their hearts glad and pure, once they reach my land shall dwell in happiness and peace secure.
May the Buddha in faith and clarity be my true witness and my proof; I make my vow before him now, and strive with all my strength for this.
World-Honored Ones of the ten directions, whose wisdom is without a wall, ever let this Honored One know the conduct of my heart through all.
Though my body should abide amid all bitter poisons’ pain, my practice shall go forward still, and I shall bear it without regret.
Verses in Praise of the Buddha

The Buddha said to Ānanda: “When the bhikṣu Dharmākara had spoken this praise, he said to the Buddha: ‘Yes indeed, World-Honored One! I have brought forth the mind of supreme perfect enlightenment. May the Buddha for my sake proclaim the scriptures and the Dharma far and wide. I shall practice them and gather in the Buddha-lands — pure, adorned, and immeasurable wondrous lands — and cause myself quickly to attain perfect enlightenment in this world, and pluck out the root of the bitter toil of birth and death.’”

The Buddha said to Ānanda: “Then the Buddha World Sovereign King said to the bhikṣu Dharmākara: ‘As for the adornment of Buddha-lands through the practices you undertake, you yourself should know them.’ The bhikṣu said to the Buddha: ‘This meaning is vast and profound, and beyond my range. I beg the World-Honored One to unfold and expound for me at length the practice of the pure lands of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas. Hearing it, I shall practice as spoken and bring my vows to fulfillment.’ Then the Buddha World Sovereign King, knowing the height of his mind and the depth and breadth of his vow, spoke this scripture to the bhikṣu Dharmākara: ‘Suppose a man should measure out the great ocean with a single dipper; through the passing of kalpas he could still reach its bottom and obtain its wondrous treasures. If a man with the utmost mind presses forward and seeks the Way without ceasing, he is sure to win the fruit — what vow could he fail to gain?’” Then the Buddha World Sovereign King at length proclaimed for him the lands of the two hundred and ten koṭis of Buddhas, and the good and evil of the devas and humans there, and the coarseness or subtlety of those lands, and in accord with his mind’s wish he caused it all to appear before him. Then that bhikṣu, hearing the Buddha speak of those adorned and pure lands and beholding them all, brought forth a supreme and matchless vow. His mind was still and quiet, and his aspiration clung to nothing. Nothing in all the world could equal him. For five full kalpas he pondered and gathered in the pure practice of adorning Buddha-lands.”

Ānanda said to the Buddha: “How long is the span of that Buddha’s life?” The Buddha said: “That Buddha’s life was forty-two kalpas. Then the bhikṣu Dharmākara gathered in the pure practice of the two hundred and ten koṭis of wondrous Buddha-lands. Having practiced thus, he came to where that Buddha was, bowed his head at the Buddha’s feet, walked around the Buddha three times, stood with palms joined, and said to the Buddha: ‘World-Honored One! I have gathered in the pure practice of adorning Buddha-lands.’ The Buddha said to the bhikṣu: ‘You may now speak, for this is the time to make it known and to rouse and delight the whole great assembly. When bodhisattvas hear it, they will practice this dharma and so fulfill their boundless vows.’ The bhikṣu said to the Buddha: ‘I beg you to hear and consider it. As I have vowed, so shall I now set it all forth:
If, when I attain Buddhahood, there should be hells, hungry ghosts, or animals in my land, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and humans in my land should, after the end of their lives, again fall into the three evil paths, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and humans in my land should not all be of the true golden hue, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and humans in my land should differ in form and appearance, some fair and some foul, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and humans in my land should not know their former lives, even to the extent of knowing the affairs of a hundred thousand koṭis of nayutas of kalpas, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and humans in my land should not obtain the celestial eye, even to the extent of seeing a hundred thousand koṭis of nayutas of Buddha-lands, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and humans in my land should not obtain the celestial ear, even to the extent of hearing all that a hundred thousand koṭis of nayutas of Buddhas teach and receiving and upholding it in full, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and humans in my land should not obtain the knowledge of others’ minds, even to the extent of knowing the thoughts of the living beings in a hundred thousand koṭis of nayutas of Buddha-lands, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and humans in my land should not obtain the spiritual foot, so that in a single thought they cannot pass beyond a hundred thousand koṭis of nayutas of Buddha-lands, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and humans in my land should give rise to thoughts that reckon and cling to a self, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and humans in my land should not dwell in the certainty of the assembly and be sure to reach parinirvāṇa, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
If, when I attain Buddhahood, my light should be limited, so as not to illumine even a hundred thousand koṭis of nayutas of Buddha-lands, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
If, when I attain Buddhahood, my life should be limited, so as to last only a hundred thousand koṭis of nayutas of kalpas, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the hearers in my land should be such that they can be reckoned — even if living beings in worlds as many as three thousand great thousand worlds all became solitary Buddhas and together for a hundred thousand kalpas calculated and numbered them — and their number could be known, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and humans in my land should have lives that can be measured, except as their own vows may make them free to be long or short, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and humans in my land should so much as hear the name of anything unwholesome, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
If, when I attain Buddhahood, the countless Buddhas of the ten directions should not all praise and proclaim my name, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, living beings of the ten directions, with the utmost mind of faith and gladness, wishing to be born in my land, should call my name even ten times and yet not be born there, may I not attain perfect enlightenment. Only those who commit the five grave offences and slander the true Dharma are excepted.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, living beings of the ten directions who bring forth the mind of enlightenment, cultivate all virtues, and with the utmost mind make vows, wishing to be born in my land, should not, at the end of their lives, be met by a great assembly appearing before them, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, living beings of the ten directions who hear my name, hold my land in mind, plant the roots of every virtue, and with the utmost mind transfer the merit, wishing to be born in my land, should fail to accomplish it, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and humans in my land should not all be complete in the thirty-two marks of a great being, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, bodhisattvas from other Buddha-lands who are born in my land should not surely reach the stage of one remaining rebirth, except as their own vows may set them free to transform beings at will, may I not attain perfect enlightenment. For the sake of living beings they don the armor of the great vow, accumulate the roots of virtue, deliver all beings, walk through all Buddha-lands, practice the bodhisattva conduct, and make offerings to all Buddhas and Tathāgatas of the ten directions; they open and transform living beings as countless as the Ganges’ sands, establish them in the supreme true Way, surpass the common ranks, and in the practices of the grounds visibly cultivate the virtue of Samantabhadra.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in my land, by the Buddha’s spiritual power, should make offerings to all Buddhas, and in the space of a single meal cannot reach every one of countless, immeasurable koṭis of nayutas of Buddha-lands, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in my land, before all Buddhas, should manifest the roots of their virtue, and the offerings they seek and desire should not be as they wish, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in my land should be unable to expound the wisdom of the All-Knowing, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in my land should not obtain bodies of diamond, hard as Nārāyaṇa, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, all things in my land — the devas and humans, all the ten thousand things, adorned and pure, bright and fair, of forms and colors beyond the common, fathoming subtlety and reaching the wondrous, beyond all power to weigh — should be such that living beings there, even with the celestial eye, could discern and reckon their names and numbers, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in my land, even those of the least merit, should not know and see the immeasurable light and color of the tree of enlightenment, four million li in height, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in my land who receive, read, recite, and uphold the scriptures and the Dharma, and who chant, keep, and expound them, should not obtain eloquence and wisdom, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
If, when I attain Buddhahood, the wisdom and eloquence of the bodhisattvas in my land should be measurable, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, my land should not be so pure that in that purity one sees, as in a bright mirror one sees one’s own face, all the countless, immeasurable, inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, all things in my land, from the ground up to the empty sky — palaces, towers, terraces, ponds, streams, flowers, and trees, and every one of the ten thousand things — should not all be wrought together out of immeasurable precious substances of many kinds and a hundred thousand perfumes, adorned and wondrous beyond all devas and humans, with that fragrance pervading the worlds of the ten directions, so that bodhisattvas who smell it all practice the Buddha’s conduct, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, living beings of the countless, immeasurable, inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, when my light touches their bodies, should not become soft in body and mind, surpassing the devas and humans, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, living beings of the countless, immeasurable, inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, hearing my name, should not obtain the bodhisattva’s patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas and all profound dhāraṇīs, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, there should be women in the countless, immeasurable, inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions who, hearing my name, rejoice in faith and gladness, bring forth the mind of enlightenment, and loathe the female body, and yet after the end of their lives should again take a woman’s form, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in the countless, immeasurable, inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions who hear my name should not, after the end of their lives, ever practice the pure life until they attain the Buddha-way, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and humans in the countless, immeasurable, inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions who hear my name should not throw themselves down with all five limbs, bow their heads in reverence, rejoice in faith and gladness, and practice the bodhisattva conduct, so that devas and worldlings all pay them respect, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and humans in my land who wish for clothing should have it come at once as their minds think of it, just as the wondrous Dharma robes praised by the Buddha, in accord with the Dharma, come of themselves upon the body, and if there should be any cutting, sewing, pounding, dyeing, or washing, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bliss enjoyed by the devas and humans in my land should not equal that of a bhikṣu whose outflows are exhausted, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in my land who wish, as they please, to see the countless adorned and pure Buddha-lands of the ten directions should not at that very time, as they wish, see them all in the jeweled trees, as in a bright mirror one sees one’s own face, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in the lands of other directions who hear my name should, until they attain Buddhahood, have faculties that are deficient, misshapen, or incomplete, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in the lands of other directions who hear my name should not all obtain the samādhi of purity and liberation, and, dwelling in that samādhi, in the instant of a single thought make offerings to countless, inconceivable World-Honored Buddhas without losing their meditative intent, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in the lands of other directions who hear my name should not, after the end of their lives, be born into noble families, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in the lands of other directions who hear my name should not rejoice and leap up, practice the bodhisattva conduct, and be complete in the roots of virtue, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in the lands of other directions who hear my name should not all obtain the samādhi of universal equality, and, dwelling in that samādhi, until they attain Buddhahood, ever behold all the countless, inconceivable Buddhas, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in my land should not hear at once, of themselves, the Dharma they wish to hear according to their vows, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in the lands of other directions who hear my name should not at once reach the stage of no falling back, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in the lands of other directions who hear my name should not at once reach the first patient acceptance, and the second and third patient acceptance of the Dharma, and in all the Buddha-dharmas at once obtain the stage of no falling back, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.””
The Buddha said to Ānanda: “When the bhikṣu Dharmākara had made these vows, he spoke in verse:
I build a vow that surpasses the world; I shall surely reach the supreme Way. Should this vow of mine not be fulfilled, I swear I shall not win equal enlightenment.
Through countless kalpas, should I fail to be a great giver of alms, relieving all who suffer want and poverty, I swear I shall not win equal enlightenment.
When I attain the Buddha-way, my name shall surpass the ten directions. Should there be any place it is not heard, I swear I shall not win equal enlightenment.
The Verses of the Three Vows
Free of desire and deep in right mindfulness, with pure wisdom practicing the pure life, I seek with all my heart the Supreme Honored One and become a teacher of devas and humans.
By spiritual power I spread a great light over boundless lands everywhere, dispelling the darkness of the three defilements and saving all from every peril and distress.
I shall open the eye of wisdom for them and quench this dim and blinded darkness, close up all the evil paths, and open wide the gate of good rebirths.
When my merit is fulfilled and complete, my radiance shall light the ten directions; the sun and moon shall hide their doubled glow, and the light of heaven shall not appear.
I shall open the Dharma-treasury for all and freely bestow the jewel of merit, and ever amid the great assembly speak the lion’s roar of Dharma.
Making offerings to all Buddhas, complete in all roots of virtue, my vow and wisdom fully accomplished, I shall become the hero of the three realms.
As the Buddha’s wisdom is immeasurable, penetrating all and illumining all, so by the power of my merit may I equal this most victorious Honored One.
If this vow of mine wins its fruit, the great thousand worlds shall quake and move, and all the devas of the empty sky shall rain down rare and wondrous flowers.
The Repeated Vow

The Buddha said to Ānanda: “When the bhikṣu Dharmākara had spoken this verse, at that very time the whole earth quaked in six ways, and the heavens rained wondrous flowers, which were scattered upon him. Music sounded of itself, and a voice in the sky praised him, saying: ‘He is certain to attain supreme perfect enlightenment!’ Then the bhikṣu Dharmākara fully cultivated and fulfilled these great vows — true and not vain, surpassing the world, deeply delighting in stillness and extinction. Ānanda! The bhikṣu Dharmākara, in the presence of that Buddha, amid the great assembly of devas, Māras, Brahmās, dragons, spirits, and the eight kinds of beings, made these great vows; and having made them, he set his mind wholly and single-mindedly on adorning a wondrous land. The Buddha-land he cultivated opened wide and vast, surpassing and uniquely wondrous, established forever, without decay or change. Through inconceivable millions of kalpas he accumulated and planted the bodhisattva’s immeasurable virtues and practices: he gave rise to no thought of desire, no thought of anger, no thought of harm; he did not cling to form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas; he perfected the power of patience and took no account of any suffering. Of few desires and content, unstained by anger or folly, ever still in samādhi, his wisdom unobstructed, he had no mind of falsehood, flattery, or crookedness; with a gentle face and loving words, he understood the other’s meaning before the question was asked. Brave and diligent, his vow never wearied. He sought only the dharma of purity and clarity, to benefit living beings. He revered the Three Treasures and served his teachers. With great adornment he was complete in all practices, causing all living beings to accomplish merit and virtue.

Dwelling in the dharma of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, doing nothing and arising in nothing, he looked upon all dharmas as illusion. He kept far from coarse speech, which harms oneself, harms others, and harms both alike. He practiced good speech, which benefits oneself, benefits others, and benefits both. He renounced his kingdom and gave up his throne, cut away wealth and desire, himself practiced the six pāramitās and taught others to practice them. Through countless kalpas he piled up merit and virtue. Wherever he was born, all was as his mind wished, and immeasurable treasuries of jewels appeared of themselves in answer. He taught and established countless living beings in the supreme true Way. Sometimes he was an elder, a householder, a man of great family or noble birth; sometimes a kṣatriya king, a wheel-turning sage emperor; sometimes a lord of the six heavens of desire, or even a Brahmā king. Ever with the four offerings he made offering and paid reverence to all Buddhas; merit such as this cannot be told. His breath was fragrant and pure as the utpala flower, and from every pore of his body came the fragrance of sandalwood, which perfumed immeasurable worlds. His countenance was upright and fair, his marks and beauties rare and wondrous; from his hands there ever came inexhaustible treasures — clothing, food and drink, rare and wondrous flowers and incense, banners, canopies, standards, and all the implements of adornment. Things such as these surpassed all devas and humans, and in all dharmas he attained freedom.”

Ānanda said to the Buddha: “Has the Bodhisattva Dharmākara already become a Buddha and entered parinirvāṇa? Is he not yet a Buddha? Or is he living now?” The Buddha said to Ānanda: “The Bodhisattva Dharmākara has now become a Buddha.
