He is in the west, a hundred thousand koṭis of lands from here, and his Buddha-world is named Land of Peace and Bliss.” Ānanda asked again: “How long has it been since that Buddha attained the Way?”

The Buddha said: “It is ten kalpas since he attained Buddhahood. In that Buddha-land the ground is naturally of the seven treasures — gold, silver, lapis lazuli, red coral, amber, giant clam, and agate — wrought together as one ground, vast and boundless beyond every limit, each mingled with the others and passing into one another in turn. It blazes with light and shines, subtle and wondrously fair, pure and adorned, surpassing the essence of all the treasures of every world in the ten directions; those treasures are like the treasures of the sixth heaven. And in that land there is no Mount Sumeru, nor any of the mountains of the vajra enclosure, nor great oceans, small seas, streams, channels, wells, or valleys — yet by the Buddha’s spiritual power, if one wishes to see them, one sees them. There are no hells, no hungry ghosts, no animals, none of the destinies of woe. There are no four seasons of spring, summer, autumn, and winter; it is neither cold nor hot, but ever harmonious and well attempered.”

Then Ānanda said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One! If there is no Mount Sumeru in that land, on what do the Four Heavenly Kings and the heaven of Trāyastriṃśa rest?” The Buddha said to Ānanda: “On what do the third Yāma heaven, and even the heaven of the utmost form, all rest?” Ānanda said to the Buddha: “The fruit of deeds is inconceivable.” The Buddha said to Ānanda: “The fruit of deeds is inconceivable, and the Buddha-worlds are inconceivable too; the merit and power of goodness of the living beings there rest upon the ground of deeds, and so it can be thus.” Ānanda said to the Buddha: “I do not doubt this dharma, but for the sake of living beings to come, wishing to put away their doubts and confusion, I ask this meaning.”

The Buddha said to Ānanda: “The authority and radiance of Amitābha, the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity, are the most honored and foremost, and the light of no other Buddha can equal them. Some illumine a hundred Buddha-worlds, some a thousand Buddha-worlds; to put it briefly, they illumine Buddha-lands as countless as the Ganges’ sands to the east, and to the south, west, and north, and in the four intermediate directions, above and below, it is the same. Or again, some Buddha-lights shine seven feet, some a yojana, two, three, four, or five yojanas, and so doubling on and on, until they illumine one Buddha-land. Therefore Amitābha, the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity, is called the Buddha of Immeasurable Light, the Buddha of Boundless Light, the Buddha of Unobstructed Light, the Buddha of Peerless Light, the Buddha of Blazing King Light, the Buddha of Pure Light, the Buddha of Joyous Light, the Buddha of Wisdom Light, the Buddha of Unbroken Light, the Buddha of Inconceivable Light, the Buddha of Ineffable Light, and the Buddha of Light Surpassing Sun and Moon. Whatever living beings encounter this light have their three defilements wiped away; in body and mind they grow soft, they rejoice and leap up, and a good mind arises in them. Those in the three evil paths, in places of utmost suffering, seeing this light, all find rest and are troubled by grief no more, and after the end of their lives all are delivered. The light of Amitābha, the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity, is bright and blazing, illumining the ten directions, and there is no Buddha-land where it is not heard of. Not only do I now praise his light: all Buddhas, hearers, solitary Buddhas, and the assemblies of bodhisattvas all praise it in the same way. If there are living beings who hear of the authority, spirit, and merit of his light, and day and night proclaim it with an unbroken mind, then as they wish, so shall they be born in that land. They shall be praised by all bodhisattvas and hearers, who will proclaim their merit; and when they afterward attain the Buddha-way, they shall be praised for their light by all Buddhas and bodhisattvas of the ten directions, even as I now praise it.”
The Buddha said: “Were I to proclaim the majestic and wondrous light and authority of Amitābha, the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity, for a whole kalpa day and night, I still could not finish!”

The Buddha said to Ānanda: “And the life of Amitābha, the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity, is long and enduring beyond all reckoning. Do you know it? Suppose that all the countless living beings of the worlds of the ten directions all obtained human bodies and all were brought to the stage of hearers or solitary Buddhas, and all gathered together in one place, meditating with one mind; and though they exhausted all their power of wisdom and for a hundred thousand million kalpas together calculated and compared the length of his life, they could not exhaust it or know its limit. The lives of the assembly of hearers, bodhisattvas, devas, and humans are likewise such, and cannot be known by reckoning or by parable. And moreover, the hearers and bodhisattvas there are beyond measure in number and beyond all telling; their spiritual wisdom is penetrating and their authority is free, so that they can hold all worlds in the palm of the hand.”

The Buddha said to Ānanda: “At that Buddha’s first assembly the number of hearers could not be told, and of bodhisattvas likewise. Even if there were beings like Mahāmaudgalyāyana, a hundred thousand million koṭis of them, immeasurable and countless, and for asaṃkhyeya nayutas of kalpas, until they entered parinirvāṇa, they all together calculated and compared, they could not find out how many there were. It is like the great ocean, deep and vast without measure. Suppose a man divided a single hair into a hundred parts, and with one part of a hair took up a single drop of that water: what do you think? Is the water he takes up much, compared with that great ocean?” Ānanda said to the Buddha: “The water he takes up, compared with the great ocean, is a measure of much and little that no clever reckoning, no counting, no words, no parable could ever know.” The Buddha said to Ānanda: “Just so, Maudgalyāyana and those like him, through a hundred thousand koṭis of nayutas of kalpas, might count the hearers and bodhisattvas of that first assembly, and the number they could know would be like a single drop, while what they did not know would be like the waters of the great ocean.

And in that land there are jewel trees of the seven treasures, filling the whole world all around: trees of gold, trees of silver, trees of lapis lazuli, trees of crystal, trees of red coral, trees of agate, and trees of giant clam. Some are wrought together out of two treasures, some of three, and so on up to seven treasures, each in turn combined with the rest. Some have gold for the tree, silver for the leaves, flowers, and fruit; some have silver for the tree, gold for the leaves, flowers, and fruit; some have lapis lazuli for the tree, crystal for the leaves, and the flowers and fruit likewise; some have crystal for the tree, lapis lazuli for the leaves, and the flowers and fruit likewise; some have red coral for the tree, agate for the leaves, and the flowers and fruit likewise; some have agate for the tree, lapis lazuli for the leaves, and the flowers and fruit likewise; some have giant clam for the tree, all the treasures for the leaves, and the flowers and fruit likewise.

Or some jewel trees have purple gold for the root, silver for the trunk, lapis lazuli for the branches, crystal for the boughs, red coral for the leaves, agate for the flowers, and giant clam for the fruit. Or some jewel trees have silver for the root, lapis lazuli for the trunk, crystal for the branches, red coral for the boughs, agate for the leaves, giant clam for the flowers, and purple gold for the fruit. Or some jewel trees have lapis lazuli for the root, crystal for the trunk, red coral for the branches, agate for the boughs, giant clam for the leaves, purple gold for the flowers, and silver for the fruit. Or some jewel trees have crystal for the root, red coral for the trunk, agate for the branches, giant clam for the boughs, purple gold for the leaves, silver for the flowers, and lapis lazuli for the fruit. Or some jewel trees have red coral for the root, agate for the trunk, giant clam for the branches, purple gold for the boughs, silver for the leaves, lapis lazuli for the flowers, and crystal for the fruit. Or some jewel trees have agate for the root, giant clam for the trunk, purple gold for the branches, silver for the boughs, lapis lazuli for the leaves, crystal for the flowers, and red coral for the fruit. Or some jewel trees have giant clam for the root, purple gold for the trunk, silver for the branches, lapis lazuli for the boughs, crystal for the leaves, red coral for the flowers, and agate for the fruit. Row upon row they stand matched to one another, trunk to trunk they face one another, branch to branch they are leveled to one another, leaf to leaf they turn toward one another, flower to flower they follow one another, fruit to fruit they answer one another, and their purple radiance is too great to look upon. When the clear breeze rises in its season, it sends forth the five tones, and subtle and wondrous gong and shang notes harmonize of themselves.

And the tree of enlightenment of Amitābha, the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity, is four million li in height; its root is five thousand yojanas around, and its branches and leaves spread out two hundred thousand li. It is naturally wrought of all precious substances together, adorned with the moonlight maṇi and the sea-holding wheel-jewel, king of all jewels, and all around, strung among the boughs, hang jeweled necklaces of a hundred thousand myriads of colors, of many kinds and strange transformations, with immeasurable light and flame shining beyond all limit. A rare and wondrous jeweled net is spread over it, and all adornments appear as they are wished. A gentle breeze slowly stirs and blows upon the jewel trees, sending forth immeasurable wondrous sounds of Dharma. Those sounds flow out and spread through every Buddha-land. Whoever hears them attains the profound patient acceptance of dharmas and dwells in no falling back, and until they attain the Buddha-way their ear-faculty is pure and clear and they meet with no suffering. Whoever sees its color with the eye, knows its fragrance with the nose, tastes its flavor with the mouth, touches its light with the body, or takes the Dharma as the object of the mind, all attain the profound patient acceptance of dharmas, dwell in no falling back until they attain the Buddha-way, and have their six faculties pure and clear, free of every trouble. Ānanda! If the devas and humans in that land see this tree, they attain three patient acceptances: first, the patient acceptance of sound; second, the patient acceptance of compliant gentleness; third, the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas. This is all by the power of the authority and spirit of Amitābha, the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity, by the power of his original vow, the power of his fulfilled vow, the power of his clear vow, the power of his firm vow, and the power of his ultimate vow.”

The Buddha said to Ānanda: “The kings of the world have a hundred thousand kinds of music, and from the wheel-turning sage king up to the sixth heaven, the sounds of their instruments and music surpass one another a thousand, ten thousand, a hundred million times over. Yet the ten thousand kinds of music of the sixth heaven do not equal one sound of one of the seven-jewel trees of the land of Amitābha of Immeasurable Life by a thousand million times! There too there are ten thousand kinds of music that come of themselves, and those sounds of music are none of them other than the sound of Dharma. Clear, flowing, plaintive, and bright, subtle, wondrous, harmonious, and elegant, it is the foremost of all sounds in the worlds of the ten directions.

Its lecture halls, monasteries, palaces, and towers are all adorned with the seven treasures and come into being of themselves by transformation, and are further laced and draped over with true pearls, moonlight, maṇi, and all the precious substances. Within and without, to left and right, there are bathing pools, some ten yojanas, some twenty or thirty, even a hundred thousand yojanas; in length, breadth, and depth each is of one measure. The water of the eight virtues lies clear and brimming full, pure, fragrant, and clean, tasting like sweet dew. The pool of gold has a bottom of silver sand; the pool of silver has a bottom of gold sand; the pool of crystal has a bottom of lapis lazuli sand; the pool of lapis lazuli has a bottom of crystal sand; the pool of red coral has a bottom of amber sand; the pool of amber has a bottom of red coral sand; the pool of giant clam has a bottom of agate sand; the pool of agate has a bottom of giant clam sand; the pool of white jade has a bottom of purple gold sand; the pool of purple gold has a bottom of white jade sand; or two treasures, three treasures, and so on up to seven treasures are wrought together in turn. On the banks of those pools stand sandalwood trees, whose flowers and leaves hang down and spread, their fragrance perfuming all around. Celestial utpala flowers, padma flowers, kumuda flowers, and puṇḍarīka flowers, mingled in color and rich in light, cover the water everywhere.

When those bodhisattvas and the assembly of hearers enter the jewel pools, if their minds wish the water to cover their feet, the water covers their feet; if they wish it to reach their knees, it reaches their knees; if they wish it to reach their waists, the water reaches their waists; if they wish it to reach their necks, the water reaches their necks; if they wish it to wash their bodies, of itself it washes their bodies; if they wish it to return again, the water at once returns. It tempers warmth and coolness of itself as they please, opens the spirit and delights the body, washes away the stains of the mind, and is clear, bright, and limpid, pure as if formless. The jewel sands mirror one another through and through, and there is no depth it does not illumine; the clear ripples swirl and flow back, pouring into one another, moving gently and calmly, neither slow nor hurried. The waves lift up immeasurable wondrous sounds that come of themselves, and whatever each being is fit to hear, there is none who does not hear it. Some hear the sound of the Buddha, some the sound of the Dharma, some the sound of the Saṅgha; some the sound of stillness, the sound of emptiness and no-self, the sound of great compassion, the sound of the pāramitās; some the sound of the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the dharmas not held in common, the sound of all spiritual wisdom, the sound of nothing done, the sound of no arising or ceasing, the sound of the patient acceptance of non-arising, and even the sound of the ambrosial consecration, and all the wondrous sounds of Dharma. With sounds such as these, each according to what they hear, they rejoice beyond measure.

In accord with the pure, desire-free, still, and true meaning; in accord with the power of the Three Treasures and the dharmas of no contention and not held in common; in accord with the way walked by the penetrating wisdom of bodhisattvas and hearers. There is no name of the suffering of the three evil paths, but only the sounds of natural joy and bliss; therefore that land is named the Land of Utmost Bliss.

Ānanda! All those who are reborn in that Buddha-land are complete in pure bodies of form such as these, in all wondrous sounds, and in spiritual powers and merit. The palaces they dwell in, their clothing, food and drink, all the wondrous flowers and incense, and the implements of adornment are like the things that come of themselves in the sixth heaven. When they wish to eat, vessels of the seven treasures appear of themselves before them — gold, silver, lapis lazuli, giant clam, agate, red coral, amber, moonlight, and true pearl; such vessels come as their minds wish, and food and drink of a hundred flavors brim full within them of itself. And though there is such food, there is in truth no one who eats it: they merely see its color and smell its fragrance, and with the mind they take it as food, and of themselves are filled and satisfied. Body and mind grow soft, and they have no relish or clinging; when the matter is done, it vanishes away, and when the time comes, it appears again.

That Buddha-land is pure and peaceful, subtle and wondrously blissful, next only to the way of unconditioned nirvāṇa. Its hearers, bodhisattvas, devas, and humans are lofty and bright in wisdom and penetrating in spiritual powers, all of one single kind, with no difference in form or appearance — only because they conform to the other regions are they given the names of devas and humans. Their countenances are upright and fair, rare and surpassing the world; their bearing and color are subtle and wondrous, neither deva nor human, and all receive bodies of natural emptiness and formlessness, and bodies without limit.”

The Buddha said to Ānanda: “Suppose a poor beggar in the world were set beside a king: could his form and appearance be compared to the king’s?” Ānanda said to the Buddha: “Even if this man stood beside a king, he would be blemished and foul, beyond all comparison, a hundred thousand million koṭis of times beyond reckoning. Why is this? The poor beggar is at the very bottom and lowest of all; his clothes do not cover his body, and his food is only enough to keep him alive. Beset by hunger and cold and hardship, he is worn to the dregs of human decency. All this is because in former lives he planted no roots of virtue, hoarded wealth and gave no gifts, and the richer he grew the stingier he became, wanting only to get things for nothing, greedy and insatiable. He had no faith in practicing good, and his evil deeds piled up like a mountain. Thus when his life ended, his wealth and treasures scattered and vanished. His toilsome body had heaped them up, and for them he was plagued with worry, yet they profited himself nothing, and in vain they became another’s. With no good to lean on and no virtue to rely upon, at death he fell into evil destinies and received this long suffering; when his offences were done and he escaped from them, he was born low and mean, foolish and vulgar to the utmost, showing a form like a human being. And so the kings of the world, alone honored among men, all come to this by virtue piled up in former lives. They were kind and generous, giving broadly, benevolent and loving, helping all; they kept faith and practiced good, and quarreled with no one. Therefore at the end of their lives blessings answered them and they rose to good destinies. They were born above in the heavens and enjoyed that blessing and bliss; and the surplus blessing of piled-up good has now made them human, born into a royal house, naturally honored and noble. Their bearing and countenance are upright and fair, and all revere and serve them. Wondrous clothing and rare delicacies follow their minds as they wear and use them; the blessing of former lives has followed them, and so they can bring this about.”

The Buddha said to Ānanda: “What you say is so. Reckon that a king, though honored among men and upright and fair in form and color, compared with a wheel-turning sage king is utterly mean and base, like that beggar beside a king. The wheel-turning sage king, whose majestic marks are rare and wondrous and first in all the world, compared with the king of the heaven of Trāyastriṃśa is again hideous and foul, and cannot be compared by ten thousand koṭis of times. Suppose the celestial emperor were compared with the king of the sixth heaven: a hundred thousand koṭis of times and no likeness at all. And suppose the king of the sixth heaven were compared with the bodhisattvas and hearers of the land of Amitābha of Immeasurable Life: their light and countenance and bearing and color do not come near them, by a hundred thousand million koṭis of times beyond all reckoning.”

The Buddha said to Ānanda: “In the land of Amitābha of Immeasurable Life, the clothing, food and drink, flowers and incense, necklaces, banners, canopies, and standards, the subtle and wondrous sounds, and the dwellings and palaces and towers and pavilions of the devas and humans there — all accord with their forms and colors, their height and size, whether of one treasure, two treasures, or up to immeasurable many treasures — as their minds wish and desire, so at a thought they come. And again, wondrous garments of many jewels are spread over all the ground, and all the devas and humans walk treading upon them. Immeasurable jeweled nets cover the Buddha-land all over, all woven of threads of gold and true pearls and a hundred thousand mingled treasures, rare and wondrous and precious and strange, adorned and decked in order; all around the four sides hang jeweled bells, whose light and color shine and blaze in utmost splendor. A natural wind of virtue slowly rises and gently stirs. That wind is harmonious and temperate, neither cold nor warm, mild and cool and soft, neither slow nor hurried. It blows upon the nets and all the jewel trees and sends forth immeasurable subtle and wondrous sounds of Dharma, and spreads abroad ten thousand kinds of gentle and elegant fragrant virtue. Those who hear it have the dust of affliction and the habits of defilement no longer arise; and when the wind touches their bodies, all obtain happiness and bliss, like a bhikṣu who has attained the samādhi of extinction.

And again, the wind scatters flowers that fill the Buddha-land all over; they fall in order according to their colors and are never in disorder, soft and shining, fragrant and richly scented. When one treads upon them, they sink four inches, and as soon as the foot is lifted they are as before. When the flowers have served their use, the ground at once opens and they vanish away in order, pure and leaving no trace. In season the wind scatters flowers again, and six times over it is so. And again, jeweled lotus flowers of many treasures fill the whole world all around; each jewel flower has a hundred thousand koṭis of petals, and the light of those flowers is of immeasurable kinds and colors — blue flowers with blue light, white flowers with white light; black, yellow, vermilion, and purple, their light and color blazing, glorious and radiant, illumining sun and moon. From each flower come thirty-six hundred thousand koṭis of rays of light, and from each ray of light come thirty-six hundred thousand koṭis of Buddhas, their bodies the color of purple gold and their marks and beauties rare and wondrous; and each of those Buddhas again sends forth a hundred thousand lights and proclaims the subtle and wondrous Dharma for the ten directions everywhere. Thus those Buddhas each establish immeasurable living beings in the true Way of the Buddha.”

The Buddha said to Ānanda: “Whatever living beings are born in that land all dwell in the assembly of right certainty. Why is this? In that Buddha-land there are no assemblies of wrong views, nor assemblies of uncertainty. All the Buddhas and Tathāgatas of the ten directions, countless as the Ganges’ sands, together praise the authority, spirit, and merit of Amitābha, the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity, as inconceivable. Whatever living beings hear his name, and with a mind of faith rejoice, even for a single thought, and with the utmost mind transfer the merit, vowing to be born in that land, at once attain rebirth and dwell in no falling back. Only those who commit the five grave offences and slander the true Dharma are excepted.”
The Text on the Fulfillment of the Eighteenth Vow

The Buddha said to Ānanda: “The devas and humans of the worlds of the ten directions who with the utmost mind wish to be born in that land are of three grades. Those of the upper grade leave home and abandon desire, become śramaṇas, bring forth the mind of enlightenment, single-mindedly and constantly invoke Amitābha of Immeasurable Life, cultivate all virtues, and vow to be born in that land. When the lives of such living beings are ending, Amitābha of Immeasurable Life, together with a great assembly, appears before them, and at once they follow that Buddha and are reborn in his land; there in a jeweled lotus flower they are born by transformation, dwell in no falling back, and are brave in wisdom and free in their spiritual powers. Therefore, Ānanda, whatever living beings wish to see Amitābha of Immeasurable Life in this present life should bring forth the mind of supreme enlightenment, cultivate merit and virtue, and vow to be born in that land!”

The Buddha said to Ānanda: “Those of the middle grade are the devas and humans of the worlds of the ten directions who with the utmost mind wish to be born in that land. Though they cannot go forth and become śramaṇas or greatly cultivate merit, they should bring forth the mind of supreme enlightenment, single-mindedly and constantly invoke Amitābha of Immeasurable Life, practice good in greater or lesser measure, keep the fasts and precepts, raise stūpas and make images, feed śramaṇas, hang banners and light lamps, scatter flowers and burn incense, and with this transfer the merit, vowing to be born in that land. When such a person is at the point of death, Amitābha of Immeasurable Life manifests a transformed body before them, whose light and marks and beauties are complete like the true Buddha’s, together with a great assembly. At once they follow the transformed Buddha and are reborn in that land, dwell in no falling back, and their merit and wisdom rank next to the upper grade.”

The Buddha said to Ānanda: “Those of the lower grade are the devas and humans of the worlds of the ten directions who with the utmost mind wish to be born in that land. Though they cannot perform any meritorious deeds, they should bring forth the mind of supreme enlightenment, and single-mindedly and with one intent, even to ten thoughts, call upon Amitābha of Immeasurable Life and vow to be born in his land. If they hear the profound Dharma and rejoice in faith, without giving rise to doubt, even for a single thought, thinking upon that Buddha with a most sincere mind, and vow to be born in his land — such a person, at the point of death, dreams of that Buddha and also attains rebirth, and their merit and wisdom rank next to the middle grade.”

The Buddha told Ānanda: “Amitābha, the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity, is boundless in majestic power. In the worlds of the ten directions, the immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable Buddhas and Tathagatas all praise him. In the eastern direction, in Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, immeasurable and countless bodhisattvas all journey to where the Buddha of Immeasurable Life dwells, to revere and make offerings to him and to the assemblies of bodhisattvas and hearers, to listen to and receive the sutras and Dharma, and to proclaim the teaching of the Way. In the southern, western, and northern directions, and in the four intermediate directions, above and below, it is likewise so.”
Then the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
In Buddha-lands of the east, their number like the Ganges’ sands, the bodhisattvas of those lands go to behold the Buddha of Immeasurable Enlightenment.
South, west, and north, the four intermediate directions, above and below as well: the bodhisattvas of those lands go to behold the Buddha of Immeasurable Enlightenment.
All those bodhisattvas each bring heavenly wondrous flowers, precious incense, and priceless garments, to make offerings to the Buddha of Immeasurable Enlightenment.
All together they play heavenly music, pouring forth harmonious and elegant sounds, singing in praise of the most supreme Honored One, making offerings to the Buddha of Immeasurable Enlightenment.
Fully penetrating the wisdom of spiritual powers, they enter the profound Dharma-gates; complete in the treasury of merit, their wondrous wisdom has no equal.
The sun of wisdom lights up the world, dispelling the clouds of birth and death; reverently they circle three times and bow their heads to the Unsurpassed Honored One.
Seeing that adorned Pure Land, subtle and inconceivable, they accordingly bring forth the immeasurable mind—may my land be likewise.
Then the Honored One of Immeasurable Life changed countenance and gave a joyful smile; from his mouth came countless rays of light, illumining the lands of the ten directions.
The light returned and circled his body, then after three circuits entered at the crown of his head; all the assemblies of devas and humans leaped up and rejoiced.
The great being Avalokiteshvara, adjusting his robes, bowed his head and asked, addressing the Buddha: for what reason do you smile? Pray, tell us your meaning.
The Brahma-voice is like thunder; the eight tones pour forth wondrous sound. I shall bestow the bodhisattva prediction; now I speak—listen well, good sir.
Upright men who come from the ten directions—I know all their vows: they aspire to adorn the Pure Land and, having received the prophecy, shall become Buddhas.
Awakening to all dharmas as like a dream, an illusion, an echo, they fulfill all their wondrous vows and shall surely accomplish such a land.
Knowing dharmas to be like lightning flashes, they perfect the bodhisattva way; with all the roots of their merit, having received the prophecy, they shall become Buddhas.
Penetrating the nature of all dharmas, all is empty and without self; with wisdom they seek the pure Buddha-land and shall surely accomplish such a land.
The Buddhas tell the bodhisattvas: now go and behold the Buddha of Peace and Nourishment; hearing the Dharma, take joy in practicing it, and swiftly attain the land of purity.
Arriving in that adorned and purified land, they will swiftly gain spiritual powers, and before the Honored One of Immeasurable Life they will receive the prophecy and accomplish equal enlightenment.
By the power of that Buddha’s original vows, those who hear his name and wish to be reborn all reach that land and of themselves attain irreversibility.
Bodhisattvas bring forth the highest vow—may my land be without difference—and universally resolve to save all beings; their fame shines throughout the ten directions.
Serving a hundred million Tathagatas, flying in transformation to every land, reverently and joyfully they depart and return again to the Land of Peace and Nourishment.
If a person has no good mind, he cannot hear this sutra; only the pure who keep the precepts may hear the right Dharma.
Those who have met the World-Honored One before can believe this matter; humble and reverent, they hear and practice it, leaping up in great joy.
The proud, the mean, and the indolent find it hard to believe this Dharma; those who have seen the Buddhas in former lives delight in hearing such a teaching.
Hearers or bodhisattvas cannot fathom the saintly mind; it is as with one born blind who would lead and guide others.
The Tathagata’s ocean of wisdom is deep and vast, without shore or bottom; the two vehicles cannot fathom it—only a Buddha alone understands it clearly.
Suppose all people were complete in having attained the Way, with pure wisdom like original emptiness, and for a million kalpas pondered the Buddha’s wisdom—
exhausting their powers and expounding it to the utmost, to the end of life they still would not know it; the Buddha’s wisdom has no bound—thus does one attain purity.
A human lifespan is most hard to obtain, and a Buddha’s world most hard to meet; that people have faith and wisdom is hard—if you hear, strive on and seek.
Hearing the Dharma, able to hold it in mind and, seeing and revering it, gaining great celebration—such a one is my good friend; therefore you should set your mind on it.
Though the whole world were filled with fire, one must pass through it to hear the Dharma; one will surely accomplish the Buddha-way and broadly rescue the stream of birth and death.
Verses on Going to Behold

The Buddha told Ānanda: “The bodhisattvas in that land shall all ultimately reach the stage of one lifetime from Buddhahood, except those whose original vows, for the sake of living beings, adorn themselves with the merit of their great vows, wishing universally to save and release all living beings. Ānanda, among the hearers in that Buddha’s land, the bodily radiance of each is one fathom; the radiance of the bodhisattvas shines for a hundred yojanas. There are two bodhisattvas, most honored and foremost, whose majestic radiance illumines three thousand great thousand worlds.”

Ānanda said to the Buddha: “What are the names of those two bodhisattvas?” The Buddha said: “One is named Avalokiteshvara, the second is named Mahasthamaprapta. These two bodhisattvas cultivated the bodhisattva practice in this land, and when their lives ended they were transformed and born in that Buddha’s land. Ānanda, all living beings born in that land are complete in the thirty-two marks, fulfilled in wisdom, deeply entering all dharmas, thoroughly penetrating the essential and wondrous, unobstructed in spiritual powers, with clear and keen faculties. Those of dull faculties accomplish the two forbearances; those of keen faculties attain the incalculable forbearance of the non-arising of dharmas. Moreover, those bodhisattvas, until they become Buddhas, do not undergo evil destinies; sovereign in spiritual powers, they always know their past lives. They are excepted only if born in another region of the five turbid evil worlds, where they manifest like those there, as in my own land.”

The Buddha said to Ānanda: “The bodhisattvas in that land, sustained by the Buddha’s majestic power, in the time of a single meal journey to the immeasurable worlds of the ten directions and reverently make offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones. Whatever their minds conceive—flowers and incense, music, garments and canopies, banners and pennants, and offerings immeasurable and countless—arises by transformation of itself and arrives as soon as thought of. Rare, wondrous, and surpassing, such as the world does not possess, they scatter them in offering before the Buddhas and the assemblies of bodhisattvas and hearers. In the sky they transform into flower canopies, blazing with light and color, their fragrance pervading all. Where those flowers are four hundred li around, in like manner doubling again and again, they cover three thousand great thousand worlds, and following one after another they vanish by transformation. All those bodhisattvas, rejoicing together, in the sky join in heavenly music and with subtle and wondrous sounds sing in praise of the Buddha’s virtues; hearing and receiving the sutras and Dharma, their joy is immeasurable. Having made offerings to the Buddha, before they have eaten, they suddenly rise lightly and return to their own land.”

The Buddha said to Ānanda: “When Amitābha, the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity, proclaims the Dharma to the hearers, bodhisattvas, devas, and humans, they all gather in the Hall of the Seven Treasures, where he broadly proclaims the teaching of the Way and unfolds the wondrous Dharma; none fails to rejoice, and their minds open in understanding and attain the Way. At once winds arise naturally from the four quarters, blowing on the trees of the seven treasures and bringing forth the five tones. Immeasurable wondrous flowers scatter with the wind in every direction, making offerings of themselves, and so without cease. All the devas each bring hundreds of thousands of heavenly flowers and incenses and ten thousand kinds of music, making offerings to that Buddha and to the assemblies of bodhisattvas and hearers. They scatter flowers and incense everywhere and play all kinds of music, coming and going back and forth, each making way for the other; at such a time their joy and delight cannot be fully told.”

The Buddha told Ānanda: “Whatever the bodhisattvas born in that Buddha’s land expound, they always proclaim the right Dharma, in accord with wisdom, without transgression or loss. Toward all things in that land they have no mind of ‘mine,’ no mind of defilement. In coming and going, advancing and resting, their feelings are tied to nothing. According to their wish they are sovereign, without preference or aversion; without ‘that’ or ‘I,’ without contention or dispute. Toward all living beings they gain a mind of great compassion and beneficence. Soft and tamed, they have no mind of hatred. Apart from the coverings, they are pure, with no mind of weariness or indolence. They have the mind of equality, the mind of victory, the mind of profundity, the mind of concentration, and the mind that loves, delights in, and rejoices in the Dharma. They extinguish all afflictions and are free of the mind of evil destinies. They fulfill all the practices of the bodhisattvas and are complete in accomplishing immeasurable merit. They attain profound meditative concentration, all penetrations and clear wisdom, and roam in aspiration through the seven factors of enlightenment, cultivating the mind of the Buddha-Dharma.

With the fleshly eye, clear and pure, nothing is not distinctly seen; with the divine eye, penetrating, immeasurable and boundless; with the Dharma-eye, observing, they fathom all paths; with the wisdom-eye, seeing the truth, they can cross to the other shore; with the Buddha-eye, complete, they awaken to the nature of dharmas and, with unobstructed wisdom, expound the Dharma for others. They regard the three realms equally, as empty and nothing at all; they aspire to the Buddha-Dharma, are complete in all eloquence, and extinguish the afflictions that torment living beings. Born from the Tathagata, they understand dharmas as they truly are, and are skilled in knowing the methods of the sound of gathering and cessation. They take no delight in worldly speech but rejoice in right discourse. They cultivate all roots of goodness and aspire to the Buddha-way. Knowing that all dharmas are utterly quiescent, they exhaust both the afflictions of this present body and the residues that remain. Hearing the profound Dharma, their minds feel no doubt or fear. Those who can always practice great compassion are deep, vast, and subtle, bearing and covering all. They reach the ultimate One Vehicle and arrive at the other shore; they cut through the net of doubt, and wisdom issues from the mind.

In the Buddha’s teaching they embrace all without exception; their wisdom is like the great sea, their samadhi like the king of mountains. The light of their wisdom is pure and bright, surpassing the sun and moon. The dharmas of purity are complete and perfect. Like a mountain of clouds, they illumine all merits with a single purity; like the earth, they hold no different mind toward pure or foul, good or bad; like pure water, they wash away all dust and defilement; like the king of fire, they burn up the fuel of every affliction; like a great wind, they move through all worlds without obstruction; like space, they cling to nothing in all existence; like a lotus flower, they are unstained by any world; like a great vehicle, they carry multitudes across birth and death; like thick clouds, they shake the great Dharma-thunder to awaken the unawakened; like abundant rain, they rain the sweet dew of Dharma to nourish living beings; like a diamond mountain, they cannot be shaken by demons or outsiders; like Brahma, they are foremost among all good dharmas; like a banyan tree, they cover all; like an udumbara flower, they are rare and hard to meet; like a golden-winged bird, they subdue outsiders; like flocks of birds, they hoard nothing; like the king of oxen, they are unequaled; like the king of elephants, they are well tamed; like the king of lions, they are fearless; vast as space, they are equal through great compassion; destroying jealousy, they do not begrudge the superior.

They take joy in seeking the Dharma with minds that never tire. They always wish to speak it widely, their resolve never wearying. They beat the Dharma-drum, raise the Dharma-banner, shine the sun of wisdom, and dispel the darkness of delusion. They practice the six harmonies of reverence and always give the gift of Dharma, advancing with courage, their minds never retreating or weakening. They are lamps for the world, the supreme field of merit. They are always teachers and guides, equal without hate or love, delighting only in the right path, with no other joy or grief. They draw out the thorns of desire and bring peace to living beings. Their merits are supreme; all revere them. They extinguish the three defilements and course in spiritual powers. They possess the powers of cause, condition, intention, vow, and skillful means; the powers of constancy, goodness, concentration, insight, and much hearing; the powers of giving, precepts, patience, diligence, meditation, and wisdom; the powers of right mindfulness, calm and insight, and all penetrations and clarity; and the Tathagata’s power of taming living beings. All such powers are complete in them. Their bodily form and marks, their merits and eloquence are complete and adorned, unequaled by any. They revere and make offerings to countless Buddhas and are always praised by all Buddhas together. They fulfill the bodhisattva paramitas and cultivate the samadhis of emptiness, marklessness, and wishlessness, and the samadhi-gates of non-arising and non-ceasing, far removed from the stages of hearers and solitary buddhas. Ānanda, those bodhisattvas accomplish such immeasurable merits; I have spoken of them only in brief for you. Were I to speak in full, a hundred thousand million kalpas could not exhaust them.”

The Buddha told Maitreya Bodhisattva and the assembly of devas and humans: “In the land of Immeasurable Life, the hearers and bodhisattvas, their merits and wisdom, cannot be described. Moreover, that land is so subtle and blissful, so pure as this—why do you not strive to do good? Think on the naturalness of the Way. Abide in neither high nor low, penetrate without limit; each should strive diligently and seek it for yourselves. You will surely pass beyond and be reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss, cutting across the five evil paths; the roads of rebirth close of themselves. Ascend the Way without end—easy to go, yet none go; that land does not oppose or reject, drawn by naturalness. Why not abandon worldly affairs and diligently practice the Way and its virtue? You may attain the utmost long life, with bliss without end.

Yet worldly people are shallow and vulgar, contending together over what is not urgent, and amid this fierce evil and extreme suffering they labor body and mind to provide for themselves. With no noble or base, no poor or rich, young and old, men and women, all worry over wealth; the having and the not having are the same, their anxious thoughts equal. They fret and sorrow, piling up cares and schemes. Driven by the mind, they have no hour of peace. Having fields, they worry over fields; having houses, they worry over houses. Cattle, horses, the six kinds of livestock, servants, wealth, clothing, food, and goods—they worry over all of it. With heavy thoughts and ceaseless sighs, they grieve, brood, and dread; and unforeseen calamities come upon them—fire and water, thieves, enemies, creditors—burning, drowning, seizing, plundering, scattering and destroying them. The poison of care leaves them dazed, with no hour of release. Resentment knots within the heart, never parting from grief and vexation. The mind is hard and the will fixed, with no letting go. Or they sit and are crushed; body dies and life ends, and they are cast away and gone, with none to follow. The noble and wealthy have this affliction too, with ten thousand anxieties and fears, toiling and suffering like this, accumulating all manner of chills and fevers, dwelling together with pain. The poor and lowly, pressed by want, are always without. Having no fields, they worry and wish for fields; having no houses, they worry and wish for houses; having no cattle, horses, livestock, servants, wealth, clothing, food, or goods, they worry and wish to have them. Just as they have one thing, they lack another; having this and lacking that, they think of making them equal. Just as they would have them all, they are scattered again. Thus in grief and toil they must seek anew, and cannot always obtain; their thoughts bring no benefit, and body and mind both labor, unable to sit or rise in peace, with anxious thoughts following after. Toiling and suffering like this, they also accumulate all manner of chills and fevers, dwelling together with pain; or in time they sit and meet an early death, unwilling to do good, to practice the Way, or to advance in virtue. When their lifespan ends and they die, they must go far alone, heading toward some destination, on the paths of good and evil, and none can know it.

Between people of the world—father and son, elder and younger brother, husband and wife, household and family, kin within and without—there should be mutual respect and love, with no mutual hatred or envy. Sharing what they have, they should not be greedy or grudging; their words and looks should always be gentle, never contrary or harsh. Yet sometimes, though the mind be calm, anger arises; the resentment of this life, with the slightest mutual hatred and envy, grows fiercer in later lives, until it becomes great enmity. Why is this? In the affairs of the world, people bring harm to one another; though not immediately, they should at once dissolve it. But they harbor poison and store up anger, knotting resentment in the spirit; naturally it is marked and known, and they cannot be parted from it. They must be born facing one another, each taking revenge on the other. People in the world, amid love and desire, are born alone and die alone, go alone and come alone. When they come to the places of suffering and bliss according to their bent, they must bear it themselves, and there is none to take their place. Good and evil transform, and calamity and blessing occupy different places; prepared and waiting from of old, they must enter alone, going far to another place where none can see them. Good and evil come naturally, following where one is born; dark and hidden, parted for long, their roads differ and meeting has no set time. It is very hard, very hard, to meet now as we have. Why not abandon all affairs, and while each is still strong and well, strive diligently to cultivate goodness and advance with vigor, vowing to cross over the world and attain the utmost long life? Why do you not seek the Way? What are you waiting for? What pleasure do you seek? Such worldly people do not believe that doing good brings good and practicing the Way brings the Way; they do not believe that people die and are reborn, or that giving brings blessing. The affairs of good and evil they do not believe at all, saying it is not so, that in the end there is no such thing. Only because of this, and seeing it for themselves, they look at one another, and former and latter are the same. Passing it on in turn, by the leftover commands of fathers, the ancestors of old never did good and did not know the Way and its virtue; dull in body and dark in spirit, their minds blocked and their thoughts shut. The destinies of death and birth, the paths of good and evil, they cannot see for themselves, and there is none to tell them. Good and ill fortune, calamity and blessing, they vie to bring about, and none finds it strange. The constant way of birth and death passes on in turn; or a father weeps for a son, or a son weeps for a father, brothers, husbands and wives weep for one another. Upside down and inverted, the root of impermanence—all must pass away and cannot be kept forever. They teach and guide, but few believe; thus birth and death flow on without rest. People such as these, benighted and obstinate, do not believe the sutras and Dharma; their minds take no far thought, each wishing only for present pleasure, deluded by craving and desire, not reaching the Way and its virtue, lost and drowned in anger, greedy as wolves for wealth and lust. Because of this they do not attain the Way, and must undergo still more suffering in evil destinies; birth and death have no end—alas, how pitiable!

Or sometimes within a household, father and son, brothers, husband and wife, one dies and one lives, and they grieve for one another. With love and longing, their thoughts bound and tied, their minds aching and clinging, they look back on one another day after day and year after year, with no release. They are taught the Way and its virtue, but their minds do not open; they dwell on affection and fondness, never leaving desire. Dull and benighted, blocked and shut, covered by delusion, they cannot think deeply or plan well, set their minds upright, and single-mindedly practice the Way, cutting off worldly affairs. So they spin on to the end, and when their years and life are spent they cannot attain the Way, and there is no help for it. All are muddled and restless, all greedy for love and desire. Those deluded about the Way are many, those who awaken few; the world hurries on, with nothing to rely on. Noble and base, high and low, rich and poor, honored and humble, all toil and bustle, each harboring murderous poison. Evil airs are dark and hidden, and they raise affairs in delusion, opposing Heaven and Earth, not following the human heart. Natural evil is not theirs—first it follows and gives to them, indulging what they do, awaiting the fullness of their guilt. Before their lifespan ends, it suddenly seizes them away. They fall into evil destinies, toiling through life after life, turning and turning within them for thousands of millions of kalpas, with no time of escape. The pain is beyond words—how pitiable!”

The Buddha told Maitreya Bodhisattva and the assembly of devas and humans: “I now tell you: in the affairs of the world, because of this people sit and do not attain the Way. You should think carefully and plan, and keep far from all evil. Choose what is good and practice it diligently. Love, desire, glory, and splendor cannot be kept forever; all must be parted from, and there is nothing to delight in. Meeting a Buddha in the world, you should strive with vigor. Those who with the utmost vow seek birth in the Land of Peace and Bliss may attain wisdom and clarity, and merits supreme. Do not follow the desires of your mind, failing and betraying the sutras and precepts, falling behind others. If any have doubts and do not understand the sutras, let them ask the Buddha fully, and he will explain it to them.”

Maitreya Bodhisattva, kneeling long, said: “The Buddha’s majesty and honor are revered; what you have spoken is excellent and good. Hearing the Buddha’s sutra words and pondering them through the mind, worldly people are indeed so, as the Buddha has said. Now the Buddha in compassion reveals the great Way, opening eyes and ears, so that we may long be freed. Hearing what the Buddha has said, none fails to rejoice. All the devas, humans, and crawling creatures receive your compassionate grace and are released from grief and suffering. The Buddha’s words of instruction and precept are most profound and good; his wisdom clearly sees the affairs of the eight directions, above and below, past, future, and present, and nothing is left unpenetrated. That we in this assembly have been freed is due to the Buddha’s humble toil when he sought the Way in former lives. His grace and virtue cover all; his blessings tower high, his light shines through, reaching emptiness without limit, opening for people nirvāṇa. His teaching and guidance, his authority and transformation—he moves the ten directions without end. The Buddha is the Dharma King, honored beyond all sages, the teacher of all devas and humans, and according to the wishes of their minds he brings them all to the Way. Now to meet the Buddha and again hear the name of Immeasurable Life—none fails to rejoice, and their minds open in clarity.”

The Buddha told Maitreya: “What you say is so. If any have compassion and reverence for the Buddha, that is truly great goodness. Only after long ages does a Buddha appear in the world again. Now I have become Buddha in this world and expound the sutras and Dharma, proclaim the teaching of the Way, cut the net of doubts, pull out the root of craving, and block up the source of all evil. I walk through the three realms without obstruction. Holding the essentials of wisdom, the key to all paths, I grasp the guiding principles, clear and distinct. I reveal the five destinies and save the unsaved, settling the way of birth and death and nirvāṇa.

Maitreya, you should know that from countless kalpas past you have practiced the bodhisattva path, wishing to save living beings—this for a long time. Those who have attained the Way through you, up to nirvāṇa, cannot be counted. You and all the devas and humans of the ten directions, all the four assemblies, through long kalpas have turned through the five paths, in grief, fear, and toil beyond all telling; even in this present life birth and death have not ceased, yet you have met the Buddha, heard the sutras and Dharma, and again heard of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life. How excellent, how good! I share in your joy.

You too may now weary of birth and death and the pains of old age, sickness, and suffering, of the foul and impure, with nothing to delight in. You should decide for yourselves, make your body upright and your conduct correct, and do ever more good. Cultivate yourselves, cleanse your bodies, wash away the defilements of the mind. In word and deed be loyal and trustworthy, outer and inner in accord. People may save themselves and in turn rescue one another, seeking with clarity and keenness and accumulating the roots of goodness. Though this one life be toilsome, in a moment afterward you will be born in the Land of Immeasurable Life of boundless bliss. Long will you be joined in clarity with the Way and virtue, forever pulling out the root of birth and death, with no more affliction of greed, anger, delusion, or sorrow; and if you wish for a lifespan of one kalpa, a hundred kalpas, a thousand million myriads of kalpas, freely and at will, all may be obtained. This is actionless and natural, next to the way of nirvāṇa. Each of you should strive, seeking what your mind desires, and not give way to doubt or regret and make fault for yourselves, born in the border region in palaces of the seven treasures, for five hundred years undergoing all manner of adversity.” Maitreya said: “Receiving the Buddha’s weighty instruction, I will single-mindedly study and practice, following the teaching, and dare not have doubt.”

The Buddha told Maitreya: “You are able, in this world, to set the mind upright and correct, to do no evil—this is the highest virtue, unequaled in the worlds of the ten directions. Why is that? In the Buddha-lands, devas and humans naturally do good and do not greatly do evil, and are easy to guide. Now I have become Buddha in this world, dwelling amid the five evils, the five pains, and the five burnings, in the most extreme suffering. I teach and transform living beings, leading them to abandon the five evils, to put away the five pains, to leave the five burnings, to subdue and transform their minds, to keep the five goods, to gain their merit and blessing—the way of long life in the world and nirvāṇa.”

The Buddha said: “What are the five evils? What are the five pains? What are the five burnings? How does one transform the five evils, keep the five goods, and gain the merit and blessing of the way of long life in the world and nirvāṇa?

First, the evil: devas, humans, and crawling creatures all wish to do evil; the strong overpower the weak, and each in turn injures and kills the other, devouring one another, not knowing how to cultivate goodness, perverse and without the Way. Afterward they receive the punishment of calamity, naturally bent thither. The gods record and know; the offender is not pardoned. Hence there are poverty and lowliness, beggars and the solitary, the deaf, the blind, and the mute, and the foolish, base, and evil—down to the deformed and insane and the deficient. And there are the noble and wealthy, the talented and clear-minded: all this comes from kindness and filial piety in former lives, from cultivating goodness and piling up virtue. There is a constant way in the world: the king’s law and the prisons. Yet they will not fear and be careful, but do evil and fall into crime and receive its punishment; seeking to be released, they hardly escape. Such things are seen now in the world; after death, in later lives, it is deeper and fiercer still. Entering the darkness, they are reborn and receive a body—as with the king’s law, with the utmost pain of torture.

Hence there are naturally the three evil paths, with immeasurable suffering. They trade their bodies, change their forms and their paths; the lifespan they receive is long or short. The spirit and consciousness naturally go thither. Alone they meet their end, and following one another they are born together. Each avenges the other without cease. While their evil is not exhausted, they cannot be parted. Turning and turning within, they have no time of escape, and it is hard to be freed. The pain is beyond words. Between Heaven and Earth this is natural; though it does not fall at once in sudden violence, the way of good and evil will surely come home. This is the first great evil, first pain, first burning—toil and suffering like this. It is like a great fire burning a person’s body. If one can, amid it, single-mindedly control the mind, make the body upright and conduct correct, do good alone and not do evil, then one alone is freed, gains the merit and blessing of the way of long life in the world, in heaven, and nirvāṇa—this is the first great good.”

The Buddha said: “Second, the evil: the people of the world, fathers and sons, brothers, households and couples, are all without righteousness or principle, not following the Dharma and its measure, extravagant, licentious, arrogant, and self-indulgent, each wishing only for present pleasure. They give the mind free rein, each deceiving and deluding the other; mind and mouth differ, and their words are without truth. Flattering and fawning, unfaithful, with clever words and adulation, they envy the worthy and slander the good, ruining and wronging them. When the ruler is unclear and employs his ministers, the ministers do as they please, with endless schemes and falsehoods, overstepping their measure and knowing the state of things; those in office are not upright and are deceived by them, recklessly harming the loyal and good, not according with the heart of Heaven. Ministers deceive their lords, children their fathers, brothers, husbands and wives, relatives and acquaintances deceive one another. Each harbors greed, anger, and delusion; each wishes to enrich himself and craves much. Noble and base, high and low—their minds are all the same. They ruin the family and lose their lives, giving no thought to what comes before or after. Kin within and without are destroyed with them. Or sometimes a household or acquaintance, a village or market quarter, foolish folk and rustics, turn together to such dealings; each harms or profits the other, and anger becomes a knot of resentment. The rich are stingy and will not give; they cling to what they love, their greed heavy, their minds toiling and their bodies suffering. Thus to the very end they have nothing to rely on; they come alone and go alone, with none to follow. Good and evil, calamity and blessing, follow the life where one is born; or they go to a place of bliss, or enter bitter poison—and then they repent. What use is that?

The people of the world, foolish of mind and scant of wisdom, seeing the good they hate and slander them, with no thought of emulating them; they wish only to do evil and recklessly commit what is against the Dharma. Always harboring a thievish mind, coveting others’ gain, they scatter and waste what they have and then seek for more. Their minds are crooked and not upright; they fear that others see them; they take no forethought, and only when the matter comes do they repent.

In this present life there are the king’s laws and prisons; according to their crimes they go and receive their punishment. Because in former lives they did not believe the Way and its virtue, did not cultivate the roots of goodness, and now again do evil, the gods mark and know them and record their names in the ledgers. When their lifespan ends and the spirit departs, they descend into evil destinies. Hence there are naturally the three evil paths, with immeasurable suffering; turning and turning within them, life after life, kalpa after kalpa, they have no time of escape, and it is hard to be freed. The pain is beyond words. This is the second great evil, second pain, second burning—toil and suffering like this. It is like a great fire burning a person’s body. If one can, amid it, single-mindedly control the mind, make the body upright and conduct correct, do good alone and not do evil, then one alone is freed, gains the merit and blessing of the way of long life in the world, in heaven, and nirvāṇa—this is the second great good.”

The Buddha said: “Third, the evil: the people of the world, born leaning on one another, dwell together between Heaven and Earth. The years of their lifespan—how many can there be? Above are the wise and noble elders, the honored and wealthy; below are the poor and menial, the feeble and foolish; in the middle are those who are not good. Always harboring evil, thinking only of lust, their breasts full of trouble, their love and desire in confusion, they cannot sit or rise in peace; covetous and stingy, wishing only to gain without effort. They glance sidelong at fine forms, their lewd manner showing without. They loathe and hate their own wives and steal in and out in secret, wasting the family wealth in unlawful deeds. They form ties and gather, raise troops and fight one another, attack and rob and kill, seize by force without the Way. Their evil minds are set on the outside, and they do not cultivate their own work; they steal and snatch what they can, plotting blows to accomplish their ends. By threats and force they gather wealth to give to wife and children, giving the mind free rein and taking their pleasure, indulging the body in delight. Or with their own kin, not avoiding noble or base, in the household within and without, they bring grief and suffering, and also do not fear the king’s law or its prohibitions. Such evil is plain to humans and ghosts; sun and moon shine on it, and the gods record and know. Hence there are naturally the three evil paths, with immeasurable suffering; turning and turning within them, life after life, kalpa after kalpa, with no time of escape, hard to be freed, the pain beyond words. This is the third great evil, third pain, third burning—toil and suffering like this. It is like a great fire burning a person’s body. If one can, amid it, single-mindedly control the mind, make the body upright and conduct correct, do good alone and not do evil, then one alone is freed, gains the merit and blessing of the way of long life in the world, in heaven, and nirvāṇa—this is the third great good.”

The Buddha said: “Fourth, the evil: the people of the world do not think of cultivating goodness but teach one another and do evil together—two-tongued speech, harsh speech, false speech, and idle speech; slander and treachery, strife and disorder, hating and envying the good, ruining the worthy and clear, taking joy at their side. They are unfilial to their two parents and slight and scorn their teachers and elders; among friends they are without trust and rarely honest. The noble and honored are proud and great, saying they themselves possess the Way; they run wild with power and force and encroach upon others. They cannot know themselves, are shameless in doing evil, think themselves strong and healthy, and wish others to respect and fear them. They do not revere Heaven and Earth, the gods, sun, and moon, and will not do good; they are hard to tame. Self-willed and haughty, they think it can always be so, with no care or fear, always harboring arrogance. Such evils the gods record and know. Because in former lives they did some merit and blessing, and small goodness supported and protected them, in this life they do evil, their merit and blessing are all destroyed, and the good gods and spirits each depart and leave them; they stand alone and empty with nothing to rely on. When their lifespan is spent, all evils return to them; naturally they are pressed and hurried, and together rush to seize them. Their names are recorded with the gods; calamity and guilt draw them on to the place they must go. The retribution of their crimes is natural, with no way to leave it; they can only go forward and enter the cauldron of fire, body and mind crushed, spirit in pain. At such a time, what use is regret? The way of Heaven is clear; there is no stumbling. Hence there are naturally the three evil paths, with immeasurable suffering; turning and turning within them, life after life, kalpa after kalpa, with no time of escape, hard to be freed, the pain beyond words. This is the fourth great evil, fourth pain, fourth burning—toil and suffering like this. It is like a great fire burning a person’s body. If one can, amid it, single-mindedly control the mind, make the body upright and conduct correct, do good alone and not do evil, then one alone is freed, gains the merit and blessing of the way of long life in the world, in heaven, and nirvāṇa—this is the fourth great good.”

The Buddha said: “Fifth, the evil: the people of the world lean and loiter, indolent and lazy, unwilling to do good, to cultivate the body, or to attend to their work. Their households and kin suffer hunger and cold, and when father and mother teach and admonish them they glare and answer in anger. Their words and commands are not harmonious, but contrary and rebellious, like enemies—better to have had no son. In taking and giving they know no measure, and all alike find them hateful. They betray kindness and violate righteousness, with no thought of repayment. Poor and pressed by want, unable to gain more, they seize by force and plunder, giving themselves up to idleness and roaming. Long accustomed to getting things for nothing to relieve themselves, they are addicted to drink and dote on delicacies, eating and drinking without measure, giving the mind free rein and roaming at ease, rude and obstinate. They do not know human feeling and force their will on others. Seeing others’ good, they hate it with envy. Without righteousness or propriety, with no care or scruple, self-willed and self-approved, they cannot be admonished. For the support of their six kinds of kin they feel no concern. They do not think on the kindness of father and mother, nor keep the righteousness of teacher and friend. Their minds always think evil, their mouths always speak evil, their bodies always do evil; never once a good deed. They do not believe in the sutras and Dharma of the former sages and Buddhas, do not believe that practicing the Way can bring deliverance from the world, do not believe that after death the spirit is reborn, do not believe that doing good brings good and doing evil brings evil. They wish to kill true persons and to set the assembly of monks at strife. They wish to harm father and mother, brothers, and kin. Their six kinds of kin they hate and loathe and wish dead. Such worldly people—their minds and thoughts are all alike, foolish and benighted, yet they think themselves wise. They do not know where they come from in birth, nor where they go in death. Unkind and disobedient, they oppose Heaven and Earth. And amid all this they hope for luck and wish for long life, yet in the end must die. With a compassionate mind one teaches them and makes them think on goodness, reveals birth and death and the destinies of good and evil, and that this is natural—yet they will not believe it. To speak to them with a bitter heart brings them no benefit; their minds are shut and blocked and their thoughts do not open. As the great command of life is about to end, regret and fear come together. They did not cultivate goodness beforehand, and only at the end do they repent. What use is repenting afterward?

Between Heaven and Earth the five paths are clearly divided, vast and dark, broad and boundless. Good and evil bring their retribution, calamity and blessing follow one another; each bears it himself, and there is none to take his place. The reckoning is natural, answering to what one has done; calamity and guilt pursue the life, with no release. The good person doing good passes from joy to joy, from light to light; the evil person doing evil passes from suffering to suffering, from darkness to darkness. Who can know this? Only a Buddha knows. They teach and reveal it, but few believe and accept; birth and death do not cease, and the evil paths are not emptied. Such worldly people are hard to exhaust in full; hence there are naturally the three evil paths, with immeasurable suffering. Turning and turning within them, life after life, kalpa after kalpa, they have no time of escape, and it is hard to be freed. The pain is beyond words. This is the fifth great evil, fifth pain, fifth burning—toil and suffering like this. It is like a great fire burning a person’s body. If one can, amid it, single-mindedly control the mind, make the body upright and mindfulness correct, make words and deeds accord, do all with utmost sincerity, speak as one speaks, with mind and mouth not turning apart, do good alone and not do evil, then one alone is freed, gains the merit and blessing of the way of long life in the world, in heaven, and nirvāṇa—this is the fifth great good.”

The Buddha told Maitreya: “I tell you all: the five evils of this world are toil and suffering like this. The five pains and five burnings give rise to one another; people only do all manner of evil and do not cultivate the roots of goodness, and all naturally enter the evil destinies. Or in this present life they first suffer calamity and sickness, unable to seek death and unable to seek life—the summons of their own sins, shown to all. When the body dies they follow their deeds and enter the three evil paths, with immeasurable bitter poison, each burning itself; and after long ages they together form knots of enmity, from the smallest beginning growing into great evil. All this comes from greed for wealth and lust, from being unable to give, pressed on by delusion and desire, following the thoughts of the mind; the bonds of affliction have no release. Enriching themselves and contending for gain, they take no account of anything. Wealth, honor, and glory give present pleasure; they cannot endure insult, nor attend to cultivating goodness. Their power and influence are but little, and soon wear away. The body sits in toil and suffering, and after long ages it is greatly worse. The way of Heaven stretches and draws tight, naturally correcting and indicting; the net of its guiding cords above and below answers one another, and lonely and fearful the rich enter into it. This has been so in every age—how painful, how pitiable!”

The Buddha said to Maitreya: “The world is like this, and the Buddhas pity it all. By the power of their majestic spirit they destroy all evil and lead all to goodness. Abandon what you have in mind; receive and keep the sutras and precepts, accept and practice the way of Dharma, without transgression or loss, and at the end you will attain the way of long life in the world and nirvāṇa.”

The Buddha said: “You devas and humans now, and the people of later ages, who receive the Buddha’s sutra words, should think on them deeply and be able to set your minds upright and your conduct correct. Let rulers do good and lead and transform those below them, each in turn commanding one another, each keeping himself upright. Revere the sages, honor the good, be kind and compassionate, broad in love. Toward the Buddha’s words of teaching and admonition, dare not be remiss. You should seek deliverance from the world and cut off the root of all the evils of birth and death; you should leave the three evil paths and their immeasurable hosts of grief, fear, and bitter pain. In this you should broadly plant the roots of virtue, bestow kindness and give gifts, and not transgress the prohibitions of the Way. Be patient and diligent, single-minded and wise. Teach and transform one another, establish virtue and do good. With mind upright and thought correct, pure in fasting and precepts, one day and one night surpass a hundred years of doing good in the Land of Immeasurable Life. Why is that? In that Buddha’s land all is actionless and natural, all accumulate manifold goodness, without a hair’s breadth of evil. Here, cultivating goodness for ten days and ten nights surpasses a thousand years of doing good in the Buddha-lands of other directions. Why is that? In the Buddha-lands of other directions, those who do good are many and those who do evil are few; merit and blessing come naturally, and there is no ground for doing evil. Only here is there much evil and nothing natural; in toil and suffering people pursue desire, deceiving and cheating one another, mind toiling and body weary, drinking bitterness and eating poison; in such evil business they never once rest.

I pity you and all the hosts of devas and humans, and with a bitter heart instruct and enlighten you, teaching you to cultivate goodness. According to what is fitting I guide you and bestow on you the sutras and Dharma; let none fail to receive and use them. According to the wishes of your minds, I lead you all to attain the Way. Wherever the Buddha has walked—in countries, towns, and villages—none fails to receive his transformation. The world is harmonious and compliant, sun and moon clear and bright. Wind and rain come in season, and pestilence does not arise. The country is rich and the people at peace, weapons of war are of no use. Virtue is honored, benevolence is raised, and all attend to cultivating propriety and yielding.”

The Buddha said: “I pity you devas and humans more than a father and mother think on their children. Now I have become Buddha in this world, subduing and transforming the five evils, dissolving the five pains, and utterly extinguishing the five burnings, attacking evil with good and pulling out the suffering of birth and death. I lead people to gain the five virtues and rise to the peace of actionlessness. After I pass away, the way of the sutras will gradually perish, people will be flattering and false, and again do all manner of evil. The five burnings and five pains will return as before. After long ages it will grow worse, beyond all telling; I have spoken of it only in brief for you.”

The Buddha said to Maitreya: “Each of you should ponder this well and teach and admonish one another; according to the Buddha’s sutras and Dharma, let none transgress.” Then Maitreya Bodhisattva, joining his palms, said: “What the Buddha has spoken is most good; the people of the world are indeed so. The Tathagata in universal compassion pities and grieves for them and leads them all to deliverance; receiving the Buddha’s weighty instruction, we dare not transgress.”

The Buddha told Ānanda: “Rise, and adjust your robes; with joined palms and reverence, pay homage to Amitābha, the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity. The Buddhas and Tathagatas of the lands of the ten directions constantly join in praising and lauding that Buddha, who is unattached and unobstructed.”

Then Ānanda rose and adjusted his robes, faced the west with upright body, reverently joined his palms, and prostrated himself with all five limbs, paying homage to Amitābha, the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity. He said: “World-Honored One, I wish to see that Buddha’s Land of Peace and Bliss, and the great assemblies of bodhisattvas and hearers.” When he had spoken these words, at once Amitābha, the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity, released a great radiance that illumined all the Buddha-worlds. The mountains of diamond that encircle, the king of mountains Sumeru, and all the mountains great and small—all things alike became one and the same color. It was as when the flood at the end of an aeon fills the world, and all things within are submerged and no more seen; vast and boundless, only the great water is seen. That Buddha’s radiance was likewise so. The radiance of the hearers and bodhisattvas was all concealed, and only the Buddha’s light was seen, bright and blazing. Then Ānanda beheld Amitābha, the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity, majestic in virtue like the king of mountains Sumeru, rising above all the worlds, his marks and radiance illumining all.” The four assemblies of this gathering all saw it at once; and they saw this land as well, in like manner.

Then the Buddha asked Ānanda and Maitreya Bodhisattva: “Do you see all the subtle, adorned, and naturally arisen things in that land, from the ground upward to the Pure Abode Heavens?” Ānanda answered: “Yes, I have seen them.”
Do you also hear Amitābha, the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity, with his great voice proclaiming throughout all worlds to transform living beings?” Ānanda answered: “Yes, I have heard it.”

Do you also see the people of that land, riding palaces of the seven treasures a hundred thousand yojanas in size, without any obstruction, going everywhere in the ten directions to make offerings to the Buddhas?” He answered: “I have seen it.”

Do you also see the womb-born among the people of that land?” He answered: “I have seen them. Those womb-born dwell in palaces of a hundred yojanas, or of five hundred yojanas, each receiving all manner of bliss within them, like the Heaven of the Thirty-Three, and all of it naturally so.”

Then Maitreya Bodhisattva said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, for what cause and what condition are the people of that land womb-born or transformationally born?” The Buddha told Maitreya: “If there are living beings who with a mind of doubt cultivate all manner of merit and vow to be born in that land, not understanding the Buddha’s wisdom, the inconceivable wisdom, the inexpressible wisdom, the broad wisdom of the Great Vehicle, the unequaled and matchless supreme and highest wisdom—toward these wisdoms they doubt and do not believe; yet they still believe in sin and blessing, cultivate the roots of goodness, and vow to be born in that land. Those living beings are born in those palaces and live five hundred years, never seeing the Buddha, never hearing the sutras and Dharma, never seeing the assemblies of bodhisattvas and hearers. Therefore in that land they are called womb-born. But if there are living beings who clearly believe in the Buddha’s wisdom, even to the supreme wisdom, do all manner of merit, and with a mind of faith dedicate it, those living beings are born by transformation within lotus flowers of the seven treasures, sitting cross-legged; in a moment their bodily marks and radiance, their wisdom and merit, are complete and accomplished like those of the bodhisattvas.
