Moreover, Maitreya, the great bodhisattvas of other directions, who set their minds on seeing Amitābha, the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity, and reverently making offerings to him and to the assemblies of bodhisattvas and hearers—those bodhisattvas, when their lives end, are born in the Land of Immeasurable Life and are born by transformation within lotus flowers of the seven treasures. Maitreya, you should know that those born by transformation do so because their wisdom is superior; while the womb-born are all without wisdom, and for five hundred years never see the Buddha, never hear the sutras and Dharma, never see the bodhisattvas and the assemblies of hearers, have no means to make offerings to the Buddha, do not know the rules of the bodhisattva Dharma, and cannot cultivate merit. You should know that such persons in former lives had no wisdom, and this is brought about by their doubt.”

The Buddha told Maitreya: “Suppose a wheel-turning sage king had a prison of the seven treasures, adorned in every way, furnished with beds and hangings, hung with all manner of silk canopies. If some young princes offended the king, he would at once put them inside that prison and bind them with golden chains. Their food and drink, clothing and bedding, flowers and incense and music would be like the wheel-turning king’s own, lacking nothing. What do you think? Would those princes delight in that place?” He answered: “No. By every kind of means they would seek out some great power and wish to free themselves.” The Buddha told Maitreya: “Those living beings are likewise so. Because they doubt the Buddha’s wisdom, they are born in those palaces of the seven treasures, where there is no punishment, not even a single thought of evil. But for five hundred years they do not see the Three Jewels and cannot make offerings or cultivate the roots of goodness; this they take as suffering. Though they have other pleasures, they still do not delight in that place. If such living beings recognize their own former offense, deeply repent and reproach themselves, and seek to leave that place, they at once gain their wish and go to where Amitābha, the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity, is, to revere and make offerings to him, and can also go everywhere to immeasurable and countless other Buddhas to cultivate all manner of merit. Maitreya, you should know that a bodhisattva who gives rise to doubt loses great benefit; therefore you should clearly believe in the unsurpassed wisdom of all the Buddhas.”

Maitreya Bodhisattva said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, in this world how many bodhisattvas who do not regress will be born in that Buddha’s land?” The Buddha told Maitreya: “In this world there are sixty-seven koṭis of non-regressing bodhisattvas who will be born in that land. Each one of those bodhisattvas has already made offerings to countless Buddhas, and is next after Maitreya. The bodhisattvas of lesser practice, and those who cultivate but little merit, cannot be counted, and all shall be born there.”

The Buddha told Maitreya: “Not only the bodhisattvas of my own realm are born in that land. The Buddha-lands of other directions are likewise so. The first Buddha there is named Far-Shining; he has a hundred and eighty koṭis of bodhisattvas, all of whom shall be born there. The second Buddha is named Treasure Store; he has ninety koṭis of bodhisattvas, all of whom shall be born there. The third Buddha is named Immeasurable Sound; he has two hundred and twenty koṭis of bodhisattvas, all of whom shall be born there. The fourth Buddha is named Sweet Dew Taste; he has two hundred and fifty koṭis of bodhisattvas, all of whom shall be born there. The fifth Buddha is named Naga Supreme; he has fourteen koṭis of bodhisattvas, all of whom shall be born there. The sixth Buddha is named Supreme Power; he has fourteen thousand bodhisattvas, all of whom shall be born there. The seventh Buddha is named Lion; he has five hundred koṭis of bodhisattvas, all of whom shall be born there. The eighth Buddha is named Radiance Beyond Defilement; he has eighty koṭis of bodhisattvas, all of whom shall be born there. The ninth Buddha is named Foremost Virtue; he has sixty koṭis of bodhisattvas, all of whom shall be born there. The tenth Buddha is named Mountain of Wondrous Virtue; he has sixty koṭis of bodhisattvas, all of whom shall be born there. The eleventh Buddha is named King of Humans; he has ten koṭis of bodhisattvas, all of whom shall be born there. The twelfth Buddha is named Unsurpassed Flower; he has countless and incalculable assemblies of bodhisattvas, all non-regressing, wise and bold, who have already made offerings everywhere to immeasurable Buddhas, and who within seven days can gather up the firm Dharma that great beings cultivate over a hundred thousand koṭis of kalpas. All these bodhisattvas shall be born there. The thirteenth Buddha is named Fearless; he has seven hundred and ninety koṭis of great bodhisattvas, and lesser bodhisattvas and monks beyond counting, all of whom shall be born there.”

The Buddha said to Maitreya: “Not only the bodhisattvas in these fourteen Buddha-lands shall be born there; in the immeasurable Buddha-lands of the worlds of the ten directions, those who are born there are likewise so, most many and countless. Were I to tell only the names of the Buddhas of the ten directions, and of the bodhisattvas and monks born in that land, a whole day and night for a kalpa would not exhaust them; I have now spoken of them only in brief for you.”

The Buddha told Maitreya: “Whoever hears the name of that Buddha, rejoices and leaps up, even for a single thought—you should know that such a person gains great benefit: he is complete in unsurpassed merit.

Therefore, Maitreya, though a great fire filled three thousand great thousand worlds, one must pass through it to hear this sutra and Dharma, to rejoice, believe, and delight in it, to receive and keep it, read and recite it, and practice as taught. Why is that? There are many bodhisattvas who wish to hear this sutra and cannot obtain it. If there are living beings who hear this sutra, they will never regress from the unsurpassed Way. Therefore you should single-mindedly believe and receive it, keep, recite, speak, and practice it. I now for the sake of all living beings expound this sutra and Dharma, causing them to see Amitābha, the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity, and all that is in his land. What should be done, all of it may be sought; do not, after my entry into nirvāṇa, give rise again to doubt. In ages to come, when the way of the sutras is utterly extinguished, I, in compassion and pity, shall specially preserve this sutra and keep it in the world for a hundred years. Whatever living beings meet with this sutra shall, according to the wishes of their minds, all attain deliverance.”
Maitreya’s Entrustment Passage
The Passage on Specially Preserving This Sutra

The Buddha said to Maitreya: “The Tathagata’s arising in the world is hard to meet and hard to see; the sutras and the way of the Buddhas are hard to obtain and hard to hear; the supreme Dharma of the bodhisattvas and the paramitas are also hard to hear; and to meet a good teacher and, hearing the Dharma, be able to practice it—this too is hard. But to hear this sutra and with faith and delight receive and keep it is the hardest of the hard; nothing surpasses this difficulty. Therefore my Dharma is thus made, thus spoken, thus taught. You should believe and comply, and practice according to the Dharma.”

Then when the World-Honored One had spoken this sutra and Dharma, immeasurable living beings all brought forth the mind of unsurpassed right enlightenment. Twelve thousand nayutas of people attained the pure Dharma-eye. Twenty-two koṭis of devas and humans attained the fruit of non-returning. Eight hundred thousand monks exhausted their outflows and their minds were freed. Four koṭis of bodhisattvas attained non-regression. Adorning themselves with the merit of their great vows, in future ages they shall accomplish right enlightenment. Then the three thousand great thousand worlds shook in six ways, and a great light shone throughout the lands of the ten directions; hundreds of thousands of musics arose of themselves, and immeasurable wondrous flowers fell in profusion.

When the Buddha had finished speaking the sutra, Maitreya Bodhisattva and the assemblies of bodhisattvas who had come from the ten directions, the Elder Ānanda, the great hearers, and all the great assembly, hearing what the Buddha had spoken, none failed to rejoice.
Translated by decree by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of the Great Tang
The Great Jewel Heap Sutra, Scroll Seventeen: The Gathering of Amitābha Tathagata

blocks.text: The Gathering of Amitābha Tathagata, Part One

inline.s: Thus have I heard: at one time the Buddha dwelt on Vulture Peak in Rajagriha, together with a great assembly of monks, twelve thousand in all, all great hearers known and recognized by the many. Their names were: the Venerable Ajñata-Kauṇḍinya, Aśvajit, Mahānāma, Bhadrika, Vimala, Subhadra, Sampūrṇakīrti, Gavāṃpati, Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa, Nadī-Kāśyapa, Gayā-Kāśyapa, Mahā-Kāśyapa, Śāriputra, Mahā-Maudgalyāyana, Mahā-Kātyāyana, Mahā-Kapphina, Mahā-Cunda, Pūrṇa-Maitrāyaṇīputra, Aniruddha, Revata, Upananda, Kapphiṇa, Nanda, Svāgata, Rāhula, Ānanda, and others, with these as foremost.

There were also assemblies of great bodhisattvas, namely Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, Maitreya Bodhisattva, and the assemblies of great bodhisattvas of the present Bhadra kalpa, surrounding him before and behind.

He was also accompanied by the assembly of sixteen good men including Bhadrapāla, namely the Bodhisattva Good Thought on Meaning, the Bodhisattva Wisdom and Eloquence, the Bodhisattva Contemplating Non-Abiding, the Bodhisattva Skillful in Transforming Spiritual Powers, the Bodhisattva Light Banner, the Bodhisattva Supreme Wisdom, the Bodhisattva Stillness of Faculties, the Bodhisattva Wisdom Vow, the Bodhisattva Fragrant Elephant, the Bodhisattva Jewel Banner, and others, with these as foremost.

All together they cultivated the way of Samantabhadra, fulfilled all the practices and vows of a bodhisattva, and dwelt at peace in all dharmas of merit, reaching the Buddha-Dharma and the ultimate other shore. They vowed to accomplish equal right enlightenment in every world. They further vowed to be born in the Tushita Heaven, and when their lives there ended, to descend and be born from the right side, to walk seven steps, to release a great radiance that illumined all Buddha-worlds and shook them in six ways, and to proclaim: “I am the most honored in all the world.” All the devas of Brahma and Indra came to attend him in person. They further manifested learning writing and calculation, calendrical science, grammar, the arts and crafts, medicine, the nurturing of life, and talismans and seals, and in other games and sports they excelled above others. Dwelling in the royal palace, they wearied of the realms of desire; seeing old age, sickness, and death, they awakened to the impermanence of the world. They gave up the royal throne, crossed the city wall, and went forth to study the Way. They removed all their ornaments and the kāśika cloth, put on the monastic robe, and practiced austerities for six years. They were able to make such a display in the lands of the five turbidities. Conforming to the world, they bathed in the Nairañjanā River and went toward the site of enlightenment. The naga kings welcomed and praised them; the assemblies of bodhisattvas circumambulated them to the right and sang their praises. Then the bodhisattva accepted grass, spread it himself beneath the bodhi tree, and sat cross-legged. They further saw the hosts of Mara gather around and prepare to do harm. By the power of concentration and wisdom the bodhisattva subdued the hosts of Mara and accomplished unsurpassed enlightenment. Brahma the king urged them and they turned the wheel of Dharma. Bold and fearless, their Buddha-voice roared like thunder; they beat the Dharma-drum and blew the Dharma-conch. They raised the great Dharma-banner and lit the torch of right Dharma. They embraced the right Dharma and all the meditative concentrations. They rained the great Dharma-rain, moistening and enriching living beings. They shook the great Dharma-thunder, awakening all. A great light shone throughout all Buddha-lands. Within those worlds the earth all trembled. The palaces of Mara were destroyed, and Papiyas was terrified. They broke down the city of afflictions and cast off the net of views. Far from black dharmas, they gave rise to white dharmas. They could receive and digest the food offered to a Buddha. To tame living beings they proclaimed the wondrous principle. Sometimes they showed a smile and released hundreds of thousands of rays. They ascended the stage of consecration and received the bodhi prophecy. Sometimes they accomplished the Buddha-way, and were seen to enter nirvāṇa. They caused immeasurable sentient beings all to attain the extinction of outflows, and matured bodhisattvas in boundless roots of goodness. In all such Buddha-lands they could manifest. It is like a magician skilled in the art of illusion, able to manifest the forms of men and women; yet within those forms nothing at all can be grasped. Just so, those bodhisattvas, because they have well learned the merit of boundless illusion, can manifest transformations in accord, and because they well understand the way of transformation, they manifest all Buddha-lands and reveal great compassion. Benefiting all living beings everywhere, they fulfill the vows and practices of a bodhisattva. They accomplish boundless and immeasurable gates of meaning. They penetrate the equal and all-good dharmas and are complete in their cultivation. Into all Buddha-lands they enter equally. They are constantly urged on and empowered by all Buddhas, and all Tathagatas know, recognize, and approve them. To teach bodhisattvas they act as ācāryas, constantly practicing the corresponding boundless practices. They penetrate the conduct of all Dharma-realms and well understand sentient beings and lands; they also constantly aspire to make offerings to all Tathagatas. They see all manner of bodies as like reflections. Well learning Indra’s net, they can break the net of Mara. They destroy the net of views and enter the net of sentient beings. They can transcend the retinue of afflictions and the companions and people of Mara. Far beyond the stages of hearers and pratyekabuddhas, they enter the Dharma-gates of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, and can abide in skillful means. They never delight in entering the nirvāṇa of the two vehicles, but attain the samadhis of non-arising and non-ceasing, and gain all dhāraṇī-gates. Their faculties are broad and great, their eloquence decisive. In the bodhisattva-piṭaka dharmas they are well able to understand. The Buddha-flower samadhi they enter at will. They are complete in all kinds of profound meditative concentration. All Buddhas appear before them, and in a single thought they travel throughout Buddha-lands and return, no different in time. In what is hard and what is not hard they can understand all extremes. They expound the ultimate reality and well understand its distinctions. They gain the Buddha’s eloquence and dwell in the practice of Samantabhadra. They are well able to distinguish the languages of living beings and surpass all worldly dharmas; they well understand all supramundane dharmas. They gain the perfection of sovereign mastery over requisites and bear living beings, as a friend not asked. They can hold the Dharma-treasury of all Tathagatas and dwell in it without interruption, keeping the lineage of all Buddhas. Pitying living beings, they can open the Dharma-eye. They close the evil destinies and open the door to good destinies. Beholding all living beings, they can form the thought of father, mother, and brother; and again they regard living beings as they regard their own bodies. Having realized the perfection of all praised virtues, they well understand and praise all the virtues of the Tathagatas, together with the rest of the dharmas of praise and virtue. Thus the assembly of such great bodhisattvas, immeasurable and boundless, all came together.

Then the Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, placed his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said: “Great Virtue, World-Honored One, your bodily form and all your faculties are utterly pure; your majestic light blazes like molten gold, and like a bright mirror it gathers and reflects radiance. From ages past until now I have never once seen such a sight; I am glad to behold it and give rise to a rare thought. The World-Honored One now enters the great stillness of samadhi, practices the Tathagata’s practices, all of them complete, and well establishes the practice of a great being. Pondering the Buddhas of past, future, and present—why, World-Honored One, do you dwell in this mindfulness?”
Then the Buddha said to Ānanda: “How now are you able to know this meaning? Did some devas come and tell you? Or is it because you have seen me and know it yourself?”
Ānanda said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, I saw the Tathagata’s rare radiance, and so gave rise to this thought; it was not because of devas or others.”

The Buddha told Ānanda: “Excellent, excellent! Your question now is well asked. You are able to observe the subtle and wondrous eloquence and to ask the Tathagata such a meaning. It is for the sake of all Tathagatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones, and of those who dwell in great compassion to benefit living beings, who are rare great beings like the udumbara flower appearing in the world, that you ask this meaning. And again, for the sake of pitying and benefiting all living beings, you are able to ask the Tathagata such a meaning. Ānanda, the Tathagata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is well able to reveal immeasurable knowledge and vision. Why is that? The Tathagata’s knowledge and vision have no obstruction. Ānanda, if the Tathagata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, wished to remain in the world, he could in the time of a meal remain for immeasurable and countless hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of kalpas. And were he to prolong it beyond that number, the Tathagata’s body and all his faculties would neither increase nor decrease. Why is that? The Tathagata has gained sovereign mastery of samadhi and has reached the other shore. In all dharmas he is supremely sovereign. Therefore, Ānanda, listen well and ponder it well; I shall explain it for you in detail.”
Ānanda said to the Buddha: “Yes, World-Honored One, I wish and long to hear it!”

Then the Buddha told Ānanda: “In ages past, beyond asaṃkhyeyas and countless great kalpas, a Buddha appeared named Dipankara. Long before that Buddha, beyond measure, there was a Buddha named Austerity who arose in the world. Before the Buddha Austerity there was again a Tathagata named Moon Face. Before the Buddha Moon Face, beyond measure, there was the Buddha Sandalwood Fragrance, and before that Buddha the Buddha Sumeru Heap. Before the Buddha Heap there was again the Buddha Wondrous Height Kalpa. And so in turn there were the Buddha Face Beyond Defilement, the Buddha Undefiled, the Buddha Naga Deva, the Buddha King of Mountain Sound, the Buddha Sumeru Heap, the Buddha Golden Store, the Buddha Illuminating Radiance, the Buddha Radiance Sovereign, the Buddha Lineage of the Great Earth, the Buddha Blazing Radiance of Vaiḍūrya Gold Light, the Buddha Moon Image, the Buddha Opening Flowers Adorned with Light, the Buddha Wondrous Sea of Supreme Enlightenment Sporting in Spiritual Powers, the Buddha Diamond Light, the Buddha Great Agada Fragrant Light, the Buddha Mind Beyond Affliction, the Buddha Increase of Treasures, the Buddha Bold Heap, the Buddha Supreme Heap, the Buddha Upholding the Great Merit of Dharma-gift and Spiritual Powers, the Buddha Outshining Sun and Moon, the Buddha Illuminating Vaiḍūrya, the Buddha Mind-Awakening Flower, the Buddha Moonlight, the Buddha Sunlight, the Buddha King of Flower Garland Colors Opening Spiritual Powers, the Buddha Water Moonlight, the Buddha Destroyer of the Darkness of Ignorance, the Buddha Canopy of Pearl and Coral, the Buddha Tisya, the Buddha Supreme Flower, the Buddha Roar of Dharma Wisdom, the Buddha with Lion’s Roar and Goose and Swan Voice, and the Buddha Brahma Voice Naga Roar. Such Buddhas arose in the world, each separated from the next by kalpas beyond measure. Before the Buddha Naga Roar appeared in the world, in countless kalpas before, there was the Buddha World Sovereign. Before the Buddha World Sovereign, in boundless kalpas, a Buddha appeared in the world named the Tathagata King of Freedom in the World, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, Perfect in Wisdom and Conduct, Well-Gone, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Tamer of Beings, Teacher of Devas and Humans, Buddha, World-Honored One. Ānanda, in that Buddha’s Dharma there was a monk named Dharmakara, who had surpassing vows and practices, and whose powers of mindfulness and wisdom were heightened. His mind was firm and unmoved, his merit and wisdom surpassing, his human form dignified. Ānanda, that monk Dharmakara went to where the Tathagata King of Freedom in the World was, bared his right shoulder, bowed his head to the Buddha’s feet, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and praised him in verse:
The Tathagata’s light is immeasurable and boundless; throughout the world no light can compare.
All the suns, moons, and maṇi jewels are outshone by the Buddha’s majestic light.
The World-Honored One can utter a single sound, and each living being understands it according to its kind.
He can also manifest a single wondrous body, and cause all beings to see it according to their kind.
In precepts, concentration, wisdom, diligence, and much hearing, no living being can equal him.
The stream of his mind’s awakened wisdom is like the great sea; he well understands the most profound Dharma.
Delusions exhausted and faults gone, he is worthy of offerings; such is his sacred virtue—he alone is the World-Honored One.
The Buddha has a surpassing and mighty radiance that illumines immeasurable lands of the ten directions.
I now praise all his virtues, hoping for blessing and wisdom equal to the Tathagata’s.
He can save all the worlds from the many sorrows of birth, old age, sickness, and death.
May I dwell in samadhi and expound the Dharma-gates of giving and precepts.
With patience, diligence, concentration, and wisdom, may I become a Buddha and save living beings.
To seek the unsurpassed great bodhi, I make offerings to all the wondrously awakened of the ten directions.
Hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas, as many as the sands of the Ganges.
And may I gain a great spiritual radiance, doubling its shining over koṭis of Buddha-lands like Ganges sands.
And with boundless surpassing effort, may I attain a supreme and vast pure abode.
In such an unequaled Buddha-land I shall settle living beings and benefit them.
The supreme great beings of the ten directions shall all be born there with joyful minds.
Only the Buddha’s sacred wisdom can know and bear witness; I now seek the power of firmness.
Though I sink into all the uninterrupted hells, such a vow and mind shall never retreat.
The unobstructed wisdom of all the world should know and understand such a mind.

Moreover, Ānanda, when the monk Dharmakara had praised the Buddha’s virtues, he said to the World-Honored One: “I now bring forth the mind of unsurpassed right enlightenment. I pray the Tathagata to expound such dharmas for me, that I may in the world attain the unequaled accomplishment of great bodhi and fully embrace a pure and adorned Buddha-land.”
The Buddha said to the monk: “You should cultivate for yourself a pure Buddha-land.”

Dharmakara said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, I have no such power to embrace and receive them. I pray the Tathagata to tell me of the other Buddha-lands, pure and adorned; when we have heard it, we vow to perfect them.”

Then the World-Honored One broadly expounded for him the twenty-one koṭis of pure Buddha-lands in their full adornment. When he had spoken this Dharma, a koṭi of years passed. Ānanda, the monk Dharmakara embraced all the pure and adorned matters within those twenty-one koṭis of Buddha-lands. Having embraced them, he fulfilled five kalpas in thought and cultivation.”
Ānanda said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, how long was the lifespan of that Tathagata, the King of Sovereignty over the World?”

The World-Honored One told him: “The lifespan of that Buddha was fully forty kalpas. Ānanda, the Buddha-lands of those twenty-one koṭis of Buddhas, the Buddha-land embraced by the monk Dharmakara, surpasses them. Having embraced them all, he went to where the Tathagata King of Sovereignty over the World was. He bowed his head at his feet, circled him seven times to the right, and stood to one side, saying: ‘Lord, I have embraced and gathered in a Buddha-land perfect in merit, virtue, and adornment.’
The Buddha said: “Now is the very time. You should tell it fully, so that the assembly may rejoice, and so that the great assembly may all embrace that Buddha-land and bring it to perfection.”
Dharmakara said: “May the World-Honored One in his great compassion stay and listen; I shall now set forth my peerless vows:
If I attain supreme bodhi, and there be in my land beings of the hells, of the hungry ghosts, or of the animal realm, may I never take supreme, perfect enlightenment.
If I become a Buddha, and there be beings in my land who fall into the three evil destinies, may I never take enlightenment.
If I become a Buddha, and the beings in my land are not all of one true golden hue, may I never take enlightenment.
If I become a Buddha, and the beings in my land differ in form and feature, some fair and some foul, may I never take enlightenment.
If I become a Buddha, and the beings in my land do not gain the memory of past lives, down to not knowing the affairs of a hundred thousand kalpas in koṭis of nayutas, may I never take enlightenment.
If I become a Buddha, and the beings in my land, lacking the celestial eye, cannot see even the Buddha-lands of a hundred thousand koṭis of nayutas, may I never take enlightenment.

If I become a Buddha, and the beings in my land do not obtain the celestial ear, and cannot hear the Buddha teaching the Dharma even beyond a hundred thousand koṭis of nayutas of yojanas, may I never take enlightenment.

If I become a Buddha, and the beings in my land have no knowledge of the minds of others, and do not know the mental conduct of the beings in the Buddha-lands of a hundred thousand koṭis of nayutas, may I never take enlightenment.

If I become a Buddha, and the beings in my land do not obtain spiritual powers, mastery, and the perfections, so that in a single instant of thought they cannot pass beyond the Buddha-lands of a hundred thousand koṭis of nayutas, may I never take enlightenment.
If I become a Buddha, and beings in my land give rise to even the least thought of “I” and “mine,” may I never take bodhi.
If I become a Buddha, and beings in my land are not certain to accomplish equal, perfect enlightenment and realize the great nirvāṇa, may I never take bodhi.
If I become a Buddha, and my light is limited, so that it does not illumine even the Buddha-lands of a hundred thousand koṭis of nayutas and beyond reckoning, may I never take bodhi.
If I become a Buddha, and my lifespan is limited, even to koṭis of nayutas of hundreds of thousands of kalpas and beyond reckoning, may I never take bodhi.

If I become a Buddha, and there be any in my land who know the number of its hearers: even were the three-thousand-great-thousand world filled with beings and with pratyekabuddhas who for a hundred thousand years exhausted their wisdom to reckon it, they could not know it. If there be any who know it, may I never take enlightenment.
If I become a Buddha, and the beings in my land have lifespans that are limited and bounded, may I never take bodhi — save for those who are born there by the power of their vows.
If I become a Buddha, and there be in my land any beings with an evil name, may I never take enlightenment.
If I become a Buddha, and the countless Buddhas in those immeasurable lands do not together proclaim and praise my land, may I never take enlightenment.

If, when I attain supreme enlightenment, beings in other Buddha-lands, having heard my name, turn all their roots of goodness, heart to heart, toward rebirth in my land, even to ten thoughts, and are not born there, may I never take bodhi — save for those who commit the five heinous deeds, who slander the true Dharma, and who revile the sages.

If I become a Buddha, and there be beings in other Buddha-lands who arouse the bodhi-mind and give rise to pure thoughts toward me, and who then turn their roots of goodness toward rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, and at the end of their lives I and the assembly of monks do not appear before them, may I never take enlightenment.

If I become a Buddha, and there be beings in immeasurable lands who hear my name spoken and turn their own roots of goodness toward the Land of Ultimate Bliss, and are not born there, may I never take bodhi.
If I become a Buddha, and the bodhisattvas in my land do not all perfect the thirty-two marks, may I never take bodhi.

If I become a Buddha, and all the bodhisattvas in that land do not all stand, with respect to the great bodhi, at the stage of one lifetime from Buddhahood — save for those great-vowed bodhisattvas who, for the sake of beings, don the armor of diligence, diligently practice for their benefit, cultivate the great nirvāṇa, travel through all Buddha-lands, practice the bodhisattva path, make offerings to all Tathagatas, establish beings as countless as the sands of the Ganges in supreme enlightenment, and whose practiced conduct surpasses what went before, who walk the path of Samantabhadra and thereby gain deliverance — if it is not so, may I never take bodhi.

If I become a Buddha, and the bodhisattvas in my land do not each morning make offerings to the Buddhas of other regions, even to immeasurable koṭis of nayutas of hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, and by the Buddha’s majesty return to their own land before the meal — if it is not so, may I never take bodhi.

If I become a Buddha, and the bodhisattvas in that land, whatever offerings they need for the places of the Buddhas, do not plant roots of goodness of every kind, and such things are not brought to perfection, may I never take bodhi.
If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in my land who expound the essentials of the Dharma do not skillfully enter into and accord with the wisdom of the All-Knowing, may I never take bodhi.
If I become a Buddha, and the bodhisattvas born in that land do not possess the firm strength of Narayana, may I never take enlightenment.

If I become a Buddha, and throughout my land, among all its adornments, there is no being able to expound them fully — even one with the celestial eye cannot know all its varied kinds, forms and colors, and appearances of light — and if any can know and fully expound them, may I never take bodhi.

If I become a Buddha, and my land possesses immeasurable trees of color a hundred thousand yojanas tall, and among the bodhisattvas there are those of inferior roots of goodness who cannot know them, may I never take enlightenment.
If I become a Buddha, and the beings in my land who read and recite the scriptures, teach, and expound them do not obtain supreme eloquence, may I never take bodhi.
If I become a Buddha, and the bodhisattvas in my land do not perfect boundless eloquence, may I never take bodhi.

If I become a Buddha, and the light and purity of my land is everywhere without equal, illumining immeasurable, countless, inconceivable Buddha-worlds, showing therein the faces of beings as in a bright mirror — if it is not so, may I never take bodhi.

If I become a Buddha, and within the bounds of my land, on the earth and in the sky, there are not immeasurable kinds of fragrance, and hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of jeweled censers whose fragrance perfumes everywhere throughout the realm of space, that fragrance surpassing the treasures of gods and humans and offered to the Tathagata and the assembly of bodhisattvas — if it is not so, may I never take bodhi.

If I become a Buddha, and throughout the ten directions all the beings of immeasurable, countless, inconceivable, unequaled realms who are touched by the Buddha’s majestic light do not attain peace and joy of body and mind surpassing gods and humans — if it is not so, may I never take enlightenment.

If I become a Buddha, and the bodhisattvas in the Buddha-lands of immeasurable, inconceivable, unequaled realms, having heard my name, do not realize the dharma of non-arising and obtain dharanis, may I never take enlightenment.

If I become a Buddha, and throughout the countless, inconceivable, unequaled Buddha-lands all the women, having heard my name, gain pure faith, arouse the bodhi-mind, and grow weary of the female body, yet in a future life do not forsake the female body, may I never take bodhi.

If I become a Buddha, and the assemblies of bodhisattvas in immeasurable, countless, inconceivable, unequaled Buddha-lands, having heard my name, gain the dharma of non-arising, and do not cultivate the peerless pure practice until they reach the great bodhi, may I never take enlightenment.

If I become a Buddha, and throughout the ten directions, in the Buddha-lands beyond all measure, all the bodhisattvas, having heard my name, do not bow with all five limbs to the ground and cultivate the bodhisattva path with pure hearts, and if the gods and humans do not revere them, may I never take enlightenment.

If I become a Buddha, and the clothing the beings in my land need does not come at a thought, as when the Buddha says “Come, monk,” and the Dharma robe is naturally upon the body — if it is not so, may I never take bodhi.

If I become a Buddha, and all kinds of beings, as soon as they are born in my land, do not all obtain every requisite, with pure minds and peace and joy like monks who have destroyed the defilements, may I never take bodhi.

If I become a Buddha, and the multitudes in my land cannot, as their hearts wish, see the pure lands of the Buddhas and their peerless adornments all appearing among the jewel trees, like faces seen in a bright mirror — if it is not so, may I never take bodhi.
If I become a Buddha, and beings in other Buddha-lands, having heard my name, attain bodhi with any of their faculties deficient or their virtues and powers narrow, may I never take bodhi.

If I become a Buddha, and the bodhisattvas in other Buddha-lands, having heard my name, do not all skillfully distinguish the names and words of the supreme samadhis — and while abiding in those samadhis, in a single instant, in the time of a word, cannot make offerings to immeasurable, countless, inconceivable, unequaled Buddhas, and do not realize the six samadhis — may I never take enlightenment.
If I become a Buddha, and bodhisattvas in other Buddha-lands, having heard my name, are not born after the end of their lives into noble and wealthy families, may I never take enlightenment.

If I become a Buddha, and the bodhisattvas in other Buddha-lands, having heard my name, do not in due season cultivate the bodhisattva path, gaining pure joy and the abiding of equality, perfect in all roots of goodness, may I never take enlightenment.

If I become a Buddha, and bodhisattvas in other regions, having heard my name, all obtain the gate of the samadhi of equality, and abiding in that concentration ever make offerings to immeasurable, unequaled Buddhas, and until bodhi never turn back — if it is not so, may I never take enlightenment.
If I become a Buddha, and the bodhisattvas in my land do not naturally hear the Dharma they wish to hear, according to their vows and aspirations — if it is not so, may I never take enlightenment.
If I attain supreme bodhi, and bodhisattvas in other Buddha-lands, having heard my name, turn back from supreme, perfect enlightenment, may I never take enlightenment.

If I become a Buddha, and bodhisattvas in other Buddha-lands, hearing my name, do not in that very season obtain the first, second, and third patient acceptances, and cannot realize non-retrogression with respect to all Buddhadharmas, may I never take bodhi.
At that time the Buddha told Ānanda: “That monk Dharmakara, having made these vows before the Tathagata King of Sovereignty over the World, by the Buddha’s majestic spirit spoke these verses:
Before the Tathagata I make this vow: on the day I attain supreme bodhi.
if these supreme vows are not fulfilled, may I never take the unequaled honored one of the ten powers.
If my heart cannot bear to give without cease, relieving the poor and freeing them from every pain.
benefiting the world and bringing it peace, may I never become the Dharma King who saves the world.
When I attain bodhi and sit in the place of enlightenment, if my fame does not reach throughout the ten directions.
and the immeasurable, boundless Buddha-lands beyond number do not receive it, may I never take the honored one of the ten powers in the world.
Setting out for the unsurpassed great bodhi, if I leave home to seek the realm of desire.
and in that vow have neither mindfulness nor wisdom, may I never become the tamer, the teacher of gods and humans.
May I attain the Tathagata’s immeasurable light, illumining all Buddha-lands in the ten directions.
able to quench all greed, hatred, and delusion, and to cut off the evil destinies of the world.
May I gain the light that opens the pure eye of wisdom, dispelling the darkness of all states of being.
Ending every calamity, leaving none behind, and setting gods and humans in a mighty one’s peace.
Having cultivated my original practice to purity, I shall gain immeasurable, peerless radiance.
outshining the light of sun and moon, of all the gods, and of the maṇi jewels.
The peerless husband, his practice done, becomes a hidden treasure for the poor.
perfect in wholesome dharmas and without equal, he roars the lion’s roar amid the assembly.
In former times I made offerings to the self-awakened ones, and for many kalpas diligently practiced austerities.
seeking the supreme accumulations of wisdom, fulfilling my original vows as the honored one of gods and humans.
The Tathagata’s knowledge and vision is without obstruction, and can comprehend all that is conditioned.
May I become the unequaled one, the supreme wise one, the true guide.
If I am to attain the great bodhi, may these vast vows be truly fulfilled.
and may the three-thousand-great-thousand world be shaken, with gods raining flowers from the sky.
Then let the whole earth tremble, with celestial flowers and music filling the sky.
and a rain of fine sandalwood powder, and a voice proclaiming that in the future he shall become a Buddha.

The Buddha told Ānanda: “That monk Dharmakara, before the Tathagata King of Sovereignty over the World and before the gods and humans, the demons and Brahmas, the ascetics and brahmins, and all the rest, broadly made these great and vast vows. They have all been accomplished — a rarity in the world. Having made these vows, he truly abided in them, and in every kind of merit and virtue he was complete in adornment, of vast majesty and purity of Buddha-land. While he cultivated the bodhisattva path in this way, throughout immeasurable, countless, inconceivable, unequaled koṭis of nayutas of hundreds of thousands of kalpas, he never once gave rise to greed, anger, or delusion, or to thoughts of desire to harm or to hate; nor did he give rise to thoughts of form, sound, scent, taste, or touch. Toward all beings he ever took joy in love and respect, as toward his own kin. His nature was gentle and mild, and he was easy to live with. To those who came seeking he never went against their wishes; with kind words he persuaded and instructed them, and none failed to follow his heart. He nourished himself with whatever he obtained for the support of the body. Desiring little and content, he ever delighted in emptiness and leisure. He was intelligent by nature and clear in understanding, yet without pretense. His nature was tame and compliant, without violence or evil. Toward all beings he ever held compassion and patience. His mind was without deceit or flattery, and without indolence. With kind words he urged himself onward, seeking all pure dharmas. For all beings everywhere he was brave and never turned back. Benefiting the world, his great vows were fulfilled. He served his teachers and honored the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha. In the bodhisattva path he ever wore the armor. His heart delighted in stillness and quiet, and he was free of all defilement and attachment. So that beings might ever cultivate pure dharmas, he became foremost among them in the wholesome dharmas. He dwelt in emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, in non-action and non-arising, in neither arising nor ceasing, and was without pride or arrogance. And that true one, in walking the bodhisattva path, ever guarded his speech, and never by his speech harmed others or himself. Ever by his speech-karma he benefited himself and others. When he entered royal cities and villages, though he saw many forms, his mind was undefiled. With a pure mind he neither craved nor hated. At that time the bodhisattva himself practiced giving, and also caused others to practice giving. In the perfection of morality and on through the perfection of wisdom, he set the first two practices in motion, and all were brought to perfection. Because he perfected such roots of goodness, wherever he was born, immeasurable koṭis of nayutas of hundreds of thousands of treasuries of jewels welled up of themselves. And he caused immeasurable, countless, inconceivable, unequaled and boundless kinds of beings to abide in supreme, perfect enlightenment. Thus immeasurable bodhisattvas set in motion wondrous practices, making offerings and serving the World-Honored Ones, until they became Buddhas; and all this cannot be known by language or discrimination. Whether he was born a wheel-turning king, or Indra, or the god Suyama, or a god of the Tuṣita heaven, or a god of the heaven of Good Transformation, or of the heaven of Freely Enjoying Others’ Transformations, or as Great Brahma, king of the gods, in every case he was able to serve and make offerings to all the Buddhas, and to request the Buddhas to turn the wheel of Dharma. If he was born a king of Jambudvipa, or an elder, a minister, a brahmin, or a kṣatriya, in all those clans he was able to honor and make offerings to all the Buddhas. And he could expound immeasurable Dharma-gates. Thereafter he forever abandoned the world and attained supreme enlightenment. Yet that bodhisattva could, with exquisite clothing, bedding, food, and medicine, make offerings to all Tathagatas for the whole of his life, and gain an abiding of peace and joy. All such roots of goodness brought to perfection cannot be fully bounded even by language. From his mouth there ever came the wondrous fragrance of sandalwood. That fragrance pervaded immeasurable, countless, even koṭis of nayutas of hundreds of thousands of worlds. And from every pore of his body there came the supreme fragrance of utpala flowers surpassing gods and humans. Wherever he was born, his marks and features were dignified and fair, peerless and complete. He also obtained sovereignty, the perfection of mastery, over all requisites, and every article he used was everywhere and never lacking. That is to say: jewel-incenses of every kind, flowers, banners, pennants, silken streamers, canopies, exquisite clothing, food and drink, broth and medicine, and all treasuries of hidden treasure and rare curiosities that were needed — all flowed naturally from the bodhisattva’s palms. From the pores of his body there flowed all the music of gods and humans. By these causes and conditions he was able to cause immeasurable, countless, inconceivable beings to abide in supreme, perfect enlightenment. Ānanda, I have now told of the Bodhisattva Dharmakara’s original cultivation.”
At that time Ānanda said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, is the Bodhisattva Dharmakara, who attained bodhi, of the past? Of the future? Or is he now present in some other world?”

The Buddha told Ānanda: “To the west of here, a hundred thousand koṭis of Buddha-lands away, there is a world named Ultimate Bliss. There the monk Dharmakara became a Buddha, named Immeasurable Life, and he is now present, teaching the Dharma. Immeasurable bodhisattvas and assemblies of hearers revere and surround him. Ānanda, the light of that Buddha illumines all Buddha-lands — immeasurable, countless, inconceivable. I shall now speak of it in brief: his light illumines the east, as many lands as the sands of the Ganges; and to the south, the west, and the north, to the four intermediate directions, above and below, it is likewise so. Except where the power of the Buddhas’ own original vows adds its majesty, all are illumined by it. The light of those Buddhas may extend one fathom, or one yojana, or even koṭis of nayutas of hundreds of thousands of yojanas, or it may illumine all Buddha-lands.

Ānanda, for this reason the Buddha Immeasurable Life has other names besides, namely: Immeasurable Light, Boundless Light, Unattached Light, Unobstructed Light, Light of Majestic Sovereignty, Light of Love, Light of Joy, Light of Delight, Inconceivable Light, Unequaled Light, Immeasurable and Incommensurable Light, Light That Outshines the Sun, Light That Outshines the Moon, Light That Outshines Both Sun and Moon.

That light of his is pure and vast, causing all beings to rejoice in body and mind. And it causes all the dragons, yakṣas, asuras, and the rest in other Buddha-lands to gain gladness. Ānanda, were I to open and reveal the light of that Buddha for a whole kalpa, I could not finish speaking of it.

Again, Ānanda, the assembly of hearers of that Tathagata Immeasurable Life is beyond reckoning; no one can know its limit. Even if monks were as many as koṭis of nayutas of hundreds of thousands in number, all like Mahāmaudgalyayana, with sovereign spiritual powers, who in the morning traverse a great thousand worlds and in a moment return to where they were, and they were to spend koṭis of nayutas of hundreds of thousands of years trying together to reckon the assembly of hearers at the first assembly of the Buddha Immeasurable Life — exhausting their spiritual powers, even to the end of their lives, they would not know one part in a hundred, nor one part in a thousand or a hundred thousand, nor one part in an upaniṣad either.

Ānanda, it is like the great ocean, eighty-four thousand yojanas deep: strain the eye to the utmost and its edge cannot be seen. If a man were to split the tip of a hair into fifty parts and with one of those parts take up a single drop from the great ocean — Ānanda, that drop of water, compared with the great ocean, which is the greater?”
Ānanda said: “Even a thousand yojanas of water would still be reckoned little, how much less could a single part of a hair’s tip be compared to it?”

The Buddha told Ānanda: “Even if monks were as many as koṭis of nayutas of hundreds of thousands in number, all like Mahāmaudgalyayana, and for a hundred thousand koṭis of nayutas of years they all together reckoned the assembly of hearers at the first assembly of that Tathagata Immeasurable Life, the number they could know would be like that one drop of water at a hair’s tip. The rest, beyond their measure, is like the great ocean. The assembly of bodhisattvas and mahāsattvas is likewise so, and cannot be known by reckoning. Ānanda, the lifespan of that Buddha is immeasurable and boundless; the number of his kalpas cannot be known. The lifespan of the hearers, the bodhisattvas, the gods, and the humans is likewise so.”
Ānanda said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, how long has it been since that Buddha appeared in the world, that he has obtained such an immeasurable lifespan?”

The Buddha told Ānanda: “Ten kalpas have passed since that Buddha took birth. Again, Ānanda, that realm of Ultimate Bliss has immeasurable merit and is complete in adornment. The land is rich in harvest, and gods and humans are flourishing. Their minds and wills are harmonious and at ease, and they ever dwell in peace and security. There are no hells, no animals, and no realm of King Yama. There are fragrances of every kind, spreading their perfume everywhere. Wondrous flowers of every kind also fill the land. There are seven-treasure banners set out in rows on every side. Upon those jeweled banners hang pennants and canopies and many jeweled bells, complete in hundreds of thousands of wondrous and varied colors. Ānanda, the land of that Tathagata has many jewel trees: some are of pure gold, silver, crystal, or beryl, of coral, agate, or jade; some are made of one jewel only, not mixed with others, while others are adorned with two jewels, or even up to seven. Ānanda, where gold makes the tree, gold is the root and stem, and silver the leaves, flowers, and fruit. Where silver makes the tree, silver is the root and stem, and gold the leaves, flowers, and fruit. Where agate makes the tree, agate is the root and stem, and fine jade the leaves, flowers, and fruit. Where fine jade makes the tree, jade is the root and stem, and the seven treasures the leaves, flowers, and fruit. There are also gold trees with gold for the root, silver for the stem, crystal for the branches, beryl for the twigs, coral for the leaves, agate for the flowers, and fine jade for the fruit. There are also silver trees with silver for the root, gold for the stem, and the remaining branches and fruits adorned as in the gold trees. Where crystal makes the tree, crystal is the root, gold the stem, silver the branches, beryl the twigs, coral the leaves, agate the flowers, and fine jade the fruit. Beryl, pearl, agate, and the other trees are adorned with jewels in turn, all like crystal. There are also jade trees with jade for the root, gold for the stem, silver for the branches, crystal for the twigs, beryl for the leaves, coral for the flowers, and agate for the fruit. And there are immeasurable maṇi-jewel trees and other jewel-adorned trees throughout that land. Those jewel trees blaze with a radiance nothing in the world can match, and seven-treasure nets are spread over them. Those nets are soft as karpasa cotton.

Again, Ānanda, the Buddha Immeasurable Life has a tree of bodhi, sixteen koṭis of yojanas tall, with branches and leaves hanging down for eight koṭis of yojanas. The trunk rises five thousand yojanas, and its girth is the same. Its branches, leaves, flowers, and fruit ever bear immeasurable hundreds of thousands of wondrous colors of every kind, and precious jewels, peerlessly adorning it. That is to say: the moonlight maṇi jewel, the Śakra-abhilagna jewel, the mind-king maṇi jewel, and the sea-borne flowing maṇi jewel, whose radiance illumines everywhere, surpassing gods and humans. Upon that tree are golden locks, from which hang jeweled rosaries adorning it on every side. That is to say: rucaka jewels, musāragalva jewels, and pearls red, white, and blue, all made into rosaries. There are lion-cloud-gathering jewels and the like made into its locks, adorning its jeweled pillars. And pure gold, pearls, and various jewels and bells are made into nets. Jeweled locks adorn it, covering it over. Beryl, the ten-thousand sign, and the half-moon jewel reflect and adorn one another.

When a gentle breeze stirs them, they give forth sounds of every kind, causing all the beings of a thousand worlds, each according to the differences in what they delight in, to realize the patient acceptance of non-arising in the profound Dharma. Ānanda, when the beings of those thousand worlds hear these sounds, they abide in non-retrogression from supreme bodhi. And immeasurable, countless beings obtain the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas.

Again, Ānanda, if there are beings who see the bodhi tree, hear its sound, smell its fragrance, taste the flavor of its fruit, touch its light and shadow, or recollect the tree’s virtues, by these causes and conditions, until they reach nirvāṇa, their five faculties are free of affliction and their minds are without distraction. All of them attain non-retrogression from supreme, perfect enlightenment.

And by seeing that bodhi tree they obtain three kinds of patient acceptance. Which three? The first is the patient acceptance that follows sound; the second is the patient acceptance of conformity; the third is the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas. All this is by the majestic spirit of the original vows of the Buddha Immeasurable Life, and by his grace in the seeing; by his cultivation of meditation in past lives; because he is beyond compare; because he is without deficiency; because he cultivated well; because he received well; because he accomplished well.

blocks.text: The Assembly of Immeasurable Life Tathagata, Scroll Five, Part Two

inline.s: Again, Ānanda, that realm of Ultimate Bliss has no black mountains, no ring of iron mountains, no great ring of iron mountains, no Mount Sumeru, and the like.”
Ānanda said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, since the heavens of the Four Great Kings and the heaven of the Thirty-Three do not exist there, on what do the mountains rest?”

The Buddha told Ānanda: “What do you think? Above Mount Sumeru there are the Yama heavens, and on up to the heaven of Freely Enjoying Others’ Transformations, and the heavens of the form realm as well — on what do they rest?”
Ānanda said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, they rest on the power of inconceivable karma.”
The Buddha said to Ānanda: “Can you know inconceivable karma?”
He answered: “No.”
The Buddha told Ānanda: “Can you know the roots of goodness and the power of karma of the Buddhas and of beings?”
He answered: “No, World-Honored One. In this Dharma I am truly without confusion; it is to break the net of future doubt that I have asked this question.”

The Buddha told Ānanda: “That realm of Ultimate Bliss has no seas, but it has rivers. The narrowest of those rivers is fully ten yojanas wide. The shallowest of those waters is twelve yojanas deep. Such is the measure of the depth and breadth of those rivers — some twenty or thirty yojanas, even up to a hundred. Some are exceedingly deep and broad, reaching a thousand yojanas. Their waters are cool and pure, possessing the eight qualities. The deep currents ever rush, giving forth subtle and wondrous sounds, like the hundreds of thousands of celestial musics of the gods. In the Land of Bliss those sounds are heard everywhere. Wondrous flowers of every kind drift down along the current. A gentle breeze stirs softly, giving forth fragrances of every kind. Along both banks are many sandalwood trees, with long branches and dense leaves crossing and covering the rivers. They bear fruit and open flowers, whose fragrance and radiance are a delight to behold. The multitudes of beings roam and sport there, coming and going as they wish. Some wade into the rivers, bathe in the currents, and play. They are moved by waters of the heavens that accord well with what beings desire: depth and shallowness, cold and warmth, all bend to each person’s liking. Ānanda, beneath the great rivers the ground is spread with golden sand, and there are celestial fragrances no one in the world can describe, scattered on the wind and giving forth their perfumes. Mingled with the flowing water is the scent of celestial mandārava flowers, utpala flowers, padma flowers, kumuda flowers, and puṇḍarīka flowers, covering the surface over them.

Again, Ānanda, the people of that land sometimes go wandering and gather together on the riverbanks. Some do not wish to hear the sound of the rushing currents: though they have obtained the celestial ear, they never hear it at all. Some wish to hear it, and at once they understand hundreds of thousands of kinds of delightful sounds. That is to say: the sound of Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha; the sound of stillness; the sound of non-nature; the sound of the perfections; the sound of the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses; the sound of spiritual powers; the sound of non-action; the sound of non-arising and non-ceasing; the sound of quiet; the sound of border quiet; the sound of utmost quiet; the sound of great compassion and great pity; the sound of the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas; the sound of consecration and receiving the position — having heard such sounds of every kind.

they obtain vast delight and joy, and they accord with observation, with disenchantment, with destruction, with quiet, with border quiet, with utmost quiet, with the flavor of meaning, with Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, with the powers and fearlessnesses, with spiritual powers, with stillness, with bodhi, with the hearers, and with nirvāṇa.

Again, Ānanda, in the Land of Ultimate Bliss one does not hear the names of evil destinies, nor the names of obstruction, affliction, or covering. There are no names of hells, of Yama, or of animals. There are no names of the eight difficulties, nor names of the feeling of suffering or of neither-suffering-nor-pleasure. Since even the names do not exist, how much less the actual suffering. Therefore that land is named Ultimate Bliss. Ānanda, I have now spoken of the causes and conditions of Ultimate Bliss in brief. Were I to speak of them at length, a kalpa would not suffice. Again, Ānanda, all the beings in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, whether already born, now being born, or yet to be born, all obtain such wondrous bodies, with upright form and feature and sovereign spiritual powers. Complete in the power and merit of blessing, they enjoy palaces and gardens of every kind, clothing and food, incense and flowers and rosaries. Whatever they need comes as they wish, all just as they think — like the gods of the heaven of Freely Enjoying Others’ Transformations.

Again, Ānanda, in that Buddha-land there is subtle food. The beings there never taste or eat it. Like the gods of the sixth heaven, as they think so it comes; such food and drink is the same as having eaten it. Their complexion and strength increase, and there is no excrement. There are also immeasurable wish-fulfilling and wondrous fragrances — perfumes and powdered incense — whose scent perfumes everywhere in that Buddha-land. And scattered flowers, banners, and pennants also fill it everywhere. Those who wish to smell the fragrance smell it as they wish; those who do not wish to, never receive it at all. There are also immeasurable exquisite garments, jeweled crowns, armlets and bracelets, earrings, rosaries, flower garlands, and belts and chains, adorned with every jewel, of immeasurable radiance and hundreds of thousands of wondrous colors, all complete and naturally upon the body. There are also nets of gold and silver, of pearls and wondrous jewels, hung with many jeweled bells, adorning it on every side. Whatever palaces, towers, or pavilions the beings need, at their pleasure and desire, high or low, long or short, broad or narrow, square or round, and with all the beds and seats spread with fine clothing and adorned with every kind of jewel, appear naturally before the beings. And each person says to himself that he dwells in his own palace.

Again, Ānanda, all the beings in the land of Ultimate Bliss are without marks of difference; yet in accord with the customs of other regions they are named gods and humans. Ānanda, it is like a lowly caṇḍāla before a wheel-turning king: there is no comparing them at all; majesty and virtue, and the regard of others, are wholly absent. And again, as Indra before the sixth heaven, neither majesty nor the like can reach it — gardens and palaces, clothing and varied adornments, nobility and mastery, rank and spiritual powers, and transformations beyond compare. Only in the bliss of Dharma are they without difference. Ānanda, you should know that the beings of that land are like the king of the heaven of Freely Enjoying Others’ Transformations.

Ānanda, in that realm of Ultimate Bliss, in the morning a gentle breeze stirs on every side, neither contrary nor disordered. It blows upon all the varied flowers, and the fragrance of every kind perfumes everywhere throughout the realm. When all beings are touched in body by that wind, they are peaceful, harmonious, and well attuned, like a monk who has attained the extinction-concentration. That wind moves the groves of seven-jewel trees, and the flowers drift and gather in heaps seven men’s height. The light of every color illumines the Buddha-land. It is like a man who spreads flowers on the ground and presses them even with his hand, distributing them in mixed colors in between. Those heaps of flowers are likewise so. Those flowers are subtle and wondrous, vast and soft, like karpasa cotton. When beings step on those flowers, their feet sink four fingers deep. When they lift their feet, the flowers return as before. When the morning has passed, those flowers sink of themselves into the ground. The old flowers gone, the great earth is pure and clean. New flowers rain down again and fill it once more. Thus at midday, in the afternoon, and in the first, middle, and last watches of the night, flowers drift and gather in heaps, and it is likewise so.

Ānanda, there is no vast, wondrous, and rare treasure that is not born in the realm of Ultimate Bliss. Ānanda, in that Buddha-land there are seven-jewel lotuses. Each lotus has immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of petals. Its petals have immeasurable hundreds of thousands of rare and wondrous colors of every kind, adorned with hundreds of thousands of maṇi jewels. They are covered with jeweled nets that reflect and adorn one another. Ānanda, the size of those lotuses is half a yojana, or one, two, three, or four, or even hundreds of thousands of yojanas. From each one of those flowers come thirty-six koṭis of nayutas of hundreds of thousands of rays of light. From each ray of light come thirty-six koṭis of nayutas of hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, their bodies like gold, complete in the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty subsidiary marks, peerlessly adorned, sending forth hundreds of thousands of rays of light that illumine the worlds everywhere. Those Buddhas all appear going to the east to teach the Dharma to the multitudes, all establishing immeasurable beings in the Buddhadharma. To the south, the west, and the north, to the four intermediate directions, above and below, it is likewise so.

Again, Ānanda, the Land of Ultimate Bliss has no darkness, and no firelight. Gushing springs and lakes and ponds have no place there. Nor are there names of dwelling and attachment, of households, or of groves and gardens, nor signs to mark them out, nor any kind of young child. Nor are there signs of sun and moon, of day and night. Since in every place there is no marking out, there are no names or titles either — save where the Tathagata adds his majesty.

Ānanda, all the beings of that land who are yet to be born will all reach the utmost, the place of nirvāṇa of supreme bodhi. Why is this? Because those of fixed wrong destiny and those of undetermined destiny cannot understand and establish that cause.

Ānanda, in the east there are worlds like the sands of the Ganges, and in each world Buddhas like the sands of the Ganges. Those Buddhas each and all proclaim and praise the immeasurable merit and virtue of Amitābha. To the south, the west, and the north, to the four intermediate directions, above and below, the praises of the Buddhas are likewise so. Why is this? Because beings in the Buddha-lands of other regions, hearing the name of the Tathagata Immeasurable Life, and even able to arouse a single thought of pure faith, rejoicing, loving, and delighting, all who turn their roots of goodness toward rebirth in the land of Immeasurable Life are born there according to their vows and attain non-retrogression, even to supreme, perfect enlightenment — save for those who commit the five uninterrupted evils, who slander and destroy the true Dharma, and who revile the sages.

Ānanda, if there are beings who, in other Buddha-lands, arouse the bodhi-mind, single-mindedly recollect the Buddha Immeasurable Life, and constantly plant many roots of goodness, and arouse the mind and turn it toward rebirth in that land, then when that person is at the end of life, the Buddha Immeasurable Life, with the assembly of monks before and behind him, appears before that person. And following that Tathagata, he is born in that land, attains non-retrogression, and shall realize supreme, perfect enlightenment.

Therefore, Ānanda, if good men and good women wish to be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss and wish to see the Buddha Immeasurable Life, they should arouse the supreme bodhi-mind. They should further single-mindedly recollect the land of Ultimate Bliss, accumulate roots of goodness, and hold and turn them toward rebirth. By this they see the Buddha, are born in that land, attain non-retrogression, and reach even supreme bodhi.

Ānanda, if beings of other lands arouse the bodhi-mind but do not single-mindedly recollect the Buddha Immeasurable Life, nor constantly plant many roots of goodness, but according to their own practice turn the merit of all wholesome deeds toward that Buddha, wishing to be born there, then when this person is at the end of life the Buddha Immeasurable Life sends a transformation body which, with the assembly of monks before and behind it, appears before that person. The light and marks of that transformed Buddha are no different from the true one, and receiving and guiding him, he follows that transformed Buddha and is born in that land, attaining non-retrogression and supreme bodhi.

Ānanda, if there are beings who abide in the Great Vehicle and, with a pure mind, turn toward the Tathagata Immeasurable Life even for ten thoughts, recollecting the Buddha Immeasurable Life and wishing to be born in his land, and who hear the profound Dharma and at once give rise to faith and understanding, with no doubt in their minds, and even attain a single thought of pure mind, arousing a single thought to recollect the Buddha Immeasurable Life, then when that person is at the end of life, as if in a dream he sees the Buddha Immeasurable Life, and is certain to be born in that land and attain non-retrogression and supreme bodhi. Ānanda, because of this benefit and meaning, the Tathagatas of immeasurable, countless, inconceivable, unequaled, boundless worlds all together praise the merit and virtue of the Buddha Immeasurable Life.

The Buddha told Ānanda: in the east there are worlds like the sands of the Ganges, and in each world there are bodhisattvas like the sands of the Ganges. Wishing to behold and make offerings to the Buddha Immeasurable Life and the assemblies of sages, they come to where the Buddha is. To the south, the west, and the north, to the four intermediate directions, above and below, it is likewise so. At that time the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
The Buddha-lands of the east, in number like the sands of the Ganges.
In Buddha-lands such as these, bodhisattvas as many as those sands.
All come manifesting spiritual powers, to bow to the Buddha Immeasurable Life.
The holy host of the three quarters, in reverence, return as one.
In the realm of sands their light of discourse shines.
They dwell in deep samādhi's joy, with the mind of the four fearlessnesses.
Each brings wondrous flowers of every kind, and famous incenses all delightful.
Together they play celestial music, a hundred thousand harmonious and elegant notes.
To offer to the Teacher of Devas and Humans, whose fame is heard throughout the ten directions.
Perfect in the power of awe-inspiring spirit, well learned in every Dharma gate.
Among all manner of offerings, they cultivate diligently without weariness or slackness.
The radiance of merit and wisdom can shatter every darkness.
All with reverent minds present every precious and wondrous offering.
They behold that peerless land, and the host of bodhisattvas without bound.
May we swiftly attain bodhi, and a pure realm like that of Peace and Bliss.
The World-Honored One knows their joy of desire, vast and inconceivable.
He smiles and reveals his golden countenance: it shall be accomplished as you have wished.
Knowing all dharmas to be illusory, and Buddha-lands as a dream or an echo.
Ever vowing to adorn, they shall accomplish a subtle and wondrous land.
By the power of their vows, bodhisattvas cultivate the supreme course of bodhi.
Knowing the land to be like an image or shadow, they bring forth the mind of vast vows.
If one seeks the all-pure, peerless, boundless Buddha-land,
let him hear the holy name of the Buddha, and vow to be born in the Land of Peace and Bliss.
If there be bodhisattvas whose aspiration seeks a pure land,
let them know the selflessness of dharmas, and vow to be born in the Land of Peace and Bliss.

Again, Ānanda, all the bodhisattvas in the Land of Ultimate Bliss are settled in utmost bodhi, and are one life from Buddhahood. The only exceptions are those great beings of the resolve who can roar the lion's roar and don the great armor, who for the deliverance of the host of beings cultivate the great nirvāṇa.

Again, Ānanda, the hearers in that Buddha-land all have light of body that can illumine one fathom. The light of the bodhisattvas shines as far as a hundred thousand fathoms, save for the radiance of two bodhisattvas, which forever illumines a billion worlds.”
Ānanda said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, what are the names of those two bodhisattvas?”

The Buddha told Ānanda: “Listen well now. Those two bodhisattvas: the first is named Avalokiteśvara, the second is named Mahāsthāmaprāpta. Ānanda, these two bodhisattvas, having relinquished the measure of their lives in the Sahā world, are born in that land. Ānanda, the bodhisattvas born in that Land of Ultimate Bliss all possess the thirty-two marks; their skin and flesh are soft, their faculties keen and sharp, their wisdom and skillful means such that there is no differentiated dharma they do not fully know. In meditative concentration and spiritual penetration they sport with ease; none of them are of thin merit or dull faculties. Among those bodhisattvas, those who attain the first patience, or the second, are immeasurable and boundless, and some have realized the patience of the non-arising of dharmas. Ānanda, the bodhisattvas of that land, until they attain bodhi, never fall into the evil destinies. In whatever life they are born, they can know their past lives. The only exception is those who appear in the world within lands of the five turbidities. Ānanda, the bodhisattvas of that land, every morning, make offerings to the immeasurable hundreds of thousands of Buddhas in other directions. Whatever they may wish for — all kinds of flower garlands, perfumed ointments, powdered incense, banners and streamers, silk canopies, and all manner of music — by the Buddha's spiritual power all appears in their hands, and they make offering to those Buddhas. Such offerings are vast and abundant, countless and boundless, inconceivable. Or again, if they delight to seek all kinds of famous flowers, flowers of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of lights and colors, all appear in their hands, and they scatter them in offering to the Buddhas. Ānanda, the flowers they scatter at once become flower canopies in the sky. The smallest of those canopies fills ten yojanas. If they do not again scatter fresh flowers upon them, the flowers already scattered never fall. Ānanda, some flower canopies fill twenty yojanas, and likewise thirty or forty, even a thousand yojanas; or they equal four continents, or cover a small chiliocosm, a middle chiliocosm, even a billion worlds. These bodhisattvas give rise to a rare thought and attain great joy. In the morning hour they serve, make offering to, revere, and praise immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of Buddhas, and having planted all roots of goodness, in that same morning hour they return to their own land. All this comes from the original vows and added majesty of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, and from the fact that they once made offering to the Tathāgatas, and their roots of goodness continue without deficiency, because they have cultivated them well, gathered them well, and perfected them well.

Again, Ānanda, the words spoken by the host of bodhisattvas in that Land of Ultimate Bliss accord with omniscience. In all that they make use of, they grasp at nothing. Wandering throughout Buddha-lands, they have neither love nor weariness, and no craving. They have no thought of craving, no thought of self, no thought of affliction, no thought of I, no thought of quarreling, opposition, resentment, or anger. Why is this? Because those bodhisattvas have, toward all beings, a mind of great compassion and benefit, a mind soft and without obstruction, a mind undefiled, a mind without resentment or hate, a mind equal, tamed, and still, a mind of patience, a mind of patience and taming, a mind of even and clear concentration without distraction, a mind without covering, a pure mind, a most pure mind, a shining mind, a dustless mind, a mind of great majesty and virtue, a good mind, a vast mind, an unequaled mind, a most profound mind, a mind that loves the Dharma, a mind that delights in the Dharma, a mind of good intent, a mind that renounces all clinging, a mind that cuts off the afflictions of all beings, a mind that closes every evil destiny.

They walk in the course of wisdom, and have already perfected immeasurable merit. In the factors of concentration and enlightenment they can expound well. Ever sporting in utmost bodhi, they diligently cultivate and proclaim it. The fleshly eye is opened and can discern and choose. The divine eye appears and beholds all Buddha-lands. The Dharma eye is pure and can be free of all attachment. The wisdom eye penetrates and reaches the farther shore. The Buddha eye is perfected, awakening and revealing. They give rise to unobstructed wisdom and broadly expound it for others. Within the three realms they cultivate equally and diligently. Having tamed themselves, they can also tame all sentient beings. They can cause others to attain supreme śamatha. In all dharmas they realize that nothing is attained. They can expound the Dharma well, with words ingenious and skillful. They diligently make offering to all Buddhas. They crush and subdue all the afflictions of sentient beings. They are pleasing to the Tathāgatas, and can be thus. Thinking thus, when they think thus, they can gather and see that all dharmas are unattained. By skillful wisdom they cultivate the dharma of cessation. They well know what to take and what to relinquish, and the sense of what accords with principle and what does not. In both the sense that accords with principle and the sense that does not, they are wholly skillful. In worldly speech their minds take no delight. In the scriptures that transcend the world they are faithful and diligent. They skillfully seek out all dharmas. Seeking all dharmas, they increase their understanding. They know that dharmas are originally without substance and cannot be grasped, and in the place they walk there is neither taking nor relinquishing. Released from old age and sickness, they abide in all virtues. From the very beginning they have dwelt in spiritual penetration, and diligently cultivate the profound Dharma. In the most profound Dharma they do not turn back. In the hard-to-understand Dharma they wholly penetrate. They attain the one-vehicle path and have no doubt. In the Buddha's teaching they do not awaken by means of another. Their wisdom is vast and deep, likened to the great sea. Their bodhi is lofty and broad, compared to Mount Sumeru. Their own majestic light surpasses sun and moon. Whatever they ponder and choose accords with wisdom. Like a snowy mountain, their minds are white and pure. Their light shines everywhere, with boundless merit, burning up the firewood of affliction. Compared to fire, they are not shaken by good or evil. Their minds are still and ever at peace, like the great earth. They wash away confusion as with pure water. Their minds have no master, like fire; they cling to nothing in the world, like wind. They nourish all beings like the earth, and view all worlds as empty space. They bear living beings like a fine carriage. Unstained by worldly dharmas, they are like the lotus. They spread far the sound of Dharma like a peal of thunder. They rain down all dharmas like a great rain. Their light covers the sages and worthies like that of the great seer. They can tame and subdue like the great elephant. Valiant and fearless like the lion king. They shelter beings like the banyan tree. Unmoved by other doctrines, like the Iron Ring Mountain. Cultivating boundless loving-kindness, like the Ganges. As kings of all good dharmas they can lead the way, like Great Brahmā. Accumulating nothing, like a flying bird. Crushing other doctrines, like the golden-winged king. Hard to meet and rare, like the udumbara flower. Supreme among men, their minds are upright. Without indolence, they can cultivate well. Among all views they skillfully decide. Gentle and patient, without jealousy. Discoursing on Dharma without satiety, seeking Dharma without weariness. Ever diligently expounding, benefiting beings. Their precepts are like crystal, clear within and without. Hearing all dharmas well, they become a supreme treasure. The words they speak make the assembly rejoice and submit. By the power of wisdom they raise the great Dharma banner, blow the great Dharma conch, beat the great Dharma drum. Ever delighting in diligent cultivation, they set up the markers of Dharma. By the light of wisdom their minds are without confusion. Far from all faults, they do no harm either. With pure minds they are apart from all defilement. Ever practicing generous giving, they forever renounce stinginess and greed. By nature gentle, they ever hold shame and modesty. Their minds are still and settled, their wisdom bright and discerning. They become lamps for the world, shattering the darkness of beings. Worthy of offerings, a peerless field of merit. As great guides they bring relief to all creatures. Far from like and dislike, their minds are pure and without care. Advancing bravely without fear, they are great generals of Dharma. Knowing the hells, they tame self and other. Benefiting sentient beings, they draw out the poisoned arrows. As knowers of the world, as teachers of the world, they guide the host of beings to renounce all clinging to love. Forever free of the three defilements, they sport in spiritual penetration.
